meta.note: matched_by.cas is authoritative. 'name' is an exact normalised title match; 'tokens' is a token-subset heuristic and may hide a genuinely distinct material with a similar name - review that bucket before trusting 'missing'. CAS coverage in the snapshot is ~75% (harvested from /products/{handle}.js metafields); products with no CAS fall back to name matching, so a handful of duplicates may remain.

missing.title: Acalea
missing.description: Acalea (mimosa heptanal) is a soft, powdery mimosa in bloom. Its heliotrope-and-mimosa floralcy stays fresh and dewy rather than sweet and heavy, brightened by a green lift and a light berry-fruity nuance. Creamy and rounded, it is gentle and natural, like newly opened petals. Use it in the mid-notes to build mimosa and heliotrope accords, or to add a soft, powdery roundness to white florals and fruity-floral bouquets. It rounds jasmine, smooths mixed-flower hearts, and lends a dewy, natural freshness that keeps a floral from turning cloying. Its green side also freshens sweeter compositions.

missing.title: Acetal CD
missing.description: Also known as Hyacinth Acetals or Phenylacetaldehyde Glyceryl Acetal , Acetal CD is a light floralising material that finds use in floral compounds needing a soft but very long lasting heart. With delicate nuances of dried rose, honey, black tea and, of course, hyacinth, this is a great material to overdose in an age of heavily restricted florals.

missing.title: Acetyl Propionyl
missing.description: Acetyl propionyl hits you with unmistakable buttery richness—this is the real thing, not a polite suggestion of cream. The caramel-toffee facet follows immediately, warm and inviting. Underneath sits a toasted, almost roasted almond quality that adds unexpected complexity to the dairy character. This material occurs naturally across an impressive range of foods: butter, bread, milk, yogurt, coffee, cocoa, roasted nuts, beer, wine, and whisky. In perfumery, it belongs to the essential custard note family alongside acetoin and butyric acid. When you need that authentic dairy-caramel warmth in gourmand compositions, nothing else quite matches its impact. Use acetyl propionyl sparingly—the odour strength is high, so dilute to one percent or less before evaluating. It transforms vanilla accords from sweet to genuinely custardy. The 12-hour substantivity provides solid mid-note performance. Blend with lactones and vanillin for irresistible dessert effects.

missing.title: Adoxal
missing.description: Adoxal opens with unmistakable marine freshness—ozonic, aldehydic, and immediately evocative of sea breezes and crisp clean linens. The waxy floral undertone emerges quickly, bringing lily-of-the-valley brightness without sweetness. A subtle ambergris-like warmth anchors the composition, making this far more sophisticated than simple aquatic materials. This Givaudan aldehyde has become essential for aquatic and fresh fragrance categories. Its profile sits close to Calone territory—watermelon-marine-ozonic—but with added aldehydic complexity and better performance in functional products. The 168-hour substantivity on blotter translates to exceptional longevity in finished compositions. Use it in detergent and fabric care fragrances where that fresh linen character defines the category. Deploy this material strategically at different concentrations for varied effects. Use traces (0.01-0.1%) as a floralizer that adds air and radiance to rose or jasmine. Push it to 1-5% for avant-garde metallic effects that evoke ink or cold metal. Partner it with Ambroxan for modern marine dry-downs or with Dihydromyrcenol to create that distinctive "blue" freshness.

missing.title: Alcohol C-10
missing.description: Alcohol C-10 greets the nose with a sweet, waxy warmth wrapped around a distinctly floral core - something between fresh orange peel and soft rose. A clean, fatty-oily smoothness gives it body without heaviness. On a strip, the floral-orange character holds for over four days. This material sits right between the lighter Alcohol C-8 and the heavier Alcohol C-12 Lauric in the fatty alcohol series. Its floral-orange quality makes it essential for rose accords and neroli reconstructions. It rounds aldehydic florals with the waxy bloom that makes classic perfumes feel opulent. Pair it with Aldehyde C-10 (Decanal) for a complete orange-waxy spectrum from sparkling top to warm base. In citrus colognes, a trace adds floral body beneath the volatile head. It occurs naturally in orange oil, coriander, and rose - a familiar companion to materials you already use.

missing.title: Alcohol C-12 Lauric
tags: locale:heat to melt and use bottles not pots
missing.description: Alcohol C-12 Lauric is a waxy solid at room temperature with a soft, clean, soapy aroma and an unmistakable fatty quality. Warm honey and coconut nuances sit underneath, giving it more character than you might expect. On the strip it's quiet but remarkably persistent, lasting over 80 hours. Use Alcohol C-12 Lauric to build convincing mimosa and cassie accords — its waxy-honey character is essential to both. It anchors aldehydic florals with warm soapy depth while acting as a fixative. In tuberose compositions, the coconut facet reinforces that naturally creamy undertone. Pair it with its aldehyde counterpart, Aldehyde C-12 Lauric, for a complete waxy spectrum from sparkling top to warm base. Orange blossom absolute and ylang ylang are natural partners. Everything you build around Alcohol C-12 lasts longer — it's a quiet fixative that should be in every perfumer's arsenal.

missing.title: Aldambre
missing.description: Aldambre opens with dry woody-amber character that feels remarkably clean—no dustiness, no heaviness. The distinctive hot iron facet emerges quickly, adding an intriguing metallic edge that sets this material apart from conventional ambers. Soft musky undertones provide a skin-like finish, while the overall effect remains warm without becoming cloying or animalic. You'll find Aldambre invaluable for abstracting woody bases and creating contemporary mineral effects. Add it at 0.5-2% to strip earthiness from vetiver and patchouli, leaving elegant driftwood bones. Combine with salicylates for authentic hot stone accords or pair with Ambroxan to amplify mineral facets. At higher doses, it becomes a statement material for conceptual fragrances. This heart-note musk bridges top and base beautifully, radiating outward during the crucial 1-4 hour window. Use it to modernise aldehydic florals or create that coveted "anti-perfume" aesthetic. For something truly electrifying, combine Aldambre with Metal Oxazole and Habanolide —together they create a hot metal accord that crackles with industrial heat, like a forge at midnight.

missing.title: Aldehyde C-11 Intreleven
missing.description: Aldehyde C-11 Intreleven opens with powerful clean aldehydic character—green, rosy, and immediately evocative of fresh linen and quality soap. The ozonic-marine facets add modern brightness, while citrus-orange undertones provide lift without heaviness. This is aldehydic perfumery at its most refined: sparkling, diffusive, and remarkably versatile across fine fragrance and functional applications. This material delivers a fresher, more complex profile than simple Aldehyde C-11 Undecylenic. The 400-hour substantivity on blotter translates to exceptional longevity in finished products, and the excellent stability in body lotions, shampoos, and all-purpose cleaners makes it valuable across categories. The fresh linen aspect has made it particularly popular in fabric care applications where clean, aldehydic character defines the category. Use it as a top note booster in white floral concepts, or to add aldehydic sparkle to citrus, marine, and green compositions. It blends beautifully with other aldehydes, rose materials, and fatty-floral notes. Excellent soap stability makes it a workhorse for functional fragrances. Aldehyde C-11 Intreleven vs Aldehyde C-11 Undecylenic These two C-11 aldehydes share the same carbon chain length but differ significantly in character. Aldehyde C-11 Undecylenic is waxy, fatty, and distinctly rosy-citrus with a soapy quality; one of the three aldehydes Beaux used in Chanel No. 5. Intreleven is several times stronger than Undecylenic, with a fresher, cleaner, more complex profile. Where Undecylenic leans fatty and waxy, Intreleven emphasises ozonic freshness and green-linen character. Use Undecylenic for classic aldehydic florals seeking that vintage Chanel sparkle; reach for Intreleven when you want modern fresh-linen power with superior diffusion. Both offer exceptional tenacity, but Intreleven's cleaner profile makes it more versatile in contemporary functional fragrances.

missing.title: Aldehyde C-11 MOA
missing.description: Aldehyde C-11 MOA — Methyl Octyl Acetaldehyde — hits you with explosive citrus-peel zestiness, radiant and immediately diffusive. Underneath is a waxy tangerine warmth that gives it body beyond a simple top note. The drydown settles into something clean and watery, almost marine. This is your go-to fresh aldehyde for contemporary citrus and marine accords, where its zesty radiance adds instant sparkle. Orange compositions gain authentic peel character from even small additions. Blend with dihydromyrcenol and calone for aquatic work, or with other C-series aldehydes for classic aldehydic lift. Use Aldehyde C-11 MOA sparingly — its diffusive power is remarkable. Pair with bergamot and vetiver for a modern masculine citrus, or with hedione and linalool for luminous white florals. It also brings that sparkling just-washed character to laundry and fabric care accords. MOA vs Undecylenic vs Intreleven Both carry the C-11 label — eleven carbon atoms — but they smell and behave quite differently. MOA is zesty, citrus-peel bright, and watery-marine. It's entirely synthetic and leans modern and fresh. Undecylenic is waxier, fattier, and more traditionally aldehydic: rosy-citrus with a soapy-green character. It occurs naturally in coriander leaf and is one of the three aldehydes Ernest Beaux selected for Chanel No. 5. The practical divide: MOA excels in contemporary citrus, marine, and fabric care compositions. Undecylenic is the classic aldehydic floral ingredient, delivering rich waxy warmth to bouquets and chypres. Undecylenic also lasts significantly longer on blotter. Use MOA when you want bright, sparkling citrus radiance; use Undecylenic for lush vintage aldehydic character. Intreleven is several times stronger than Undecylenic, with a fresher, cleaner, more complex profile. Where Undecylenic leans fatty and waxy, Intreleven emphasises ozonic freshness and green-linen character.

missing.title: Aldron®
missing.description: Aldron is a strange material. Some people can't smell it at all and some people (especially women) are repulsed by it when smelled pure. Why? No one really knows. But in the right amounts in a blend, it has a power to naturalise and add musky elegance that is appreciated by all and really impossible to obtain with any other materials. It's particularly valuable in enhancing sandalwood and musk accords, as well as in woody, tobacco, musk, and incense blends. It's definitely a quirky one but well worth the buy. For those who can smell it, the odour profile is animalic, woody, amber and musk (in the direction of sweaty human skin).

missing.title: Allyl Ionone
missing.description: Allyl Ionone is a unique and versatile ionone derivative with a floral-woody character and a fruity nuance. Its profile combines the powdery, violet-like facets typical of ionones with a subtly fresh and juicy note, making it indispensable for adding complexity to modern floral, fruity, and woody compositions. This material provides a dynamic lift and smooth diffusion, especially in the heart and base notes of a fragrance. Allyl Ionone pairs beautifully with woody and powdery materials such as Iso E Super , cedarwood, and musk , creating a soft and diffusive effect. It also complements floral components like jasmine and rose, amplifying their luxurious qualities. For fruity blends, combining Allyl Ionone with notes like peach, raspberry, or apricot creates a playful yet refined result.

missing.title: Almond Pyrazine
missing.description: Almond Pyrazine opens with explosive roasted intensity—imagine almonds crackling in a hot pan. This isn't the sweet marzipan of benzaldehyde but pure Maillard magic. Hazelnut and peanut facets emerge alongside smoky undertones, creating the authentic aroma of nuts transformed by heat. This pyrazine requires extreme respect—we sell it as low as 0.1% in DPG but up to pure for those who need it. At parts-per-million levels, it transforms compositions with authentic roasted character. Deploy it in coffee reconstructions where its smoky-nutty profile completes the espresso illusion, or use it to add depth to chocolate accords beyond simple sweetness. Master this material by starting at 0.0001% of your finished fragrance and building carefully. It excels when paired with coffee Arabica CO2 for ultra-realistic café effects, or combine with vanillin and ethyl maltol for sophisticated praline gourmands. The pyrazine's potency means a single drop can dominate—approach with caution and precision.

missing.title: Amber Core
missing.description: Amber Core is a member of the amber family but unlike the most common ones ( Ambrocenide , AmberXTreme, Hydroxyambran and Operanide ) it is far softer and easier to work with. Try it as an alternative to the more common wood chemicals like Cedramber which it is similar to in terms of strength. Previously able to be overdosed massively, it is now under a 1.3% restriction in IFRA 51 which is still rather generous. Amber Core blends beautifully with Operanide, Ambrocenide , florals (particularly light ones like Muguet and Lilac), and wood chemicals like Orbitone® T and Iso E Super . It is an excellent blender and is especially good at linking woods, amber and citrus materials. Amber Core features in Amouage Interlude Black Iris (0.8%), Amouage Memoir Women (0.9%), Creed Royal Oud (0.08%), YSL La Nuit de L'Homme Bleu Électrique (11%), and Gucci Pour Homme (10%).

missing.title: Ambermax® 50
missing.description: Givaudan positions Ambermax as "the most powerful and efficient dry ambery note ever". It opens with an arresting dry woodiness that shoots straight through any composition like a cedar arrow. The material presents that coveted pencil-shaving character but stripped of natural cedar's rough edges. This transparent amber effect creates remarkable vertical lift in your formulas. It also excels with citrus materials, adding depth without dulling brightness. The extreme potency means a little goes very far; overdosing creates the "spiky wood" effect common to super ambers. Blend with Karanal, Okoumal, Z11, and woody-amber materials for sophisticated bases. Layer it with Ambrox to balance its trigeminal sharpness with creamy warmth. Remember this material causes rapid nose fatigue, so take breaks when evaluating your trials.

missing.title: AmberXtreme
missing.description: AmberXtreme opens with an explosive woody-amber blast that fills space instantly. Its musky-animalic character creates warmth whilst grape-anthranilate facets add subtle fruitiness. This molecule radiates with unprecedented power, perceivable below 0.1% concentration. You'll find this material essential for modern masculine fragrances where projection and longevity define success. It excels as a volume booster in woody and fougère bases, transforming linear compositions into radiant statements. Use it sparingly—even 0.01% creates noticeable aura whilst higher doses risk overwhelming entire accords. Blend AmberXtreme with Iso E Super and Cashmeran for the legendary Cashmeran Velvet effect. Combine with Ambrettolide for enhanced musk complexity or pair with Ambroxan for marine-amber depth. This powerhouse performs brilliantly in detergents where its stability ensures lasting freshness. Comparison with Operanide and Ambrocenide AmberXtreme sits between Operanide's creamy softness and Ambrocenide's sharp aggression in the radiant amber family. Where Operanide offers controllable mossy-cedar elegance and Ambrocenide delivers piercing agarwood dryness, AmberXtreme provides balanced woody-amber power with animalic warmth. Choose AmberXtreme for maximum diffusion, Operanide for sophisticated heart notes, or Ambrocenide for cutting-edge sharpness.

missing.title: Amboryl Acetate
missing.description: Amboryl Acetate opens with a fleeting acetate sparkle that quickly settles into its true character—a remarkably soft woody-amber that sidesteps the harsh dryness plaguing many synthetic ambers. This sesquiterpenoid acetate brings together the smooth, refined woodiness of vetiveryl acetate with sandalwood's creamy richness. You'll detect subtle hints of clary sage's aromatic sweetness woven through it also. This material excels where others fail in functional perfumery, maintaining its sophisticated character through aggressive product bases that destroy lesser ingredients. Its 280-hour tenacity on blotter translates to genuine lasting power in detergents, fabric softeners, and personal care products. Deploy it at 5-15% in functional bases where you need amber sophistication without the luxury price tag—it transforms mundane household products into olfactory experiences worth remembering. Fine fragrance perfumers overlook this gem at their peril, dismissing it as merely functional when it offers unique bridging qualities between top and heart accords. Use it at up to 50% in your base to create woody-amber foundations with unusual softness and powdery nuance. Combine with Iso E Super for enhanced diffusion or layer with natural sandalwood to amplify creamy facets without breaking the budget. Its acetate functionality provides superior adhesion to skin and fabric, ensuring your creation maintains its character from first spray to final dry-down.

missing.title: Ambrarome®
missing.description: Ambrarome (also known as Ambrarome Absolute) is one of the oldest bases still made and sold by the same company that created it (Synarome). It was created in 1926 by Hubert Fraysse (co-founder of the company with his brother George) and was key to Arpège, created his brother André Fraysse who was the chief perfumer of Lanvin. Ambrarome is an intensely animalic base with a strong character of ambergris, noble labdanum fractions and aspects of leather. In fact, it was the first speciality product designed to replicate the then-already expensive ambergris. It was followed later by specialities from competing companies such as Grisambrol and Grisambrene by Firmenich. François Coty loved Ambrarome so much that upon smelling it for the first time that he reformulated his great Chypre to include it (and at the same time removed Musk Ambrette and increased the Musk Ketone ). Due to the thickness and odour strength of this material we are offering it at 50% diluted in TEC as well as pure.

missing.title: Ambrocenide Crystals
tags: locale:use gentle heat to dissolve crystals in diluted version only
missing.description: Ambrocenide is a woody amber chemical with a radiance almost impossible to believe. It can be used in the merest traces to add elegance and power but it also works surprisingly well in overdose (as evidenced by the Amrita demonstration formula below - Millennium Mysore Sandal Soap). We sell Ambrocenide as pure crystals or in a 10% solution with DPG making it easier to handle. According to Perfumery: Techniques in Evolution (a series of articles published in Perfumer and Flavorist magazine): “Ambrocenide is the best discovery in the amber-woody family […] since Ambrox was commercialised. The top note of Ambrocenide is radiant, diffusive, elegant, ambery, woody—indeed both precious, and unique.” Blends with Absolute Ambergris , Sandexol , Miraclewood , Iso E Super , Norlimbanol Dextro , Z11 MIP, Cetonal , the ionones and, in truth, almost everything.

missing.title: Ambrox® DL
missing.description: When is Ambrox® not Ambrox? When it's Ambrox DL! Ambrox DL is a Firmenich product which blends around 30% captive Cachalox® with 70% Cetalox (9-epi Ambrox). While most Ambrox on the market ( Ambrox Super , Ambrofix , Orcanox , Ambroxan ) is Laevo-ambrox, Cetalox is the racemic version and has a more linear, clean dry wood character. It is subtler and less diffusive than Ambrox and it has less tendency to overwhelm other light materials. Laevo-Ambrox will give a richer, warmer and more intense result than Cetalox but Cetalox, on the other hand, can sometimes be perceived as more elegant. The other part of Ambrox DL is Cachalox, which is related to but has a weaker odour than Laevo-Ambrox. It does, however, have heightened fixative and diffusive properties. Ambrox DL is often a solid or pasty thick liquid at room temperature and some heat (typically hotter than tap or faucet hot) may be needed to loosen it up for pipetting. Notable as an example of oriental style perfumery, Areej Al Shouk by Ajmal uses just over 1% Ambrox® DL to boost the rich woody notes whilst giving lift to the tonkin deer fond (a blend of Muscenone ® Delta and Muscone Laevo ) and sparkle to the florals. Some other perfumes that incorporate Ambrox® DL are Not A Perfume (2010) by Juliette Has A Gun in which it is the only ingredient, Interlude Black Iris (2020) by Pierre Negrin for Amouage, Patchouli Absolu (2014) by Richard Herpin, Neroli Portofino (2011) by Rodrigo Flores-Roux and Tobacco Vanille (2007) by Olivier Gillotin all for Tom Ford; Philosykos (1996) by Olivia Giacobetti for Diptyque, and Amouage's Jubilation XXV (2007) by Bertrand Duchaufour. It should be noted that Cetalox is currently undergoing a regulatory recategorisation that may see it come under legislative fire and consequent IFRA/EU restriction.

missing.title: Amyl Benzoate
missing.description: Amyl Benzoate is a lovely soft fruity floral material with balsamic nuances that works extremely well as a general floraliser and blender. It isn't exploited much in modern fragrances but it really should be as it is quite distinctive and there is great potential to create novel accords with it. Its fruity aspects make it ideal for honeysuckle and sweet pea fantasy blends and it can be used at a very high dose in a fragrance as it is IFRA safe to 100%.

missing.title: Amyris Alcohol
missing.description: Amyris Alcohol (also known as Amyrol) is the pure heart of Amyris oil. It has a softer and sweeter quality than the essential oil (from Amyris balsamifera ) and can be used one for one wherever Amyris is used. Amyrol is particularly good for sandalwood accords or fragrances needing a high dose of natural wood materials that don't impart too strong a character of their own. It is well suited to modern fragrances that like to represent naturals in a more abstract or minimal way, just as Patchoulol and Olibanol do the same for Patchouli notes and Olibanum respectively. Amyris Alcohol blends beautifully with Sandexol® , Sandalwood Imperial , Rose products and woods .

missing.title: Andrane
missing.description: Andrane opens with a structured cedarwood character that quickly reveals an earthy, patchouli-like depth and a distinctive dry ambergris quality. There is subtle tobacco warmth in the background. The overall impression is of a precious, aged wood — complex, noble, and extremely tenacious, lasting for days on a blotter. Use andrane to add woody-amber depth and earthiness to your orientals, chypres, and masculine compositions. It modifies and extends patchouli accords beautifully, adding a cleaner, more structured framework. In cedarwood blends it contributes an ambergris-like dryness that elevates the entire accord. Pair with patchouli and vetiver for a rich, earthy woody base. Try it alongside ambroxan and sandalwood for modern amber-wood accords. Blend with Iso E Super and cashmeran for a contemporary, transparent woody heart with lasting power.

missing.title: Anisyl Acetone
missing.description: Anisyl Acetone opens with an immediate burst of intense sweetness—ripe raspberries crushed with cherries, but this isn't simple fruitiness. The material quickly reveals sophisticated floral facets reminiscent of mimosa and cassie absolute, creating a powdery-sweet effect that bridges fruit and flower. This remarkable complexity extends to subtle anise and licorice notes that link to its "Anisyl" heritage, while woody-balsamic undertones add unexpected depth to what might otherwise be a purely sweet material. Utilise Anisyl Acetone strategically in accords where you need fruity sweetness with floral sophistication. In Oriental bases, it provides essential berry-sweet facets that prevent heavy ambers from becoming cloying—use at 0.5-2% to add lift without overwhelming warmth. For sweet floral accords, it excels as a Heliotropin modifier, offering similar powdery sweetness without the discolouration issues that plague many formulations. In Fougère structures, small amounts (0.1-0.5%) sweeten harsh aromatic notes while maintaining masculine sophistication. Its true genius emerges in raspberry and cherry accords where it provides authentic fruit character with unusual persistence. Anisyl Acetone finds its most sophisticated applications in complex bases where its multifaceted nature truly shines. In vanilla accords, it contributes essential fruity complexity that prevents flat sweetness—combine with Vanillin and Ethyl Vanillin at 2-3% for three-dimensional warmth. For licorice compositions, its natural anise facet creates seamless bridges between star anise and sweet base notes. In modern Oriental bases, layer it with benzoin and labdanum where its raspberry-mimosa character adds contemporary freshness to traditional warmth. The material's exceptional stability in alkaline conditions makes it invaluable for functional perfumery, maintaining its character in challenging soap and detergent bases where many fruity materials fail. The “Anisic” Family Understanding the anise

missing.title: Anisyl Alcohol
missing.description: Anisyl Alcohol opens with an immediate powdery sweetness that distinguishes it as the softest member of the anise family. Where its relatives can be sharp or intensely fruity, this alcohol whispers rather than shouts—a gentle hawthorn blossom accord with lilac's purple sweetness woven throughout. The material brings that coveted heliotrope character perfumers seek: almond-like creaminess married to powdery florals, but without the stability headaches that plague heliotropin in alkaline bases. This alcohol excels in creating naturalness within synthetic floral bouquets, particularly in mimosa and cassie reconstructions where its powdery-balsamic profile adds authentic depth. Deploy it at 1-10% in fragrance compounds to round sharp edges and add volume to flat florals. Its moderate tenacity (30 hours on blotter) provides excellent support through the heart phase without overwhelming delicate top notes. The material's superior stability in soap, creams, and antiperspirants makes it invaluable for functional perfumery where aldehydic alternatives would discolour. Beyond its primary floral applications, Anisyl Alcohol serves as an exceptional modifier in gourmand and oriental compositions, where its vanilla-honey facets enhance edible qualities without adding excessive sweetness. Combine with benzyl salicylate and coumarin for classic powder accords, or pair with methyl eugenol to create stunning lilac soliflores. Its chemical stability and IFRA restrictions (varying from 0.21% in fine fragrance to lower levels in leave-on products) demand careful formulation, but the results justify the effort. The “Anisic” Family Understanding the anise family quartet clarifies each material's unique role: Anisic Aldehyde (p-Anisaldehyde) delivers the most intense powdery-almond character with pronounced mimosa and baby powder associations—sharp and aldehydic. Anisyl Acetate broadens the palette with complex fruity-floral notes, adding plum, raspberry, and narcotic sweetness alongside

missing.title: Antillone™
missing.description: Antillone™ is typically pineapple but with nuances of other fruit. It is a natural molecule and a speciality of V. MANE Fils. Beyond any doubt this chemical is a must-have for anyone wanting to add naturalness for a fruit blend or to create more characterful and rich natural pineapple notes. John Wright wrote an article about this molecule in Perfumer & Flavorist and said: “ The character of this chemical is somewhat similar to allyl hexanoate. It is sharp and fruity in a similar way to allyl hexanoate and instantly recognisable as pineapple. It fits equally well into pineapple flavors, adding brightness and freshness. In some ways it is preferable because it has a higher level of the dry, almost dusty, note that is reminiscent of the fresh fruit.”

missing.title: Aphermate
missing.description: You can never have too many fruity and fresh materials and the marine quality of this formate from IFF makes it an extra interesting product. Aphermate is, first and foremost, fruit (apple to be precise) followed by hints of pine tree and the seashore. It is a lovely material to add interest to the more classic freshies such as Calone and Cascalone. It also has an unusual opening note that hints at burnt plastic. Aphermate blends well with the Rose Ketones , Ethyl Safranate , Theaspirane , Amazonia, and Verdantol .

missing.title: Apo Patchone Coeur
missing.description: Upon smelling Apo Patchone Coeur it is easy to imagine hand-cobbled leather shoes, dusty Parisian lofts and antique suitcases waiting in dark corners for the outing that will never come. Apo Patchone Coeur is a refined patchouli-derived material which softens the loamy and musty top that can overshadow patchouli compositions, instead, delivering a smooth, woody-amber signature with a subtle but notable leather nuance. This makes it versatile in both masculine and unisex fragrances. Its leather-like quality often emerges as a sleek, suede-like dryness rather than the raw, animalic leather we tend to associate with birch tar or castoreum (which, it must be said, blends extremely well with this chemical). Its nuanced, tactile impression of soft leather supports other richer materials without dominating. Apo Patchone Coeur works beautifully with our Royal Leather base and needless to say it blends exceedingly well with other leather aroma chemicals such as Iso Butyl Quinoline . However, don't neglect its floral side — pairings with rose materials are fascinating and worth experimenting with for novel modern accords. Typical Usage At lower concentrations (0.5–1%), it provides a subtle, smooth enhancement to woody, leathery, or amber accords, adding depth without dominating. At higher concentrations (2–3%), it becomes more prominent, contributing a sleek suede-like leather quality and a modern patchouli twist that can define a composition

missing.title: Aprifloren®
missing.description: A lovely fruity lactone which is more powerful that similar materials such as Gamma Undecalactone. It can be used with those materials to create a velvety and complex stone fruit accord, or on its own for a different impression of peach or apricot. We highly recommend it. Aprifloren blends beautifully with Persicol , Paradise Molecule , extreme dilutions of grapefruit odourant Thiocineole , Edenolide, Ambrofix ™, Floralozone , AmberXTreme, Kephalis and all the lactones .

missing.title: Apritone
tags: locale:heat to melt and use bottles not pots
missing.description: Apritone is ripe, fleshy apricot — warm, sweet, and disarmingly realistic. But it's far more than simple fruit: peach and jasmine undertones layer underneath, with a subtle rose ketone-like facet and ambrette creaminess adding unexpected complexity. Exceptionally tenacious on the strip. Use Apritone wherever you need apricot that persists deep into the dry-down — most fruit esters vanish quickly, but this terpenoid ketone stays. It anchors peach and jasmine accords with real tenacity. Try it in woody compositions where its fruity warmth adds a supple, rounded quality you wouldn't expect. Combine Apritone with gamma-undecalactone and damascones to build full-bodied stone fruit accords. Prunolide strengthens the apricot realism. Layer it with sweet musks for a skin-scent effect where the fruit feels intimate and worn-in rather than bright and projecting — this is not a top note material.

missing.title: Aquaflora
missing.description: Aquaflora smells of fresh lily of the valley, clean and gently green. The muguet floralcy stays light and watery, almost see-through, with none of the usual heaviness. A touch of cyclamen and soft fruit rounds off the edges. Use Aquaflora to build airy muguet and cyclamen accords, or to open a floral with a fresh, just-watered lift. It adds body and a clean aquatic feel without turning soapy or sharp. Even at low levels it threads a transparent green floralcy through the top and heart.

missing.title: Armenian Wood Base
missing.description: Armenian Wood Base opens with a wave of sweet, resinous warmth — vanilla-rich benzoin interwoven with a soft cinnamic spice and a faint trail of woodsmoke. It calls to mind the experience of burning Papier d'Armenie, that traditional French incense paper soaked in Siam benzoin resin. The effect is at once cosy and quietly exotic. This is a ready-made accord built around Siam benzoin as its central axis, but it goes much further than a simple benzoin reconstitution. Soft sandalwood and powdery woody notes provide structure, while a subtle animalic funk — likely from styrax-type components and a trace of civet character — gives the base surprising depth and longevity. Reach for it whenever you need instant balsamic richness in oriental, amber, or incense accords, or use it to add smoky sweetness beneath a floral heart. Treat Armenian Wood as a shortcut to complex resinous warmth. It pairs beautifully with oud, patchouli, and frankincense for dark oriental work, and it will soften and sweeten woody-amber frameworks when used at low levels. A few percent can transform a flat vanilla into something layered and smouldering.

missing.title: Aurantiol®
missing.description: Aurantiol is the most common of the Schiff bases, a product resulting from the chemical reaction of methyl anthranilate with an aldehyde, in this case hydroxycitronellal. While there are many suppliers of Aurantiol (and you can even make it yourself by blending the two key materials in a ratio of roughly 56:44), not all Schiff bases are created equal. Poor quality versions are everywhere — the result of wrong proportions or incomplete (or worse still non-existent) dehydration of the final product. Because the process produces water as a side effect, you will often see inferior qualities which are cloudy and should be avoided. Our Aurantiol is perfectly dehydrated and has excellent clarity and a fine aroma. Aurantiol has the distinct scent of orange flowers and honey and it is in those contexts that it is most often used. Our Aurantiol is intensely yellow and very viscous (though easily pourable with a little heat). We offer it pure and in dilution due to its thickness.

missing.title: Aurelione
missing.description: Aurelione opens with a gentle, powdery warmth that settles into a soft balsamic musk with an intimate, skin-like quality. There is nothing sharp here - just a smooth, enveloping radiance with the faintest animalic whisper beneath. It recalls the warmth of clean skin on a summer evening. This is a macrocyclic ketone built on a sixteen-membered carbon ring, sold as a mixture of positional isomers including Globanone. At low doses it rounds off floral accords with invisible warmth; push it higher and you get a clean, billowing fabric-softener effect. It particularly excels at enhancing floral notes - experienced perfumers note it outperforms its close relative Globanone in this regard. Try Aurelione at 1-5% to give florals a gentle halo of warmth and persistence. In musky skin scents, push it well above 10% for full effect - it can handle overdose gracefully. Combine it with other macrocyclic musks and lactones for complex, layered musk accords that never turn harsh.

missing.title: Avobenzone
missing.description: Avobenzone is the most effective UVA absorber available to perfumers. This crystalline powder shields the full UVA range (320–400 nm, peaking at 357 nm) — the long-wave light that yellows liquids and breaks down vanillin. At typical use levels, it adds no perceptible odour to your composition. Dissolve Avobenzone in a co-solvent — benzyl benzoate, IPM, or Octinoxate — by heating to 80–85°C until completely clear. Its solubility in pure ethanol is poor (under 1%), so alcohol-based fragrances need a carrier oil in the formula. Compositions containing vanillin or citrus oils benefit most from its protection. The catch: Avobenzone is photounstable and degrades in light unless stabilised. Always include Oxynex ST at 0.5% — it quenches the reactive excited state that causes degradation, boosting photostability dramatically. Never combine Avobenzone with Octinoxate alone — without a stabiliser, the two accelerate each other's breakdown. Avobenzone vs Octinoxate Avobenzone and Octinoxate protect against different portions of the UV spectrum. Avobenzone absorbs UVA (320–400 nm) — the longer-wavelength light responsible for yellowing liquids and degrading vanillin and other phenolics. Octinoxate absorbs UVB (280–320 nm) — the shorter-wavelength radiation that attacks terpenes, aldehydes, and other volatile components. Avobenzone is a crystalline powder that must be heated to 80–85°C in a co-solvent to dissolve; Octinoxate is a pourable liquid that incorporates instantly and can dissolve up to 26% Avobenzone by weight. In theory they make a perfect pair, but they destabilise each other through photocyclisation unless a photostabiliser like Oxynex ST is included as a third ingredient. With Oxynex ST present (just 0.5% of the finished formula), the combination provides excellent broad-spectrum UV protection for your fragrances.

missing.title: Azarbre
missing.description: Azarbre is a herbal material that can add wonderfully delicate orris and honey nuances to a fragrance. It is an infrequently seen material that is used to great effect in the Dior Private Collection fragrance Bois D'Argent (2004) by Annick Menardo which is enormously popular with French Hip Hop stars. See our demo formula below. According to A. B. Camps: “This material […] is missing from most laboratories. Azarbre is less agrestical than Opalal and more woody-honey-rooty, with notes of dry flowers. Azarbre mixes well with rooty essential oils such as corydalis or Cyperus scarious and all kinds of agarwood oils as well. The material forms great accords with isophorone, phenylacetic acid , oxophorone, tobacco absolute, ionones , damascones, phenylacetates, nectarol, the usually great myrrhone, dihydroionol, and osmanthus [.]” Azarbre blends well with Aetoxylon Oil , Fenchone Alpha , Geosmin , Linalool Oxide , Amazonia ™ and Miraclewood ™.

missing.title: Bacdanol®
missing.description: Bacdanol opens with immediate sandalwood warmth enhanced by creamy, almost cosmetic milkiness. Its sweet gourmand character suggests vanilla whilst subtle rose facets add floral sophistication. This powerful material radiates with impressive diffusion, creating lasting woody depth. You'll find Bacdanol invaluable for building cost-effective sandalwood accords where diffusion and longevity matter. It excels at supporting floral hearts, particularly rose and jasmine, whilst adding creamy depth to woody bases. Use it at 0.5-2% where its power provides excellent value compared to natural sandalwood without sacrificing quality. Blend Bacdanol with Javanol for enhanced floral-sandalwood complexity or combine with Ebanol for deeper leather nuances. Pair with Iso E Super where transparent woody diffusion amplifies its creamy character. This material bridges floral hearts with amber bases beautifully, particularly with musks. Bacdanol vs Dartanol Whilst chemically similar, these materials offer distinct olfactory profiles perfumers value differently. Bacdanol presents sweeter, creamier, more gourmand character with vanilla-milky richness ideal for modern compositions. Dartanol delivers drier, more natural sandalwood with cedar-like texture and radiant elegance preferred for premium fragrances. Choose Bacdanol for cost-effective sweetness and powerful diffusion; choose Dartanol for authentic sandalwood refinement.

missing.title: Benzoin Oliffac
missing.description: Benzoin Oliffac 63 opens with a creamy, vanillic sweetness (almost milkshake-like) that sits deeper and rounder than typical vanilla materials. There's a soft powdery quality underneath, dusted with faint cinnamon and almond nuances. The effect recalls warm resin tempered into something smooth and immediately usable. This IFF base solves the notorious handling problems of crude benzoin gum—no heating, no filtering, no wax precipitation. It dissolves completely in ethanol and pours cold from the bottle, which saves you time in production. At 1–3% of your concentrate, it adds soft vanillic sweetness without announcing itself; at 5–10%, it becomes the structural backbone of amber and oriental accords. Use Benzoin Oliffac when you need the classic benzoin character without the laboratory drama. Pair it with labdanum and vanillin for traditional amber structures, or blend with tuberose and jasmine to round harsh indolic edges. Its 400+ hour tenacity on blotter makes it exceptional in functional products—candles, detergents, fabric care—where heat stability and lasting warmth matter most.

missing.title: Benzyl Acetone
missing.description: Benzyl acetone is an indispensable chemical for adding a fruity nuance to oud replacers or as a modifier to the much more delicate benzyl acetate. Benzyl acetone is very powerful and very small amounts are perceptible in a fragrance. This material is also a key component of the scent of cocoa and the most bee-attracting chemical in many flowers. Benzyl Acetone has nuances of tobacco, cinnamon, pineapple, banana and white flowers. NOTE: this product should not be confused with Benzyl Acetate, the common chemical used to reproduce the scent of jasmine and ylang-ylang.

missing.title: Bergamote 000136
missing.description: Bergamote 000136 from Firmenich opens with bright, sparkling citrus — clean bergamot zest with a subtle herbaceous-tea undertone. It reads as brighter and more lifted than the natural oil, with a fizzy, almost champagne-like quality. Firmenich captive molecules give it a character you cannot build yourself. Natural bergamot oil is phototoxic. Remove the offending compounds and you get bergamot FCF, which solves the safety problem but often loses character in the process — most FCF oils are stripped flat. This base gives you the full Calabrian bergamot impression without that compromise, and with batch-to-batch consistency natural oil cannot guarantee. Use Bergamote 000136 as a direct substitute for bergamot oil or FCF in any fine fragrance formula. Fraterworks also carries its own bergamot reconstruction, Bergamot Reggio, built to the same purpose but with different character. Try both side by side to find your preference.

missing.title: Berryflor
missing.description: Berryflor opens with a soft, fruity raspberry impression wrapped in jasmine warmth and anisic transparency. The effect reads more floral than fruity — ripe berries filtered through something clean and sweet. A gentle balsamic backdrop smooths everything into a quietly complex whole. This Givaudan creation works best as a modifier — quiet on its own, transformative in a blend. Even trace amounts soften floral accords and add convincing berry realism. Use too much and the composition drifts toward a muddy, damp character, so dose with care. Pair Berryflor with beta-ionone and raspberry ketone for lush berry hearts. It harmonises naturally with Isoraldeines and ionones, bridging fruit and flower within woody or musky bases. Twenty-four hours on blotter gives your fruity accords genuine staying power.

missing.title: Beyond Blue™
missing.description: The Fraterworks® Perfumer's Palette™ is a range of dyes that can be used alone or in combination with each other to add vibrance and colour to your perfumes or cosmetic products. Our proprietary blend of FD&C and D&C colours are sold in liquid form. Perfumer's Palette colours contain distilled water which is perfectly safe for alcoholic perfumes in the quantities needed for colouration. Typical use is from 0.01–0.5% of finished product. At these low levels, staining of clothing or skin is minimal to none but you should always test your finished product against white cloth or paper.

missing.title: Bicyclononalactone
missing.description: Bicyclononalactone is a creamy and sweet lactone but with a distinctly tonka and hay character. Its has a subtle earthiness that makes it far more interesting than many of the other lactones that tend to be variations on a theme of coconut or peach. Use it as an interesting alternative to Coumarin in a classic fougère and as a replacer for Dihydrocoumarin which is prohibited in many places except when naturally occurring in plant extracts. Bicyclononalactone is used to great effect in such scents as Ambre Narguile (2004) by Hermès where it is found at an enormous 4% and Grand Soir (2016) of Maison Francis Kurkdjian at a more reasonable 1.5%.

missing.title: Biocyclamol
missing.description: Biocyclamol opens deceptively mild—patience rewards you here. Give it time on the blotter and a beautiful muguet-cyclamen character emerges with impressive tenacity and diffusive power. The green-floral heart feels genuinely natural, lacking the ozonic, aldehydic, or lactonic distractions common in modern muguet materials. This sesquiterpene alcohol is chemically related to farnesol but offers a distinctly different olfactory experience. Found naturally in cyclamen flowers, it brings authentic botanical character to your compositions. The material works at remarkably low dosages while delivering substantivity exceeding 36 hours—exceptional performance for a floral note. Use Biocyclamol to anchor muguet accords with clean, smooth naturalism. It pairs beautifully with Takasago's Biomuguet for extended linear radiance into the drydown. The material also enhances neroli compositions unexpectedly well, adding floral volume without heaviness.

missing.title: Biomuguet
missing.description: Biomuguet delivers a muguet character unlike the classical aldehydes. This is abstract, luminous, faintly metallic — more ozonic radiance than sweet lily. A creamy floral body sits underneath the aldehydic lift, with subtle citrus and green facets that give it a distinctly modern feel. Takasago produces this from sugarcane-derived farnesene, making it bio-based though not classified as natural. With Lilial and Lyral banned in Europe, Biomuguet offers an unrestricted muguet building block for compositions that need floral luminosity. It softens harsh green and citrus notes while adding shape, rhythm, and diffusive volume. Pair Biomuguet with Biocyclamol (it's related alcohol) for the complete muguet experience — the aldehyde provides top-note radiance while the alcohol extends into the drydown. It also works beautifully with Hedione in jasmine-muguet accords. Strong at the top but moderate longevity on its own.

missing.title: Bisabolene
missing.description: Bisabolene opens with an immediate recognition factor—this is the warm, resinous sweetness you detect at the heart of genuine myrrh and opoponax absolutes. The material presents a remarkably complex profile that explains its pivotal role in recreating some of perfumery's most precious naturals. Beyond its primary balsamic-spicy character lies a sophisticated interplay of woody warmth, subtle citrus facets, and even delicate floral whispers that allow it to bridge multiple fragrance families with extraordinary grace. This material's true genius lies in its ability to recreate the authentic signatures of prohibitively expensive natural materials. Deploy bisabolene at 0.5-3% when reconstructing myrrh or opoponax accords—it provides the crucial molecular backbone these resins are built upon. More remarkably, it makes an important contribution to the recreation of oud, offering perfumers a lower cost pathway to this increasingly rare material. Its presence in natural bergamot and lemon oils explains why it adds such authentic depth to citrus reconstitutions, transforming flat synthetic citrus into living, breathing recreations. Use it as a fixative for neroli at 0.1-0.5% to anchor those fleeting orange blossom notes without masking their delicacy.

missing.title: Blackwood Base 199939 RF17
missing.description: Blackwood Base defies its name entirely. The opening is bright and rosy with a strong rosewood-linalool character — almost sparkling and citrus-touched. It feels modern and clean, nothing like the dark, brooding wood the name suggests. That brightness is what makes this base so versatile. As it develops, a serious woody-amber character emerges in the heart and base. The rosewood facets recede and a dry, leathery quality takes over, anchored by potent woody captives including Acetarolle, Mysoral, and Myrrhone Neo. Use it in masculine compositions where you want complexity without heaviness, or layer it to build skeletal oud-style effects. Blackwood Base excels as a structural backbone. Pair it with real oud for added dimension, or combine with patchouli and labdanum for a contemporary chypre foundation. In feminine work, keep it below the point where the pungent topnotes dominate — let the amber drydown do the talking instead.

missing.title: Bois d'Encens
missing.description: Bois d'Encens is a Robertet all-natural speciality in which olibanum is co-distilled with cedarwood . Co-distillation is the process in which two or more materials are turned into a single essential-oil type material by combining them prior to or during distillation. Bois d'Encense has the sweetness of fine Virginian cedarwood with the majesty and richesse of exotic frankincense. It is a wonderful material that can be used at quite high amounts. Replace all of some of the cedarwood in your scent for a more oriental touch, or just wrap it in some refined musks or a monolithic accord like Grojsman Plus for a finished perfume. Bois d'Encens blends wonderfully with smoky Cade oil or Birch tar but don't neglect the Fraterworks treasure Bouleau Pyrogene 1840 which is enormously popular. This also combines marvellously with Artemal and, if you are not tied to IFRA requirements, pure Tree Moss Absolute .

missing.title: Boisambrene Forte
missing.description: Boisambrene Forte presents a distinctive woody-amber fragrance, characterised by refined cedar-like notes combined with warm ambergris nuances, creating a dry, sophisticated aroma. Its subtle, elegant scent provides depth without being overwhelming, balancing medium intensity with exceptional tenacity. In perfumery, Boisambrene Forte excels as a powerful, long-lasting base note and effective fixative, significantly enhancing fragrance longevity and structure. Its versatility makes it ideal for woody, amber, masculine, and unisex compositions, and its notable stability in soaps, shampoos, and detergents further broadens its application in both fine and functional perfumery.

missing.title: Boisiris®
missing.description: Boisiris is a rich woody heart note with iris connotations which can be used in traces to add volume to a fragrance or in overdose, as in the case of Royal Oud by Creed where it forms a full 12% of the fragrance. Boisiris' versatility can be seen in its broad uses: in the great Fixobois base of Firmenich (which was sadly recently reformulated) it adds a blending and smoothing effect, while in their Civettte Synthetic it contributes volume and a woody nuance to the animalics. Boisiris is also found in Duro (2007) by Nasomatto, Candy Aoud (2005) and Elysium Pour Homme (2017) by Roja Dove, Colors Man Black Intenso (2021) by Benetton and 212 Heroes Forever Young (2022) by Carolina Herrera.

missing.title: Bornafix®
missing.description: Bornafix opens with a distinctive warmth that sits between dry cedarwood and dusty amber. Unlike the transparent smoothness of Iso E Super, this material has genuine texture - a green, mossy density that evokes sun-baked Mediterranean hillsides thick with rosemary and thyme. The herbal facets emerge gradually, lending an agrestic, almost landscape-like quality that sets it apart from cleaner synthetic woods. Consider Bornafix when modernising fougère structures - its thyme and lavender-spike facets bridge traditional aromatic herbs to contemporary musky bases. Combine it with Iso E Super and vetiver for complex modern woods, or layer it beneath citrus accords to give them staying power.

missing.title: Boronal
missing.description: Boronal opens with a sweet, caramel-touched floral impression that immediately recalls violets, iris and boronia absolute. Hay and soft leather emerge as it develops, alongside a bran-like warmth. The drydown is the revelation: a powdery ambergris character that lasts for days. This Symrise aldehyde works as a genuine bridge between floral hearts and woody bases. Pair it with ionones and methyl ionones for complex violet accords, or combine with Ambroxan and sandalwood for ambery depth. It adds fruit-forward warmth to osmanthus constructions and powdery richness to orientals. Blend Boronal with dihydro-beta-ionone for lush orris effects, or with mate absolute and myrrh for dark, resinous florals. It performs well in soap and powder formulations but avoid body lotions where stability suffers. It gives you boronia absolute character at a fraction of the cost.

missing.title: Bourgeonal®
missing.description: Bourgeonal opens with a burst of fresh, watery lily-of-the-valley — clean, dewy, and immediately recognisable. A bright aldehydic edge rides on top, giving it sparkle without harshness. Underneath, a quiet woody-sandalwood depth anchors the freshness and extends the drydown. This is the muguet note you build accords around. It slots naturally into aldehydic florals, green bouquets, and fresh compositions where you need a clean floral heart. Pair it with Hedione and hydroxycitronellal for a convincing lily-of-the-valley that reads as lifelike, not soapy. With Lilial no longer available in the EU, Bourgeonal covers similar muguet territory with its own greener, more openly aldehydic character. Evaluate from a 10% dilution; neat, the aldehydic top can mislead. Avoid pairing with Aldehyde C-11 (Undecanal) — it suppresses the muguet.

missing.title: Brahmanol
missing.description: Brahmanol smells of rich, creamy sandalwood with a warm musky glow underneath — soft, enveloping, and remarkably close to santalol, the heart of natural Mysore oil. It lacks the delicate floral top of the real thing, but that creamy, skin-like warmth is unmistakable, and a touch of hindinol can be used to fill that gap. Brahmanol lasts over 400 hours on a blotter. Use it as the foundation of sandalwood accords, either alone at high concentrations or blended with other sandalwood materials for a more complete picture. It adds creamy depth to floral compositions — tuberose, jasmine, and ylang-ylang all benefit from its warm, musky support. It is one of the most versatile and underrated sandalwood materials available. Where it sits in the sandalwood basic synthetics family matters. Sandalore is the most widely used replacer — sweet, creamy, powerful, with a slightly synthetic edge at high doses. Sandela is drier and more transparent, a background contributor. Ebanol is the most powerful of the group, rich and milky-sweet with a buttery maple quality. Bacdanol splits the difference between creamy and rosy, with a distinctive milky sweetness. Brahmanol is none of these. It is more musky and less floral than the natural oil, more restrained than Ebanol, warmer than Sandela, and less overtly sweet than Sandalore. Think of it as the workhorse sandalwood — reliable, tenacious, and honest. Hindinol , Polysantol , Firsantol and Javanol pack the power of the bunch and, so, are typically used in smaller amounts.

missing.title: Butylated Hydroxytoluene (BHT)
missing.description: BHT arrives as white crystalline powder with the faintest whisper of phenolic character that vanishes entirely once dissolved at working strength. This near-odourless profile makes it the perfect silent protector in perfumery. You'll detect nothing at the 0.1% level typically used to stabilise volatile aldehydes and citrus oils. Transform your most fragile materials into shelf-stable champions by adding BHT directly to pure aldehydes upon receipt. Watch as those temperamental aliphatic aldehydes maintain their sparkling character instead of degrading into rancid acids. Citrus oils retain their zesty freshness for years rather than developing stale terpene notes. Dissolve crystals directly in your fragrance concentrate before dilution for seamless incorporation and complete protection. Combine BHT with tocopherols for synergistic antioxidant power that outperforms either alone. Add citric acid to chelate trace metals that catalyse oxidation. This multi-pronged approach delivers superior stability using lower total antioxidant levels—perfect for meeting modern formulation demands whilst maintaining exceptional performance.

missing.title: Camphor Crystals
missing.description: Camphor Crystals hit the nose with an immediate sharp, cooling blast — clean, dry, and purely camphoraceous. A herbal-minty quality underneath connects it to rosemary and lavender. This is a trigeminal material: you feel it in your sinuses as much as you smell it. Use camphor in traces to add sharp freshness and clarity to aromatic and fougère compositions. It cuts through heavy materials like patchouli and myrrh, bringing air and definition. In lavender accords, a touch reinforces the natural camphoraceous facet that's already present in good lavender oils. Pair camphor with eucalyptus and rosemary for medicinal-aromatic effects, or with bright citrus for a clean, bracing opening. Small doses alongside incense and resinous materials create an unexpected cool contrast to warm, smoky bases. Dose carefully — camphor overwhelms everything if overdone.

missing.title: Canthoxal
missing.description: Canthoxal is a light anise aroma chemical with facets of liquorice and a very delicate wateriness. Canthoxal blends beautifully with Armoise Oil , Basil Oil, Spanish Anise Oil, Toscanol, Anisic Aldehyde (and others members of the same family). Canthoxal has the very rare distinction of having had its IFRA limit considerably liberalised in the latest standard, going from 0.82% to the much larger 2.5%.

missing.title: Canthoxalia
missing.description: This material offers a richly layered profile built around a persistent, inviting sweetness that defines its charm. At its heart lies a distinct anise or liquorice note, evoking the nostalgic depth of root beer, with a soft hawthorn edge that feels both floral and faintly medicinal. A powdery veil lends refinement—delicate, cosmetic, and unmistakably vintage—tempering the sweetness with a soft-focus finish. Balancing its warmth is a green-fresh brightness, adding lift and subtle complexity, at times reading as marine or dewy. It draws frequent comparison to mimosa absolute, sharing that same warm, honeyed floralcy with a plush, gently animalic undertone. Hints of orange blossom add radiance, while a whisper of spice and a dry cortex-like texture round out the base. Due to the viscous nature of this material, we are selling it diluted to 50% in TEC or pure.

missing.title: Cantryl®
missing.description: Cantryl smells wild — damp undergrowth, crushed herbs, pine needles, and hay all at once. It has a raw, almost untamed quality that instantly reads as "outdoors." There is real woody depth underneath the herbal freshness, with hints of juniper berry and rosemary. Despite being a top-note material, it lasts remarkably well — over 40 hours on a blotter. The practical value here is twofold. First, Cantryl strengthens and lifts herbal notes — lavender, rosemary, clary sage — without adding sweetness or distortion. A small amount makes these familiar materials smell more vivid and natural. Second, it is exceptionally stable in difficult bases including shampoos and acidic cleansers, where many green-herbal materials fall apart. Use Cantryl in fougère compositions alongside lavender, coumarin, and oakmoss for a green-herbal lift. It adds a natural, peely freshness to citrus accords and brings realism to violet leaf notes. Work from a dilution — it is potent and can dominate unexpectedly at higher concentrations. A little goes a long way.

missing.title: Caramel Acetate
missing.description: Caramel acetate has a fascinating dual personality. At full strength you get warm toffee, brown sugar, and molasses with a baked-bread quality. Dilute it to traces and it shifts to a soft, sweet strawberry. This concentration-dependent behaviour makes it versatile — a single material serving two very different roles. Use caramel acetate in your gourmand and oriental compositions where you need authentic caramel warmth and toffee sweetness. At higher levels it builds convincing brown-sugar accords. At lower levels it contributes a fruity strawberry facet that blends beautifully into floral and fruity hearts. Pair with vanillin and ethyl maltol for rich caramel-gourmand effects. Try it alongside lactones for creamy toffee depth. Blend with fruity esters to exploit its strawberry side — even a trace adds a soft, sweet, berry-like warmth that lifts an entire composition.

missing.title: Carbinol Muguet
missing.description: Carbinol Muguet opens with soft, clean floral freshness—delicate yet substantial. The lily and hyacinth character feels natural and unforced, while sweet rose undertones add warmth. A gentle violet nuance and mild herbaceous quality round the profile beautifully, creating something that feels lifted yet grounded. Arctander considered this material "probably the most valuable and versatile of all the so-called carbinols"—high praise indeed. It combines the best qualities of linalool and terpineol without their drawbacks: none of linalool's volatility and none of terpineol's woody-piney character. Use it as a structural floraliser at levels from 2% up to 25% of your concentrate. It builds floral body in muguet, rose, jasmine, and magnolia compositions while working equally well as an undertone in chypres and non-florals. The 244-hour substantivity makes Carbinol Muguet exceptional value for floral work—your lily character persists beautifully into the drydown. Blend with linalool and linalyl acetate for lifted muguet effects, or pair with lindenol, orris, and cinnamyl alcohol for complex floral hearts. It serves a similar structural role to benzyl salicylate but with a distinctly different character.

missing.title: Carbitol™
missing.description: Carbitol is a low gravity low odour diluent with the faintest hint of an alcoholic scent. It is the best solvent for cardboard and car diffusers and it finds use in many historic animalic bases in rather high amounts where its delicate odour contributes more than just solubility. Carbitol may primarily be a solvent but it is not a stranger to fine fragrances, being found in fairly decent amounts in 212 For Men (1999) by Alberto Morillas for Carolina Herrera, Moon Dance (2014) by Juliette Has A Gun, YSL's Opium Pour Homme (1995, Jacques Cavallier), and Pour Lui (1980) by Oscar de la Renta.

missing.title: Carvacryl Methyl Ether
missing.description: Carvacryl Methyl Ether opens with the sun-baked essence of Mediterranean herbs, capturing oregano's warmth without its medicinal edge. This methylated derivative strips away carvacrol's harsh phenolic character, revealing cleaner herbal facets. Its dry spiciness mingles with subtle citrus peel notes, creating natural complexity. This middle-note material bridges fleeting citrus tops with heavier bases beautifully. You'll find it invaluable for extending aromatic themes deep into your composition's heart, preventing abrupt transitions between volatility levels. It modernises classic fougères by adding garrigue warmth to lavender hearts, while in contemporary chypres it creates intriguing herbal contrasts against bergamot and patchouli bases. Use it at 0.5-3% to naturalise synthetic accords or boost authenticity in herb-forward compositions. Pair it with black pepper for vibrant spicy diffusion, or combine with vetiver to accentuate dry earthiness. In trace amounts, it adds unexpected spicy depth to carnation reconstructions and green texture to white florals.

missing.title: Caryophyllene Acetate
missing.description: _*]:min-w-0 gap-3"> _*]:min-w-0 gap-3"> _*]:min-w-0 gap-3"> Caryophyllene acetate delivers a smooth, dry, woody-amber character with a distinctive vetiver-like earthiness. It is far more refined than raw caryophyllene, which can feel harsh and dusty. Subtle fruity and spicy facets warm the drydown, and the overall impression is of a polished, amber-tinged wood — versatile and easy to blend. Use this material to add dry woody depth and vetiver-like character to your orientals, chypres, and woody compositions. It extends and refines vetiver accords beautifully, contributing a cleaner amber warmth. As a fixative it is outstanding, anchoring volatile top notes while adding its own woody signature to the base. Blend with vetiver and patchouli for a rich, earthy woody foundation. Try it alongside sandalwood and ambroxan for modern amber-wood accords. Pair with oakmoss and clove for classic chypre constructions where its smooth woodiness adds lasting depth.

missing.title: Caryophyllene Oxide
missing.description: Caryophyllene Oxide opens with a crystalline woody sweetness that immediately distinguishes itself from its precursor β-caryophyllene. You'll detect a refined dryness reminiscent of aged cedar and antique furniture with none of the dusty harshness. Its spicy warmth suggests clove and black pepper but smoothed and mellowed through oxidation. It seamlessly connects spicy top notes to woody bases while adding depth to oriental structures. You'll find it indispensable for creating realistic spice reconstructions where it provides the warm woody body beneath sharper phenolic notes. Its unique dry-sweet character prevents fruity accords from becoming cloying while lifting heavier base materials.

missing.title: Cassis Base 345B
missing.description: This classic blackcurrant base from Firmenich is so ubiquitous you'll recognise it immediately upon smelling even if you've never purchased it before. It features in an overdose in Un Jardin Sur Le Nil by Jean-Claude Ellena for Hermès where it forms part of his green mango accord, and is found in traces in virtually every modern department store fragrance. When you need blackcurrant, this is the base you should turn to. Use it in amounts up to 0.1% to add nuance, radiance and a light fruity connotation to the opening of your fragrance, or in higher amounts for a distinctly blackcurrant note. And don't be fooled by the name, Cassis Base 345B is also floral (particularly in the rose direction), green and minty. The versatility of this base cannot be overstated. We stock 345B because it is the favoured version of this base. Firmenich also makes a cheaper 345F. Cassis Base 345B delivers warm, fruity notes with ripe blackcurrant sparkle, consistently producing professional results. It offers reliability and sophisticated depth that perfumer wearers appreciate. 345B's exceptional warmth provides that perfect finish most projects demand. 345F exists as a cooler, greener option, but lacks the refinement and balance of 345B.

missing.title: Cedramber
missing.description: Cedramber delivers a powerful woody and velvety amber note with remarkable strength and diffusiveness. Its deep cedar-like character is complemented by a warm amber quality, making it indispensable for perfumers. It gives structure and sophistication to a scent while enhancing spicy-woody accords. Cedramber pairs beautifully with Iso E Super , Vertofix Coeur , and Cashmeran to create luminous and modern woody blends. In florals, it adds dryness and balance, while in orientals, it melds with labdanum , patchouli and vanillin to deliver a luxurious depth and richness. Cedramber lends its characteristic elegance to fragrances like Yves Saint Laurent’s Opium for Men (1995), enhancing its spicy oriental depth, and Bleu de Chanel (2010), where it provides a radiant structure to fresh-woody accords. It also demonstrates its wonderful ability to lift rich wood scents in Ajmal's masterpiece Dahn Oudh Al Shams (0.4%).

missing.title: Cedrene Alpha
missing.description: Alpha-cedrene is the sharp, dry topnote of cedarwood — the pencil-shavings character that hits you first when you snap a cedar branch. It lacks the sweet, balsamic warmth of cedrol or cedryl acetate. This is cedar stripped back to its lightest, driest essence. Use it to add crisp woody dryness to leather accords, chypres, and masculine fougères. It anchors compositions without adding sweetness, giving you the top fraction of cedarwood oil in isolated, controllable form. It also makes an excellent starting point for building custom cedar accords by blending with richer cedarwood materials. Pair it with cedryl acetate and cedrol for a full-spectrum cedar effect, or with vetiver and patchouli for dark woody depth. It works beautifully with Iso E Super and its derivatives, adding definition to their transparent warmth. A true workhorse of the woody palette.

missing.title: Cedroxyde®
missing.description: Cedroxyde is a refined woody molecule which, unlike traditional cedarwood notes, has a subtle ozonic quality, imparting a slightly aquatic, invigorating facet. It gives lift to heavy woody accords and pairs beautifully with other synthetic ingredients like Iso E Super, Cashmeran , or Ambroxan. It works exceptionally well in marine-inspired creations, fresh woods, and contemporary fougères, often serving as a heart or base note enhancer. Its nuanced drydown reveals a touch of creamy smoothness that tempers its otherwise vibrant edge. Cedroxyde excels when used alongside Sandalwood oils and lactonic elements to create creamy, smooth wood accords. Pair it with bright citrus notes like bergamot or grapefruit for a zesty, refreshing top, or mix it with synthetic amber molecules like Ambrofix or Orcanox for a more profound, resinous base. For green compositions, the ozonic cedar aspect integrates seamlessly with galbanum oil and vetiver aromachemicals like vetiveryl and vetiver acetate . Notable appearances of this material include Henry Jacques Galileo (2019) by perfumer Christophe Tollemer, Elysium (2017) Roja Dove, Dior Homme Sport (2021) by François Demachy, and Bleu de Chanel Parfum (2018) by Olivier Polge. Cedroxyde also features in the luxurious Bakhoor Al Arais (2012) by Swiss Arabian.

missing.title: Cedryl Acetate, Crystals
missing.description: Crystals are the purest form of this aroma chemical and far less common (and much harder to find) than the liquid form. Also sometimes known as Cedrenyl Acetate, this material is a wonderfully soft woody note and has no IFRA restriction unlike the closely related (olfactorily) Cedrene and Cedrol. This very long-lasting material is wonderful as a soft wood in floral bases, but also works extremely well as an alternative to Sandalwood, Vetiver and Cedarwood. Simply add it to your formula in its solid form as the crystals melt very easily.

missing.title: Celeriax
missing.description: We use celery seed in perfume to give tuberose brightness and uplift. It works in a similar way to cis-jasmone in fact. Celeriax is a molecule that does a similar thing at a slightly lower cost and with more power. Furthermore, behind its salted-skin façade lies a maple syrup note and a distinct umami quality. This is a base note material for sure which gives it some interesting potential uses as a booster for restricted oakmoss , and an extender for expensive naturals like opoponax essential oil . Synergies with celeriax can be found in Immortelle, fig leaf , and nutty notes where it can be effective in bridging nuts and wood. This is an aroma chemical you don't know you need, until you try it, at which point you'll be trying to find excuses to pop it into every blend!

missing.title: Centifolether
missing.description: Centifolether opens with fresh, dewy rose petal character reminiscent of Rosa centifolia, the hundred-petalled rose of Grasse. A metallic oxide-like facet adds a modern, lifted sparkle. Subtle anisic and exotic fruit nuances round out an aroma that reads completely natural. Use Centifolether as a rose oxide enhancer or substitute — it delivers the same rosy-metallic sparkle with far superior stability. In fine fragrance it lifts rose accords at trace levels without ever dominating. Its exceptional chemical stability makes it equally valuable in demanding functional products like laundry detergents and bleach-based cleaners. Blend Centifolether into green accords where its rosy freshness adds floral complexity. Pair it with linalool and geraniol for classic rose construction, or with citrus oils for sparkling floral-fruity top notes. Its three-hour tenacity on blotter makes it a true top note — layer over longer-lasting rose materials for naturalistic evolution.

missing.title: Cervolide®
missing.description: CERVOLIDE® is a rare macrocyclic musk known for its radiant softness and deeply soothing character. A molecule of exceptional pedigree, it blends the airy, fruity grace of Ambrettolide with the sleek, metallic warmth of Habanolide —delivering a musky signature that is both elegantly skin-like and subtly enveloping. CERVOLIDE® reveals itself not as a brute force base note, but as a gentle anchor: quiet, complex, and tenacious. Its musky presence doesn’t just linger—it soothes, offering you a rare chance to design not just for olfactory impact, but also emotional atmosphere. Perfumery Usage CERVOLIDE® excels in fine fragrance, personal care, and functional formulations, where it imparts a natural, second-skin effect. It has remarkable synergy with ambers , florals, and woods, and enhances blooming materials such as orange flower , jasmine , or rose by extending their drydown without altering their core identity. Use it to round sharpness, amplify warmth, or infuse a composition with creamy diffusion and elegant longevity. In white musk accords, it provides a quiet sophistication that cheaper musks often lack. Performance CERVOLIDE® is highly stable in soaps, shampoos, and emulsions, with excellent retention on skin and fabric. Despite its fixative strength, it maintains a clean, biodegradable profile—a modern musk aligned with green chemistry values. Its ultra-low vapor pressure allows it to act as a fragrance extender with minimal environmental footprint. Background CERVOLIDE® was first described in the late 20th century and quickly gained cult status among perfumers for its unique musk tone—softer than Muscone , richer than Galaxolide , and more complex than Exaltolide . It featured in iconic formulas like The Body Shop’s White Musk and Guerlain’s Derby (both formulas can be found below), where its subtle fruity-woody nuance added sensual warmth. Today, CERVOLIDE® remains a quietly powerful tool for perfumers seeking depth, longevity, and modern musk elegance. Note:

missing.title: Cetonal®
missing.description: Cetonal is a fascinating material with nuances of tobacco, leather, iris, animals and wood. It has a low odour profile but is surprisingly long lasting and quite profound in its effects at even very low doses (below one percent). According to Givaudan, “Orris, Woody, Powerful. Cetonal is an elegant ingredient used in woody, orris accords as well as with leather, tobacco and animal notes where it acts as an excellent blending agent and adds to the harmony of a fragrance.” Its softness shines in accords with Cashmeran, dihydro-ionones, and amber notes, pairing brilliantly with Norlimbanol , Ambrocenide, Boisambrene, Operanide, and Somalian frankincense oil

missing.title: Cetylic Alcohol
tags: locale:heat to melt and use bottles not pots
missing.description: Cetylic alcohol is not an aroma chemical — it is a white waxy solid that melts at around 50°C and resolidifies into a smooth, silky mass. You buy it for what it does, not what it smells like. Its near-total lack of odour makes it an ideal carrier that lets your fragrance speak without interference. It melts gently with warmth and sets to a smooth, waxy solid at room temperature. Blending it with beeswax and a carrier oil gives you the classic base for solid perfume — a format that is experiencing a genuine revival among niche perfume buyers. It also helps oil and water stay mixed in creams and lotions, giving them that rich, velvety slip. If you are purely a fine fragrance compounder working in alcohol, you will never need this material. But if you are building scented products beyond the spray bottle — solid perfumes, body balms, scented candles, cream perfumes — cetylic alcohol is foundational.

missing.title: Chamomile Isobutyrate
missing.description: Chamomile Isobutyrate (also known as Isopentyrate) captures the smell of fresh chamomile flowers: fruity, clean and naturally herbaceous, with a soft floral warmth. It reads as bright and true rather than medicinal or sharp. A single material that does the work of a whole chamomile accord. This is one of the rare materials that genuinely makes things smell more natural. Add it at low levels to synthetic compositions and you'll notice an immediate lift in diffusion and a convincing botanical quality that's hard to achieve any other way.

missing.title: Chloroxylenol
missing.description: Chloroxylenol opens with an unmistakable antiseptic sharpness that immediately evokes clean, clinical spaces. This powerful phenolic material carries the signature Dettol aroma. Its penetrating medicinal quality cuts through compositions with surgical precision. You'll find this material invaluable for creating authentic hospital or medical environments in conceptual fragrances. At extreme dilution, it adds a subtle phenolic dryness to leather accords. Blend it with vanillin to create intriguing, sweet-medicinal contrasts that evoke vintage apothecary preparations. Use Chloroxylenol sparingly—its potency demands respect. A mere trace transforms woody bases into something darker and more complex. Combine with creosol and guaiacol for intense tar-leather effects that push boundaries in avant-garde perfumery. Of note, the reason for its dettol like smell is because this is actually a component of Dettol; it has amazing anti-microbial and preservative properties, and while we sell it mainly as an interesting odour chemical, those other facets are a bonus.

missing.title: Cinnamic Alcohol ex Styrax
missing.description: In crafting his fragrances, Edmond Roudnitska, the greatest perfumer of his generation, would put as much thought and care into the aroma chemicals as he would the naturals. He would use benzyl acetate ex Ylang-ylang or Jasmine, Geraniol ex Palma Rosa , Linalool ex Bois de Rose , Cinnamic Alcohol ex Styrax and on and on. This 100% natural Cinnamic Alcohol ex Styrax (a speciality of Payan Bertrand) has to be smelled to be believed. It is so good you simply want to melt into it and fade away in to a world of odour perfection.
