Use it in small amounts for a richesse impossible to obtain otherwise, or go wild and overdose in a floral base! It is useable to a very respectable 2.18% of your finished product. NOTE: because this is a natural isolate, it contains approximately 55% cinnamic alcohol with the remainder being made up of natural phenyl propyl alcohol and natural cinnamic aldehyde from the same extraction source (see associated SDS for more details). This also means the product is in a liquid state making it far easier to use than pure cinnamic alcohol which is a solid at room temperature.

missing.title: Cinnamoxal™
missing.description: Cinnamoxal™ opens with sweet cinnamic warmth characteristic of authentic cassia bark from which it naturally crystallises as stearoptene. This material delivers the oily-woody texture found in genuine Cinnamomum cassia oil. The paper-like dryness and medicinal-phenolic undertones create sophisticated depth beyond simple cinnamon sweetness. You'll find Cinnamoxal essential for building authentic cassia and cinnamon bark accords. Use at 0.5-5% for sweet spicy warmth with woody-resinous character. The material's natural occurrence in cinnamon bark and leaf oils makes it crucial for reconstructing these naturals. Its medicinal nuances add complexity that distinguishes fine oriental compositions from simple spice blends. The compound excels in creating authentic bark effects with its characteristic oily texture and woody depth. Combine with eugenol for complete cinnamon bark reconstruction, coumarin for sweet hay-like warmth, or benzoin for enhanced balsamic character. Found naturally in cassia oil alongside cinnamaldehyde, it provides unique facets the simpler molecule cannot achieve. Difference from Cinnamaldehyde While cinnamaldehyde delivers the sharp, bright, almost aggressive cinnamon heat familiar from red-hot candies and cinnamon toothpicks, Cinnamoxal offers a completely different interpretation. The ortho-methoxy group transforms the molecule's character entirely - where cinnamaldehyde is hot and piercing, Cinnamoxal is sweet and rounded. Cinnamaldehyde can read as synthetic or candy-like at higher doses; Cinnamoxal maintains natural bark authenticity. The added woody-oily texture, paper-like dryness, and medicinal depth make Cinnamoxal ideal for sophisticated orientals, while cinnamaldehyde suits fresh spicy top notes. Think of cinnamaldehyde as ground cinnamon's sharp bite versus Cinnamoxal as the complex aroma of cassia bark steeping in warm oil.

missing.title: Cis-3-Hexenyl Cis-3-Hexenoate
missing.description: Cis-3-Hexenyl Cis-3-Hexenoate ( Williams Ester) opens with a burst of pure pear juice—not sweet or candied, but the fresh, watery essence of biting into ripe fruit. This double-unsaturated ester captures something most materials miss: the textural sensation of pulpiness. You smell the saccharine flesh of the pear, complete with its characteristic ethereal quality. This material transforms beyond simple pear into complex territory. Its green tomato leaf facets add sharp, vegetal sophistication whilst metallic undertones prevent any cloying sweetness. You can leverage these complex secondary notes to build modern green compositions or use its exceptional 13-hour longevity to anchor fruity top notes deep into the heart. Use Williams Ester when you need to transcend ordinary fruit notes. Its natural occurrence in gardenia makes it perfect for floral modifications, whilst its melon and tropical facets open doors to aquatic compositions. The key lies in understanding its dual nature—intensely fruity yet surprisingly green. If you need help understanding the very complex myriad of leaf alcohol esters, check out our comprehensive blog article The Scent of Broken Leaves .

missing.title: Cis-3-Hexenyl Propionate
missing.description: This green ester (a material made when an acid is reacted with an alcohol - in this case Cis-3 Hexenol and Propionic acid) captures something extraordinary—not just the smell of fruit, but its tactile quality. When you encounter this material, you immediately recognise the waxy skin of a fresh apple or unripe pear. This textural element separates it from basic fruity esters that smell flat and confectionary. This material transforms ordinary fruit accords into photorealistic experiences. Its waxy character prevents compositions from becoming overly sweet or artificial, whilst the green-leafy backbone connects seamlessly to floral hearts. You can use it to create the impression of biting into crisp fruit or walking through a dewy orchard at dawn. Apply this when you need precision over power. Its strength lies in refinement—a few drops can shift an entire accord from synthetic to natural. Build your pear and apple notes around this foundation or use traces to add sophisticated texture to tropical fruit compositions. If you want to make a hyper-realistic pear, this is a must have in combination with Pear Ester and a sneaky trace of Safraleine to boost that gritty pear flesh texture. Try it - you won't believe how real it is! If you need help understanding the very complex myriad of leaf alcohol esters, check out our comprehensive blog article The Scent of Broken Leaves .

missing.title: Cis-3-Hexenyl Salicylate
missing.description: Cis-3-Hexenyl Salicylate is probably the most versatile of the green family, owing to its lightness and blending capabilities. Often replacing the hugely popular Benzyl Salicylate of the past, Cis-3-Hexenyl Salicylate offers virtually all of the same benefits with the added fresh connotations. Cis-3-Hexenyl Salicylate is balsamic, floral, green and orchid-like. It adds freshness and a sense of space to perfumes and could be considered beneficial to virtually every scent type. This material blends beautifully with its relatives, particularly Cis-3-Hexenyl Benzoate , Cis-3-Hexenol and Cis-3-Hexenyl Acetate . Like the benzoate, this also blends nicely with herbaceous oils like Clary Sage Oil and Lavender Oil and Absolute .

missing.title: Cis-3-Hexenyl Tiglate
missing.description: Cis-3-Hexenyl Tiglate opens with distinctive warm green character that immediately sets it apart from typical leaf alcohol esters. This unique material captures fresh-cut mushroom earthiness - not mouldy but clean and vegetal - combined with unexpected banana-melon fruitiness. The subtle gardenia-chamomile floralcy adds sophisticated depth that transforms simple green accords into complex botanical stories. You'll find Cis-3-Hexenyl Tiglate invaluable for adding naturalistic warmth to green compositions that feel too sharp or synthetic. Use at 0.5-5% where its earthy-herbaceous character provides the missing link between bright green top notes and heavier base materials. Found naturally in honeysuckle flowers and comprising 1.34% of gardenia headspace, it's essential for authentic white floral reconstructions requiring green warmth. The material excels in fougère compositions where its mushroom-earth facets enhance lavender's herbal character while adding modern complexity. Combine with lavender for enhanced naturalness, gardenia bases for authentic headspace effects, or violet leaf for sophisticated green depth. Its unusual banana-melon fruitiness bridges green and tropical territories brilliantly. The Tiglate Signature Tiglates possess a distinctive warm, slightly spicy-sweet character inherited from tiglic acid that sets them apart from common acetates or propionates. While simple esters like cis-3-hexenyl acetate deliver straightforward fresh-cut grass, tiglates add unexpected warmth and complexity - think of the difference between cold salad greens versus herbs warmed by the sun. This warmth manifests as earthy-mushroom notes in hexenyl tiglate, rose-honey in phenethyl tiglate, or minty coolness in isopropyl tiglate. The branched structure of tiglic acid creates more persistent, complex esters that feel more natural and less synthetic than their straight-chain counterparts.

missing.title: Cistulate
missing.description: Cistulate (fix carboxylate) smells like a walk through a sun-warmed pine forest. Crisp fir needles and fresh green pine lead, clean and natural, while a soft cistus-resin warmth glows underneath. A light woody, faintly fruity edge rounds it off, fresh and lifted, never heavy or dark. Use it to freshen and lift pine, fir and juniper accords, giving them a natural, outdoorsy sparkle at the top. It brings a green, resinous diffusion to fougères and aromatic colognes, and its cistus warmth lets it bridge fresh coniferous notes into softer woody and amber bases.

missing.title: Civettal
missing.description: Civettal (Animal Quinoline), or tetrahydro para methyl quinoline, is a powerful animalic material that is indispensable when creating non-natural civet blends or where a civet note is needed without the full complexity of the real product. It also works well in honey and tobacco blends. Civettal has a leather nuance but far less than the more common isobutyl quinoline. The two cannot substitute for one another. An excellent fixative when dosed right. Because of its strength, we sell this pure and diluted to 10% and 1% with Dipropylene Glycol. As with all high odour materials, we ship this in a sealed foil bag.

missing.title: Claritone
missing.description: Claritone is a multi-layered beast. It is herbal (in the direction of clary sage), peony floral, vaguely fruity and, to top it off, it sparkles like a coupe of champagne! While its most obvious use will be fougères, it can add diffusion and interest to all types of fragrances and it shouldn't be relegated to masculines only. It is a nice top note modifier in small amounts, but you can also push it to the extreme in overdose. Claritone was used at 1.5% in Clive Christian 1872 .

missing.title: Clearwood®
missing.description: Clearwood® is an all-natural product made by Firmenich to mimic the sweetest and cleanest properties of patchouli oil whilst removing anything even hinting at dirt. This is effectively a natural blend of a selection of the preferred molecules found in natural patchouli. Rich in patchouli alcohol (patchoulol), Clearwood is closest to our wonderful Patchoulol Crystals PA99 but about half the strength owing to the inclusion of other molecules. It blends wonderfully with Iso E Super and other light wood materials and can be used as a one for one replacer of natural patchouli oil. Use it in traces up to overdose. According to Firmenich: “ Created from white biotechnology, Clearwood delivers all the rewards of modern ingredient design. Beaming with light, it offers the creamy warmth of amber and a dark woody character reminiscent of patchouli. ” We also now offer the extraordinary Clearwood PRISMA range, launched by Firmenich in 2024. Contains 0.05% of Tocopherol as a preservative.

missing.title: Clearwood® PRISMA
missing.description: Clearwood® PRISMA is an exciting 2024 release from Firmenich. It is previously a captive 100% natural (ISO 9235) and sustainable biotech product and marks the ten year anniversary of Clearwood , one of the company's most iconic products. We are excited to be the first retailer to offer this marvel. Clearwood® PRISMA boasts an astounding 90–99% patchoulol content and so, in pure form, it is solid (similar to candle wax) but at certain warmer temperatures it may be liquid. Firmenich also makes this product at 50% blended in Hedione® (product code 970961) due to the performance boost found in the their laboratory tests and as a prevention against solidification; we certainly concur with their master-perfumers and scientists — the Hedione Clearwood blend is a revelation. However, for those customers who prefer it, we also offer Clearwood PRISMA at 50% in odourless IPM. In Firmenich's own words: “Clearwood® Prisma, at low dosage, adds a sheer touch, harmonizing with a nuanced patchouli background. Compared to Clearwood® and Patchouli Indonesia , it reigns with sheer brilliance, keeping the citrusy sparkling notes and the spicy ones, while its counterparts, though voluminous, seem to veil the citrus and spice in their embrace. Clearwood® Prisma gives a new chypre-like vibe.” Clearwood® PRISMA blends with classic Clearwood®, Iso E Super and other light wood materials and can be used as a one for one replacer for natural patchouli oil. Use it in traces up to overdose. Undiluted Clearwood® PRISMA can serve as a stand in for the marvellous 99% pure Patchoulol Crystals that we also stock. From an olfactive perspective, Clearwood PRISMA is more intensely patchouli than the non-PRISMA product. It is still cleaner than classic patchouli oils but it has far more interesting facets than traditional Clearwood.

missing.title: Clonal™
missing.description: Clonal (Dodecane Nitrile) is a powerful citrus top note with intensely metallic nuances. It is perfect for boosting the sparkle on a cologne or fougere or for creating a modern and exciting fragrance with sci-fi characteristics. Be careful of this one! It's definitely strong and a little goes a long way. We recommend diluting it to 1% or 0.1% in DPG before using it.

missing.title: Cocoa Hexenal
missing.description: Cocoa Hexenal captures dark chocolate's bitter edge rather than its sweetness—think roasted cocoa nibs and nutshells, not milk chocolate bars. The aldehydic opening brings sharpness that transitions into warm, brown, nutty tones. Green vegetative hints recall cocoa pods on the tree while subtle honey and mocha facets round out the profile. This material forms the backbone of authentic chocolate accords where pyrazines alone fall short. Work it into gourmand compositions at 2-8% of your concentrate for recognisable cocoa impact, or use traces below 1% to add subtle brown richness to orientals and ambers. It brings unexpected depth to tobacco reconstructions and enhances hazelnut and praline effects without obvious chocolate character. Handle Cocoa Hexenal with precision—its power demands restraint but rewards careful dosing. Combine it with vanillin and tonka for classic chocolate effects, or pair with patchouli and labdanum for dark, resinous warmth. Layer it with coffee materials in masculine fragrances or work it alongside Honey Supreme where its aldehydic bite prevents cloying sweetness.

missing.title: Coffee Pentenolone
missing.description: Coffee pentenolone (ethyl cyclopentenolone) delivers a dark, complex sweetness that goes well beyond simple caramel. Coffee, rum, whiskey, and brown sugar notes intertwine with a subtle smokiness that gives it depth. Where cyclotene (methyl cyclopentenolone) gives you clean maple-syrup sweetness, this material is darker, more brooding, and more layered — think burnt toffee rather than fresh syrup. The potency is extreme. Work from a pre-diluted stock (the material is supplied at 50% in propylene glycol for this reason). At proper dosage — parts per million — it contributes a warm, gourmand sweetness that smells expensive and authentic. Overdose quickly turns compositions cloying and unrecognisable. Vanillin and tonka bean absolute bring out the caramel side. Coffee CO2 and tobacco absolute amplify the roasted facets. In leather accords a trace contributes a subtle sweet-smoky dimension. Labdanum and benzoin provide a balsamic foundation for its dark warmth to rest upon.

missing.title: Coranol
missing.description: Walking a tightrope between the scent of linalool and coriander, Coranol is a wonderful floral fresh heart note that is practically indispensable in modern perfumes. Traces added freshness, overdoses add a much-loved modern character. Coranol is the warm blow of tropical holiday air. On first sniff it is obvious why this is such a beloved aroma chemical. In the words of Perfumery: Techniques in Evolution (a series of articles published in Perfumer and Flavorist magazine): “[Coranol is o]ne of the most important chemicals used today. Coranol has an extremely fresh, floral, somewhat vibrant rosy-metallic note that is really almost impossible to replace. It combines exceptionally well with Dihydromyrcenol … imparting to every fragrance its freshness, its strength and its diffusion. It blends exceptionally well with citrus, florals, woody, spicy and musky notes and harmonises with green-metalic products such as Stemone, Paradisamide, Labienoxime or Buccoxime.” Coranol is found in Aventus at around 2%, 3.5% in 1 Million Elixir , 3.5% in 212 Men Aqua by Carolina Herrera, 2% in Aqua di Gio Profondo , 2.7% in Aqua Pour Homme by Bulgari, and a whopping 6.5% in Light Blue by Dolce and Gabbana.

missing.title: Corinal® 184008B
missing.description: Corinal® 184008 B is an intense leather base featured prominently in such fragrances as Sublime by Jean Kerleo for Patou, a huge 5% in Habit Rouge (1965) by Jean-Paul Guerlain for Guerlain, and in a lesser amount in Vetiver (2000) by the same. It was also used in the more recent 2015 Pierre Guillaume scent Metal Hurlant . Corinal blends exceptionally well with Lavender and Lavandin, Vertofix Coeur , Aerolide ®, Styrax Resinoid , and all patchouli oils.

missing.title: Corps Racine
missing.description: The most intense and longest lasting green chemical in the perfumer's arsenal, Corps Racine has a powerful note of crisp freshly shelled peas, green peppers and the bitter green of snapped twigs. Corps Racine is a powerful, green pyridine with unparalleled strength and persistence, lasting months longer than alpha-santalol. Like citronitrile, it extends the impact of volatile notes without diminishing them. Essential for any perfumer's toolkit, it blends beautifully with Verdantol™ and all of our luxurious muguet bases . Due to its unbelievable power, we are offering this at 1% diluted in dipropylene glycol (DPG) or pure for those with the need for it. Note, however, that even at 1% this is incredibly strong and we recommend further dilution to at least 0.1% in the carrier of your choice.

missing.title: Coumarone
missing.description: Incredibly powerful, coumarone is a distinctly tonka / coumarin like synthetic with a very powerful nuance of orange blossoms. With the very high restrictions on methyl naphthyl ketone (oranger crystals) and coumarin itself, coumarone really comes into its own as a booster for both those materials. Coumarone can also be used to create interesting fragrances that present tonka beans and orange blossoms in whole new light. A wonderful material that all perfumers should have in their organ.

missing.title: Cyclemax™
missing.description: Cyclemax opens with an unmistakable transparency—a clean, dewy floralcy that sits somewhere between lily of the valley and cyclamen. What sets it apart is a crisp, juicy melon-rind facet that feels modern and aquatic rather than powdery or old-fashioned. A subtle metallic-green edge, inherited from its cuminyl heritage, gives it the naturalistic snap of freshly snipped flower stems. This material has become essential in the post-Lilial era, offering similar diffusive power without the regulatory concerns that ended its predecessor's reign. Use it to build the transparent backbone of muguet soliflores, or add it at trace levels to citrus accords where it amplifies juiciness and extends perceived freshness deep into the heart. It bridges heavier florals like Florol with sparkling top notes, acting as the engine that propels a composition outward.

missing.title: Cyclohexyl Ethyl Alcohol
missing.description: Cyclohexyl Ethyl Alcohol greets you with clean, waxy floral freshness — cool and dewy, like morning moisture on peony petals. Lily and rose facets emerge alongside a green, faintly minty undertone. The overall impression is soft, transparent, and unmistakably floral. This is Phenylethyl Alcohol's cooler, waxier cousin — translucent where PEA is warm and rosy. That icy quality makes it ideal for dewy peony and lily-of-the-valley accords that need crisp, clean radiance. Blend with hydroxycitronellal, linalool, and hedione for sheer white florals. Use Cyclohexyl Ethyl Alcohol freely — it tolerates concentrations from traces to high doses without distortion. Soap, shampoo, and detergent bases that destroy other florals leave this one intact. Add it to rose or gardenia for a cool, waxy transparency that lifts the entire heart.

missing.title: Cyclopidene
missing.description: Cyclopidene masterfully delivers a "salicylate/cresyl harmony" within a single molecule. This provides radiant, solar warmth whilst contributing naturalistic animalic depth. Perfumers utilise this powerful aroma chemical primarily as a modifier at 0.1-0.5% to create vibrant, multifaceted floral accords. Use Cyclopidene at trace levels for authentic white floral impact. Combine with hedione to amplify diffusion and salicylates to enhance solar facets. Apply sparingly—its potency easily dominates compositions when overdosed. This material works effectively as a strategic replacer for restricted cresyl derivatives in modern formulations. Beyond traditional floral applications, Cyclopidene finds remarkable utility in masculine fougères where its cresylic facet adds unexpected depth at 0.05%. In functional fragrances, it survives harsh detergent environments whilst maintaining radiance on wet fabrics. When combined with ylang-ylang oil, Cyclopidene acts as a powerful booster, enhancing the natural characteristics of the oil, increasing its diffusion, and adding its unique solar and lactonic complexity. This synergy compensates for IFRA restrictions on ylang by amplifying its presence at lower concentrations—use 0.2% Cyclopidene to double the perceived ylang impact without exceeding regulatory limits. Synergies: Ylang-ylang oil, Phenyl Ethyl Alcohol, Hedione®, Cis-3-Hexenyl Salicylate, Benzyl Salicylate, para-Cresyl Acetate, Indole, Citronellol.

missing.title: Cycloverdyl Propionate
missing.description: Cycloverdyl propionate opens with a soft, sweet floral-herbal character that sits somewhere between jasmine and fresh basil. A gentle anise undertone weaves through the heart, giving it unexpected depth. Green-woody facets round out the base, fruity and oily rather than sharp. This is the softer, longer-lasting cousin of Verdyl Acetate (Jasmacyclene) — where the acetate is bright and forcefully green, the propionate trades sharpness for refined herbal-floral warmth. It adds depth to jasmine and green-floral accords without dominating. Fougères and fresh compositions benefit from its sweet herbal backbone. Blend it with Hedione and benzyl acetate for a herbal-jasmine heart, or with dihydromyrcenol and coumarin for a green fougère. At 144 hours on a strip, tenacity is exceptional for such a gentle material. It works from traces up to 8% without turning aggressive. It is important to note that this material is also often referred to simply as Verdyl Propionate. They are the same thing.

missing.title: Cyclozonal
missing.description: Cyclozonal opens with a sharp, metallic freshness that captures the scent of air after rain - clean, cool, and almost silvery. This aldehyde combines ozonic transparency with subtle floral nuances, creating an impression of dewy lily-of-the-valley blooming in crisp mountain air. Its unique character bridges the gap between high-impact marine notes and sophisticated modern florals. This material is a powerful booster for citrus accords — even small additions amplify bergamot, lemon, and grapefruit with crystalline lift. It excels in fougères and colognes where you need that clean, just-showered effect. Its stability across all classical applications makes it equally valuable in functional products. Use Cyclozonal when you need to cut through heavy base odours in functional products or when building contemporary fougères that demand crisp, clean openings. It pairs brilliantly with citrus oils, aldehydes, and woody materials like vetiver. Its metallic-ozonic facets bring remarkable diffusion and a sense of spaciousness to dense compositions.

missing.title: Damascol 4
missing.description: Damascol opens with a distinct peppery bite before revealing a deep, dark rose absolute character underneath. The overall effect is rounded and warm rather than bright, with woody undertones and subtle fruity facets. A faint iris-like powderiness lingers in the drydown. Use this to extend and darken rose accords where you want depth rather than brightness. It stretches rose absolute beautifully, adding spicy warmth without shifting the floral identity. In geranium compositions it works as a rich modifier that adds sophistication. Start at low doses and build up, as the pepper note can dominate unexpectedly at higher levels. Combine with alpha-damascone and damascenone for a complete dark rose palette. It pairs particularly well with black pepper, vetiver, and cedar for spicy-woody floral structures.

missing.title: Dartanol®
missing.description: Dartanol is the highest quality Laevo form of Bacdanol. It is the same chemical but the purest and finest version. It can be used one for one in place of Bacdanol for a richer and more cosmetic result. Blends of Dartanol with Polysantol and Firsantol are supreme but significantly more Dartanol can be used in a fragrance because a) it is not restricted by IFRA, and b) it is less powerful than the others. But despite that, you should not be fooled into thinking Dartanol is not a powerful and rich sandalwood chemical. It is, in fact, one of the finest substitutes for natural sandalwood in chemical form and a simple combination of Dartanol with Ebanol is a truly classic combo. Perfumery: Techniques in Evolution (a series of articles published in Perfumer and Flavorist magazine) sings the praises of this material thus: “[Dartanol] is better than Bacdanol. It is similar but more beautiful, more radiant, possessing a more natural sandalwood character. It is also more diffusive. I believe [Dartanol] will slowly replace Bacdanol because, although similar, it is both comparably priced and livelier. The material’s uses are similar to those of Bacdanol.” For more information on Sandalwood aromatics, see our Sandalwood Synthetics Primer .

missing.title: Datilat
missing.description: Datilat smells like a bowl of dried fruit: figs, dates, raisins and prunes, waxy and dense, with a brandy-like warmth rising off them. Behind the sweetness sits a greener fig-leaf facet that stops it turning sticky. Neat it can seem slightly plasticky; once diluted, the fruit comes sharply into focus. Use it for any dried-fruit or boozy effect. It gives fig accords their fruit, deepens oriental bases with date and raisin, and supplies the raisin character that makes a cognac accord read true. In florals a trace adds a fruity twist and underlines the plummy side of the damascones. For a fig theme, balance it with green leaf notes and creamy peach materials. For dates or plums, pair it with davana and beta-damascone ; for cognac, add rum ether and a touch of ethyl crotonate. In an oud composition it builds the boozy, raisiny sweetness of a good aged spirit.

missing.title: Delphol HC
missing.description: Delphol HC opens with green jasmine freshness — clean, airy, and immediately reminiscent of magnolia blossom. A tea-like quality adds translucent brightness. Beneath that, delicate peach fruitiness and an earthy warmth recall the celery-seed facet of its cousin cis-jasmone. This dsm-firmenich creation belongs to the Hedione family — a by-product of methyl jasmonate synthesis. At trace levels in fine fragrance, it adds volume and body to white floral accords. Push it higher in functional bases for convincing celery-seed and exotic fruity effects. Pair Delphol HC with hedione and benzyl acetate for luminous jasmine hearts. Its 48-hour tenacity on blotter gives your magnolia and tea accords lasting presence in the drydown. Exceptional chemical stability across all bases — including laundry and cleaning products — makes it a true workhorse.

missing.title: Delphone
missing.description: Delphone hits the nose with immediate jasmine power — diffusive, complex, and unmistakably floral. A celery-seed spiciness adds unexpected bite. Coconut-lactonic warmth and an oily green-herbal quality round out the profile, making this far more interesting than a simple jasmine substitute. Born as a by-product of Hedione synthesis, Delphone shares the jasmonate family's gift for radiance. It functions primarily as a white floral booster — even at trace levels it adds volume, body, and diffusion to floral accords. The lactonic facet gives it surprising versatility in fruity compositions built around peach and mango. Use Delphone sparingly in fine fragrance — it is powerful enough to dominate at anything above trace levels. Blend with hedione and methyl dihydrojasmonate for layered jasmine complexity. Its 16-hour tenacity anchors floral hearts effectively, though it works best paired with longer-lasting base materials.

missing.title: Diethyl Hexyl Adipate
missing.description: Diethyl hexyl adipate is not a fragrance material — it is a tool. This colourless, odourless liquid serves as a neutral carrier and diluent for concentrated aroma chemicals and fragrance oils. Its complete lack of smell means it dilutes without distorting, letting your materials express themselves cleanly. The main application is in candle and wax fragrance work. Diethyl hexyl adipate is compatible with waxes, does not block wicks, and is non-flammable — solving three common problems at once. It allows you to achieve higher fragrance loads in candle formulations without the flash-point issues that alcohol-based solvents create. It also works as a co-solvent for rich, heavy fragrance oils that need thinning. Beyond candles, use it to dilute potent aroma chemicals for easier handling, or as an emollient carrier in skin-safe fragrance balms and lotions. It is universally compatible with fragrance materials and leaves no residual odour. Think of it as the perfumer's equivalent of a clean glass — it holds whatever you pour into it without adding anything of its own.

missing.title: Diethyl Tartrate (DET)
missing.description: Diethyl Tartrate opens with barely-there character—vinous, faintly fruity, and pleasantly neutral. Unlike commodity solvents that contribute nothing to your composition, DET adds subtle wine-like body and a caramellic warmth that supports rather than suppresses. This is living space, not dead space. Derived from tartaric acid—the compound that gives wine its structure—DET shares chemical lineage with grapes and cognac. This makes it the solvent of choice for vintner-style accords where authenticity matters. Use it to add mouthfeel and viscosity to brandy, cognac, and wine notes; pair it with Brandy CO2 for boozy compositions that feel genuinely alcoholic rather than synthetically fruity. The subtle polarity helps sustain volatile top notes that standard solvents would flatten. Use Diethyl Tartrate as a carrier for precious floral absolutes—rose, osmanthus, boronia—where DPG might mute the sparkling top notes you paid premium prices for. It excels at dissolving difficult crystalline materials like vanillins and synthetic musks, providing a warm, non-chemical solvent profile that vintage perfumers appreciated. Note: DET is polar, making it excellent for absolutes and polar crystals but less suitable for waxy citrus oils.

missing.title: Dihydro Gamma Ionone
missing.description: Both the finest and most noble member of the family, Dihydro Gamma Ionone is found naturally in tincture of ambergris to which it contributes a refined tobacco quality. This elegant aromachemical is complex, rich and extremely nuanced. Less fruity and earthy than Dihydro Ionone Beta, and more intense and warm than Dihydro Ionone Alpha, this is a first choice material that all perfumers should have in their organ. Dihydro Ionone Gamma blends exceedingly well with Irisone® Alpha , Isoraldeine® Cetone Alpha , Iralia® , Iraldeine Delta and Dihydroactinidiolide in which it accentuates the delicate tea and tobacco qualities. We also stock Dihydro Alpha Ionone and Dihydro Beta Ionone .

missing.title: Dihydroactinidiolide
missing.description: Dihydroactinidiolide (also known as musk coumarin) is a wonderful long-lasting lactone found naturally in black tea, tobacco, fenugreek, and in the scent glands of the red fox. It also functions as a pheremone in red fire ants and certain fruit flies. A very uncommon musk, dihydroactinidiolide is a unique material that enhances and blends with tea chemicals and accords and harmonises wonderfully with tobacco, coumarin and tonka materials. It also has delicate nuances of spices, peach and medjool dates.

missing.title: Dihydroambrate
missing.description: Dihydroambrate opens with a warm, rounded woody-amber impression — not sharp, not sweet, just quietly rich. There is a subtle ambrette-like quality in the heart, a gentle seed-musk warmth that makes the material feel organic and skin-close. Dry cedar facets give it structure without making it smell specifically like cedarwood. Givaudan designed this to do one thing extremely well: add richness and balance. Drop it into a composition and everything gets warmer, fuller, more three-dimensional. It does not impose its own character on your blend — instead it amplifies what is already there, smoothing rough transitions between notes and giving thin compositions genuine body. It works at concentrations up to several percent without becoming intrusive. Its stability is remarkable. Dihydroambrate survives virtually every functional base — fabric softeners, detergents, soap, shampoo — which made it a staple in consumer products. But its real beauty shows in fine fragrance, where its quiet woody-amber warmth provides the kind of invisible foundation that makes everything above it smell more expensive. Pair it with Ambroxan for a modern amber, or use it under sandalwood materials for added depth and projection.

missing.title: Dihydroanethol
missing.description: Dihydroanethole is anethole's softer sibling. The sharp crystalline bite that makes pure anethole so assertive has been smoothed away. What remains is a rounder anise character: warm black liquorice, sweet fennel, a hint of sassafras root. It smells like the memory of anise rather than anise itself. That softness is the reason to stock it alongside anethole. Where anethole dominates and announces itself, dihydroanethole blends. It slides into oriental bases and fougères without elbowing other materials aside. Use it beneath lavender and coumarin in a fougère for herbaceous sweetness that reads as vintage and complex. In orientals, it provides the same sweet-spicy warmth that absinthe brings to a classic Guerlain structure. It is also more stable than anethole in certain formulation conditions — less prone to oxidation. If you need anise character in a product with a long shelf life, dihydroanethole is the safer choice. It works well with star anise oil, tarragon, basil, and coumarin.

missing.title: Dihydrolinalool
missing.description: Dihydrolinalool opens with an airy, clean floral sweetness that immediately signals freshness. You'll detect subtle blueberry and green-weedy undertones alongside its primary lily-of-the-valley character. This remarkably stable material bridges citrus top notes to floral hearts with exceptional grace. In compositions, dihydrolinalool serves as both harmoniser and problem-solver. Its chemical resilience allows fresh floral character to survive harsh detergent bases where natural linalool would degrade. Combine it with dihydromyrcenol and white musks to create the iconic "clean laundry" accord that defines modern fabric care fragrances. Use dihydrolinalool at 20-30% in white floral hearts for diffusive freshness. Partner it with hedione for transparent jasmine effects or layer with lilial substitutes for amplified muguet. In functional fragrances, deploy it generously—its stability masks base malodours whilst contributing pleasant floralcy that persists through product use.

missing.title: Dihydromyrcenol
missing.description: A perfumery critic one said this chemical was "lavender on steroids" and while there is much merit to such an idea, Dihydromyrcenol is so much more. It is such an easy material to blend that it can't simply be pigeonholed into the lavender family. Dihydromyrcenol in overdose is the classic material for masculine top notes but in small amounts it adds a modern and very inimitable twist to feminine top notes as evidenced in Gabrielle by Chanel and myriad other scents. Dihydromyrcenol is almost as indispensable as a high quality Bergamot FCF and Linalool these days. A 1:1 ratio with the best Lavender oil you can buy is beautiful and a supremely addictive synergy is created when the same is modified with a touch of Allyl Amyl Glycolate. Ours is a fine quality from Ventos.

missing.title: Dihydromyrcenyl Acetate
missing.description: Dihydromyrcenyl Acetate opens with a juicy bergamot character softened by lavender undertones. Where its parent alcohol Dihydromyrcenol can feel sharp and metallic, the acetate ester reads sweeter, rounder, and more elegant. You get that same citrus-cologne sparkle but wrapped in a velvety fruitiness that feels more refined and versatile. This material bridges the gap between aggressive top notes and the floral heart of your composition. Its tertiary ester structure gives it remarkable stability in alkaline environments where natural citrus oils and standard esters like Linalyl Acetate rapidly degrade. Reach for it when you need lasting citrus freshness in soaps, detergents, and household products where other citruses fail miserably. Blend it alongside Dihydromyrcenol to temper the alcohol's harshness while extending its citrus-lavender signature. It pairs beautifully with Linalyl Acetate for synthetic bergamot accords and with Allyl Amyl Glycolate for modern aromatic-fruity effects. Use it in lime fragrances to support and extend fleeting citrus top notes into the heart.

missing.title: Dihydrorose Oxide
missing.description: Dihydrorose oxide captures the whole rose experience—not just petals but the green calyx, thorny stems and morning dew. This piercing, vibrating quality cuts through heavy florals with its characteristic metallic sharpness. You'll find it creates that elusive "living rose" quality missing from traditional rose absolutes. In fine fragrance, combine it with phenylethyl alcohol and citronellol at 0.1-0.5% for photorealistic roses. For exotic fruits, it's your secret weapon—essential for authentic lychee accords and adding the bitter green skin note to mango compositions. Use dihydrorose oxide to bridge citrus tops with floral hearts, exploiting its grapefruit nuance. Its exceptional diffusion ensures immediate impact whilst the metallic facet provides modern edge. Apply it sparingly in masculine fougères with dihydromyrcenol for that steely urban freshness. Dihydrorose Oxide vs Rose Oxide Think of rose oxide as the loud, confident sibling—sharp, penetrating, and impossible to ignore even at trace levels. It announces itself with brilliant green-metallic freshness that can dominate a composition. Dihydrorose oxide is the gentler version: same family character but softer, rounder, and far more forgiving. Where rose oxide demands careful handling lest it overwhelm everything around it, dihydrorose oxide blends in politely while still contributing that distinctive green-geranium-rose signature. Use rose oxide when you want a material that punches above its weight; reach for dihydrorose oxide when you want the effect without the drama.

missing.title: Dimethyl Anthranilate Natural 50% TEC
missing.description: Also known as Methyl N Methylanthranilate, Dimethyl Anthranilate is a key component of mandarin oil (from which this product is isolated). It has a wonderfully grape-like and dusty quality which makes it very useful for the recreation of fruit and floral notes. Unlike its counterpart Methyl Anthranilate, this product won't form Schiff bases with aldehydes and is far less likely to cause discolouration. The caveat, however, is that it has a very low maximum IFRA use of 0.1%. Due to DEA restrictions, we sell this product at 50% diluted in natural Triethyl Citrate, maintaining its 100% natural status. Odour profile: neroli, grape, powdery, musty, wine, phenolic.

missing.title: Dimethyl Benzyl Carbinol
missing.description: Dimethyl benzyl carbinol (DMBC) is a key material in fine fragrance, valued for its rosy character and exceptional diffusion. It bridges accords seamlessly, ensuring structural integrity and enhancing floral compositions throughout the dry-down phase. DMBC’s versatility makes it essential in modern perfumery. Its warm, inviting profile refines mainstream fragrances, elevating them to luxury status. At optimal dilutions, it blends effortlessly, enhancing compositions with a signature depth and technical precision.

missing.title: Dimethyl Cyclormol
missing.description: Dimethyl Cyclormol opens with a cool diffusive freshness that has immediate impact. Beneath this sits an unmistakable fungal-mushroom character—damp cellar floors, freshly picked button mushrooms, the underside of forest logs after rain. The woody backbone is dry and rather neutral — neither creamy nor pencil-like. Pair this interesting material with Veramoss to build convincing modern moss accords that boost (or sidestepentirely) IFRA-restricted oakmoss or treemoss. In florals like hyacinth, muguet, or mimosa, a trace adds a realistic "growing in soil" texture. Oriental and leather bases benefit from its camphoraceous cut because of its ability to aerate heavy labdanum and amber resins, preventing cloying sweetness.

missing.title: Dimethyl Hydroquinone
missing.description: This material opens with intensely sweet, sharp-green notes reminiscent of crushed hyacinth stems and fresh fennel. Use it in traces to create the classic "foin coupé" (mown hay) accord when combined with coumarin. Its remarkable tenacity despite low molecular weight makes it invaluable for bridging top to base notes. The powerful herbaceous character transforms floral compositions, particularly white florals where naturalness proves elusive. In hyacinth reconstructions, this material provides the essential sweet-green foundation that defines the flower's character. Tobacco and oriental bases benefit from its warm, nutty facets that add sophisticated aromatic dimension without overwhelming sweetness. Surprisingly this material is naturally found in violet flowers. Traces can be useful in constructing a complex and true-to-life violet accord.

missing.title: Dimetol®
missing.description: Dimetol AKA Freesia Heptanol is used in the same way as dihydromyrcenol but for some reason it has never attracted quite the same superstar level of appeal despite being universally liked. Nevertheless it has still found fairly wide use in gentlemen's scents such as the original Polo Green , Pour Lui by Oscar de la Renta, Van Cleef and Arpels for Men and Paco Rabanne . This material has a natural brightness reminiscent of lime and lemon zest, making it suitable for modern, fresh, and clean compositions. Its unique character contributes a green sparkle and lively diffusivity to the top and heart notes of a fragrance.

missing.title: Dimyrcetol
missing.description: Dimyrcetol is IFF's proprietary blend of dihydromyrcenyl formate and dihydromyrcenol. The formate is the key component, and it gives Dimyrcetol a fresh, citrus-lime character with herbal and marine facets that broaden the profile beyond straightforward citrus. This is a rare material that most perfumers will not have encountered. Strip life is modest — under three hours — but that number tells only part of the story. On skin and in the air, Dimyrcetol projects powerfully, with a cool, clean diffusion that carries well beyond what the blotter suggests. That projection is its most distinctive quality. Bergamot and linalool complement the citrus side naturally. Lavender brings out the cologne character. Hedione, Iso E Super, and white musks all support it in modern accords, while ambroxan in the base adds amber warmth. Dimyrcetol and dihydromyrcenol are distinct materials that are easily confused. Dihydromyrcenol is the well-known metallic-lime freshness found in Davidoff Cool Water and countless masculine fragrances. Dimyrcetol is this IFF blend — primarily dihydromyrcenyl formate with some dihydromyrcenol — offering a rounder, more herbal-marine profile with greater projection but shorter blotter life. We also stock Dihydromyrcenyl Acetate .

missing.title: Diphenyl Oxide
missing.description: Diphenyl oxide has a geranium-like odour with green, leafy and metallic facets, and nuances of rose and powder. This material provides exceptional diffusion and can dramatically extend the persistence of volatile citrus components. Its geranium-like character transforms conventional rose accords into strikingly modern blends. Incorporate diphenyl oxide at low concentrations, around 1%, to avoid harshness. Combine with classic florals like lindenol ™ (terpineol) and geranyl acetate , or green notes like citral , for balanced blends. Its metallic character brings a modern edge, but requires careful handling in fragrance creation.

missing.title: Dipropylene Glycol (DPG)
missing.description: Dipropylene Glycol (DPG) is the most common diluent and solubiliser in perfumery today. It is sometimes used to pad out a formula (bringing its total to 1,000 for uniformity) and it can offer some minor benefits as a fixative, but an intelligent combination of musks is usually a better option for that purpose. DPG is almost odourless — in general it has a very faint almost alcohol-like odour that some only some people can perceive. Unlike alcohol, however, it is non-flammable having a closed cup flash point of 138°C (280°F). It has a higher viscosity than water. Some fragrances contain very large amounts of DPG to lower their cost or even their strength as we see in Baccarat Rouge 540 which uses nearly 50% in the finished formula for Eau de Parfum (compared to almost none in the Extrait). DPG is not readily soluble in fixed oils such as Fractionated Coconut Oil and can cause turbidity. If you are working with fixed oils a better option is ethanol or IPM (MIP). When DPG passes its expiry (usually after three or four years) it can develop an unpleasant bready-sour note. This can make it unsuitable for some long-term dilution needs. TEC, DEP and IPM are potential alternative options for those cases. NOTE: This must not be used in food or vape juices. Dipropylene Glycol is not a safe alternative to Propylene Glycol. Do not consume.

missing.title: Dreamwood™ 184270B
missing.description: From Firmenich: “Dreamwood Base takes its inspiration from the iconic Mysore Sandalwood, also known as the “royal tree” in the Mysore district of Karnataka, India. Created around Dreamwood, our latest breakthrough captive ingredient from white biotechnology, Dreamwood Base is designed for pure performance. It brings naturality and natural effect, impressive tenacity, warmth and creaminess to any fragrance. The traditional woody creamy warms of sandalwood is also brought to light by our best sandalwood molecules, some of which captive.” Boost the otherwise mild Dreamwood with our rich and powerful Sandexol ® base. Dreamwood also blends well anywhere Sandalwood is used.

missing.title: Dulcinyl
missing.description: You'll recognise this as raspberry preserves spread on warm brioche. The heliotrope character adds powdery depth, while cassie and mimosa undertones bring sophisticated floral complexity. This is sweetness done elegantly, never cloying despite its intensity. This IFF molecule (also known as heliotropyl acetone) bridges the gap between fruity and floral families with remarkable grace. The 400-hour substantivity on blotter makes it one of the longest-lasting berry materials available, ensuring your raspberry effect persists well into the drydown. Use it in jasmine compositions where its fruity juiciness adds the realistic touch that separates fine florals from generic sweetness. Work with Dulcinyl at up to 15% of your concentrate, though lower doses often suffice given its medium strength. The recrystallised form handles easily despite being a solid at room temperature. Blend with raspberry ketone, ionones, vanillin, and jasmine absolutes for complex fruity-floral effects.

missing.title: Dupical
missing.description: Dupical is an incredibly powerful and transparent muguet aldehyde. It carries the fresh, green, slightly watery character of lily-of-the-valley petals without the heavy indolic side. Underneath the floral top sits a light marine-aldehydic quality that keeps the whole thing airy. But be warned: a trace is very perceptible. This is one of the most overpowering lily chemicals you'll experience. Use it to reinforce muguet accords where Lilial, Lyral or Florol feel too heavy or too sweet. A small amount gives lift and watery freshness to fresh floral compositions, cologne structures and marine-floral accords. It also pulls back the waxy thickness of hydroxycitronellal. Pair with Lyral , Florol and hydroxycitronellal to build a lily-of-the-valley heart, or use against citrus and green notes in cologne tops. A trace in aquatic accords reinforces the watery character. Dose it low — overdose flattens subtler materials around it. Something important to note with Dupical is that it can be perceived as a very dense note — so while it does have a watery odour quality, it benefits from opening up with an ozonic or freshie like floralozone . This is a material that, in traces, can represent your entire muguet note, preventing the need for bulk additions of the classics like florol and hydroxycitronellal.

missing.title: Dynascone
missing.description: Dynascone hits with astonishing power—this is one of perfumery's most diffusive materials. The green-galbanum character dominates, but a juicy pineapple fruitiness weaves through alongside delicate hyacinth floral notes. It is pungent but, when properly controlled, reminiscent of ripe pineapple with green pepper heat. Use Dynascone in traces only—even at 10% dilution, it demands respect. Fine fragrance concentrations run 0.04% to 0.1%, while functional products tolerate slightly more. It pairs beautifully with cis-3-hexenol , and galbanum oil . The 348-hour substantivity ensures your green note persists through to drydown. Dynascone vs Neobutenone Alpha While sharing the same CAS number, these materials differ meaningfully in character. Dynascone delivers pronounced pineapple fruitiness alongside its galbanum character—juicy, pungent, and somewhat tropical. Neobutenone Alpha represents the purer alpha isomer, which is greener, less fruity, and closer to natural galbanum in character. Neobutenone Alpha is the "the Paradisone of green materials" and it is vastly superior for achieving authentic green effects. It features in fragrances like Creed Aventus, where traces create that inimitable green-fruity top note. If you want prominent pineapple-galbanum punch, choose Dynascone; if you want cleaner, more naturalistic greenness, Neobutenone Alpha is the better choice.

missing.title: Ebanol
missing.description: Ebanol opens with an intense sandalwood-musk fusion that's immediately recognisable for its creamy, almost edible quality. This isn't just woody—it's rich and buttery with a distinctive maple syrup sweetness. The material delivers exceptional depth and volume to woody accords while maintaining remarkable stability across pH ranges. You'll find Ebanol transforms simple woody structures into complex, multidimensional bases. Its musky character amplifies when combined with macrocyclic musks, creating exponential warmth and diffusion. In floral compositions, particularly jasmine and lily-of-the-valley, it provides the tenacious backbone these delicate notes need. The material excels at rounding sharp edges in fruity accords while contributing its signature creamy texture. Combine with Javanol for radiant sparkle or layer with Sandalore for fuller dimensionality. Its 400-hour tenacity on blotter makes it indispensable for extending top note longevity—perfect for functional fragrances requiring exceptional substantivity.

missing.title: Elemol ex Elemi
missing.description: Elemi is a lovely fresh citrusy resin, and at its heart is pure Elemol. Elemol is to Elemi oil as Olibanol is to Frankincense and Amyrol is to Amyris Oil. Because Elemol is an isolate, it is a more refined form of the oil. Elemol has lovely nuances of antique wood, roses and citrus. For something akin to the wonderful Versailles candle of Cire Trudon (mimicking the scent of the polished wood floors of the Versailles Palace), Elemol would be a perfect starting point with Virginia Cedar Wood and enhancements from Honey Supreme and Birch Tar Oil . Elemol is a light fluid making it easy to use and is 100% natural so compliant with the various natural perfumery standards.

missing.title: Ethyl Safranate
missing.description: Ethyl Safranate is a powerful and diffusive fruity rose aroma chemical this is not exploited anywhere near as much as it should be. Where the rose ketones end, Ethyl Safranate begins. With no restriction at all from IFRA and a scent profile like a more characterful damascone delta meets damascone alpha, this material deserves to be front and centre in more contemporary fragrances. Blends with Persicol are sublime and exploit its fruity side. Its bashful minty side can be extended and enhanced with touches of Peppermint Oil “Black Mitcham”, or use it to add a sultry Saffron note to a damascone rich rose base. In vanillin base amber accords it can lend a wonderful gloss when dosed correctly. Ethyl Safranate is indispensable and shockingly addictive.

missing.title: Ethyl Tiglate
missing.description: This remarkable ester opens with an immediately recognisable tutti frutti burst that captivates from the first encounter. The sweet, juicy character mirrors the authentic complexity found in ripe strawberries and fresh apples. Its unique dual personality sets it apart from conventional fruity esters that often smell synthetic. The magic unfolds in its heart where warm caramel notes emerge, creating a cooked-fruit effect that transforms simple compositions into sophisticated gourmand accords. This facet makes it invaluable for baked apple creations, strawberry tart effects, and tropical fruit blends where depth matters. Your formulations gain the naturalistic complexity that distinguishes professional work from amateur attempts. Its most distinctive feature appears in the drydown—an earthy, green olive note that prevents the sweetness from becoming cloying. This unusual characteristic allows you to build fruit accords with remarkable realism. Use it to bridge the gap between bright top notes and substantial heart materials in both functional and fine fragrance applications.

missing.title: Ethyl Undecylenate
missing.description: Ethyl Undecylenate opens with waxy fruitiness — clean, soapy, and unexpectedly smooth. A creamy sweetness fills out the body. Warm cognac-like undertones sit beneath, lending unexpected depth and boozy richness to what first reads as a straightforward fruity ester. This is your secret weapon for gourmand accords — the cognac-wine character brings authenticity to rum, brandy, and dried fruit compositions. It also lifts creamy-soapy florals with its clean waxy facet. Blend with ethyl maltol and vanillin for rich boozy warmth, or with aldehydes for sophisticated soapiness. Use Ethyl Undecylenate at moderate levels — its fatty character dominates if overdosed. The waxy warmth is remarkable in amber and oriental bases. Its 20-hour tenacity on blotter gives lasting body to fruity and boozy accords that would otherwise fade too quickly.

missing.title: Exaltenone
missing.description: Exaltenone® is one of the classic synthetic musks, valued for its ability to enhance the diffusion, depth, and longevity of a fragrance. Some perfumers even consider it superior to muscone (and muscone laevo), the natural musk ketone found in deer musk. Traces are all you need to get a real boost but this can be an overdose musk. To compare this product (which is usually liquid at room temperature but can solidify) and the very similarly named Exaltone [ Cyclopentadecanone ] we can say that E xaltone is more powdery, natural, and elegant with a focus on fixative strength, whereas Exaltenone is more powerful, opaque, and animalic, offering a creamier and robust musk note. Their differences make them suitable for slightly different roles in perfumery, and choosing between them depends on the desired scent profile and budget. Because it is costly we are also offering it diluted to 10% in DPG. Note: Firmenich refers to this product as CAS 35720-57-1 but it is also commonly referred to by the CAS 14595-54-1. The two are the same. missing.title: Filbertone
missing.description: Wonderful for gourmand or woody scents, Filbertone (AKA filbert heptenone) naturally contributes to the odour of hazelnuts and is also a minor component of the scent of chocolate. Due to its astonishing power, we are offering this at 1% diluted in dipropylene glycol (DPG) but we also offer it pure for those who have need of it. Often mistaken as a flavouring, this chemical is a hidden gem in perfumery, creating remarkable accords when properly diluted. At just 0.1%, it delivers fresh, fruity, green, and nutty nuances, effortlessly boosting citrus and floral blends. Pair it with Tropathiane , Oxane, or Passifloran , and you’ll discover vibrant, near-addictive shades that defy easy description. Even the smallest amounts can work magic. Filbertone blends beautifully with Sandexol® , Ambrexol™ , Wild Cherry and Fleur de Cassie .

missing.title: Fir Balsam Oliffac
missing.description: Fir Balsam Oliffac opens with a rush of fresh pine-needle greenness that quickly unfolds into something far more complex. The resinous heart carries an unexpected jammy sweetness—think raspberry preserves meets forest sap - anchored by smoky, mossy undertones that evoke the damp forest floor. This isn't the sharp terpenic bite of raw needle oils; it's a noble, rounded woody character with exceptional tenacity. If you want to capture the scent of Christmas without messing around with thick balsams and astringent wood oils, this is the tool for you. You'll find this material indispensable for building authentic coniferous accords that need more than just green freshness. The jammy-fruity facet adds warmth and approachability to masculine fougères whilst the powerful balsamic backbone provides serious fixative strength in orientals and chypres. Pair it with lavender and oakmoss for classic barbershop structures, or push it into gourmand territory by emphasising its berry-sweet qualities with vanilla and tonka. Pair with geosmin for damp-forest earthiness, or layer with Douglas fir and Canadian fir needle oils for a complete coniferous accord. Evernyl and cedrol in the formula contribute mossy-woody persistence. This is incredibly synergistic with Artemal . What is an Oliffac? IFF Oliffacs are a range of proprietary bases. They are IFF’s own standardised reconstructions of recognisable natural notes and genre materials (e.g., balsams, fruits, woods, animalic themes), often built around IFF specialties/captives that you cannot source elsewhere.

missing.title: Firascone
missing.description: Firascone captures the dark, concentrated floralcy of red rose petals intertwined with berry-like fruitiness. This isn't fresh tea rose - it's rich, jammy, and voluptuous with an integrated saffron note that adds dry, spicy leather texture. Secondary apple and mint facets provide roundness and lift, preventing cloying sweetness whilst maintaining sophisticated depth. This material solves the damascone restriction problem elegantly. You can work with Firascone from traces to 1% in fine fragrance without regulatory anxiety, unlike its ketone cousins that require extreme dilution. Use it to boost small doses of restricted rose ketones, extending fruity-floral volume whilst staying compliant. Build jammy rose accords by combining Firascone with phenylethyl alcohol and geranium oil. Create sophisticated saffron profiles by pairing it with safraleine - Firascone provides the softer, floral-integrated saffron facet that commercial compositions demand. Its three-hour tenacity positions it perfectly as a heart note, bridging fruity top notes into woody-floral bases. Because of its price and strength, we are offering this pure or diluted to 10% in DPG.

missing.title: Firsantol®
missing.description: Firsantol is a superstar of the synthetic sandalwood family and yet it still tends to go unused when Javanol and Polysantol are available. Why this is I do not know as Firsantol really is one of the most diffusive and luminous wood chemicals; a trace goes a long way. Blends with Polysantol and Dartanol (Laevo Bacdanol) are outstanding. A good comparison of the various chemicals is that Javanol is the most powerful and truest to the scent of sandalwood oil, Polysantol (nearly as strong as Javanol) has more sweetness and is an excellent all-round blender, and Firsantol is slightly weaker in odour intensity but the most diffusive in power. The following blend creates a nice mixture in which Dartanol adds the creamy milkiness of natural sandalwood, polysantol adds fruity brightness and boosts radiance and firsantol adds diffusion and a drier woody note to prevent the accord from being overly lactonic or sweet. 45 Dartanol 35 Polysantol 20 Firsantol For use in a floral scent you might consider the following tweak where Javanol adds the link to the florals (especially good with rose) and further increases the power. 40 Dartanol 35 Polysantol 20 Firsantol 5 Javanol Non sandalwood materials that work well with Firsantol are Norlimbanol (normal and Dextro), Amyris Wood Oil, Cedramber, Ambrocenide, Myrrh Resinoid, Helvetolide and Habanolide.

missing.title: Fleur de Cuir
missing.description: Sublime is the only word that can be used to describe this incredible natural product of Payan Betrand. Fleur de Cuir is a co-distillation of fruity osmanthus flowers into a molecular distillation of finest cedarwood oil. The end result is the most perfect balance of floral and woody notes in a purely natural extraction. Even more extraorardinary is the wonderfully complex almost oud-like leather top note which is utterly addictive. This is truly one of the masterpieces of modern perfume science. Fleur de Cuir is best used boldly — up to 5.035% of your finished product for both IFRA 50 and IFRA 51. Fleur de Cuir is so good you can simply add florals and musk and sign off on a completed fragrance. The cost of this blend is extremely good, making liberal use possible. And while our 4g price is affordable for most, we are also offering 1g sample pricing because everyone needs to try this. Even if you think you don't need or want it, add a 1g sample to your cart.

missing.title: Fleuramone™
missing.description: Fleuramone opens with the unmistakable character of jasmine blossoms, delivering concentrated floral power reminiscent of cis-jasmone. Its lactonic quality creates creamy depth whilst green facets keep it fresh. The peach-like undertone emerges as it develops, maintaining freshness for hours. You'll find this ketone essential for building jasmine, honeysuckle and reseda accords where natural extracts prove prohibitive. It excels when combined with macrocyclic musks and undecanolide, creating sophisticated white floral compositions. Use it to add unexpected freshness to lavender and herbal fragrances where its rue note provides intrigue. Blend Fleuramone with hedione for radiant jasmine diffusion or combine with benzyl acetate and linalool to construct complete jasmine reconstructions. Pair with indole for authentic indolic jasmine character. This material bridges floral hearts with fruity top notes seamlessly.

missing.title: Floralate
missing.description: Despite its name, this is not a floral chemical. It's synonym, in fact, gives a better idea of what it is used for: Citrolate. Floralate is a dry bitter-fresh grapefruit material with (as is so often the case with aromatics of this type,) rhubarb nuances. It lacks the juiciness of citrus which makes it an interesting material to take a cologne in a very novel direction. It is long lasting so it is useful for extending citrus oil (not just grapefruit) into the heart of a perfume. A touch of Nootkatone and a judicious use of vetiver Haiti can further extend it into the dry down. For stewed fruit accords which may be on the sickly side, floralate can offer a much needed dryness.

missing.title: Floramat
missing.description: Floramat opens with intriguing spicy-woody warmth that immediately recalls damascone territory. The floral tendency adds softness without becoming overtly rosy, while green-herbal facets provide freshness. It delivers a complex, multifaceted character that bridges spicy, woody, and floral worlds beautifully. Floramat offers perfumers damascone-like effects at a fraction of the cost and significantly higher safe usage amount. Use it in floral compositions where you want rosy body with spicy warmth, or in fougères and lavender accords where its woody-herbal character supports aromatic notes. The material adds fruity accent to citrus blends and enhances rose-fruity compositions. At 92-hour substantivity, your spicy-floral effect persists well into the heart and drydown. Work with Floramat at up to 5% in your concentrate. It excels alongside actual damascones where it extends and supports their effect, or as a cost-effective alternative in functional applications. The material shows excellent stability across fragrance types including flower shop accords, spicy orientals, and woody compositions. Blend with rose materials, lavender, and woody notes for sophisticated modern florals.

missing.title: Florex®
missing.description: Florex (also known as Tonka Undecanone) is a powerful and long lasting lactone with a clearly coumarin note but nuances of wood and amber. In Firmenich's own words: “A very powerful and tenacious balsamic, Tonka-like note with a unique tangy quality. It has a sweet yet tart character that suggests tobacco and coconut with a green nuance. It can be used in all types of perfumes but has especially interesting effects in white florals, citrus and fruity accords.”

missing.title: Fraistone
missing.description: _*]:min-w-0 gap-3"> _*]:min-w-0 gap-3"> _*]:min-w-0 gap-3"> _*]:min-w-0 gap-3"> Fraistone delivers a tart, bright fruitiness that sits between strawberry, green apple, and plum. There is a subtle anisic quality underneath — a faint liquorice hint that adds complexity without dominating. The overall character is clean, fresh, and inviting, with none of the heaviness that many fruity materials carry. Use fraistone to add fruity sparkle to your floral compositions. It lifts rose, tuberose, jasmine, and orange blossom accords with a tart freshness that keeps them feeling modern. It also builds convincing strawberry and apple effects when combined with other fruity esters and lactones. Blend with rose absolute and damascone for a fruit-forward rose accord. Try it alongside neroli and hedione for a sparkling fruity-floral opening. Pair with lilac and peony bases where its tartness creates a convincing spring-fruit character. You can dose generously — it works well up to high levels in your concentrate.

missing.title: Framboise Base 184039 D
missing.description: Framboise smells exactly like a handful of ripe raspberries — the balance between sweet and tart is spot on. There is a juicy, jammy quality that feels convincingly natural, plus a subtle seedy greenness that stops it from tipping into candy territory. The overall effect is fresh and appetising. Firmenich originally recommended this base for modifying chypre compositions, and that remains one of its best applications. The fruity tartness lifts mossy-woody accords beautifully. It also works as a standalone berry note in fruity-floral compositions, where its finesse and stability give it an edge over cruder raspberry reconstructions. Pair Framboise with blackcurrant bud absolute for a rich dark-berry accord, or layer it with rose for a classic raspberry-rose combination. Beta-ionone adds realistic depth, while ethyl maltol can push the sweetness for gourmand work. This base rewards subtlety — a little goes a long way.

missing.title: Freskomenthe
missing.description: Mint has a habit of seeming medicinal (think toothpaste or cleaners) and almost entirely masculine, hence its common appearance in fougéres. But Freskomenthe bucks the trend with its woody and slightly fruity undertone (in the direction of black currant and berries). Its agrestic and woody facets make it more of a dried mint leaf material. It is longer lasting that peppermint oil and able to stand up to some fairly harsh aroma chemicals making it ideal for functional perfumery. Use it with lavender and dihydromyrcenol in place of peppermint oil. It combines exceedingly well with floralozone when you're seeking a cold effect.

missing.title: Fruitate
missing.description: Fruitate opens with a burst of sweet, ripe fruitiness that carries a distinct rum-candy warmth. A citrus nuance adds brightness while subtle floral facets give it dimension beyond a simple fruit note. The woody undertone in the drydown keeps it grounded and blendable. This material's real strength is its exceptional diffusion and staying power, lasting six days on blotter. Use it to give fruity top notes persistence they normally lack, or to add ripe sweetness to jasmine and tuberose accords. It blends particularly well with bergamot and lavender. Try Fruitate at low levels as a fruity enhancer wherever you need more bloom and radiance. At higher doses the rum-candy warmth becomes prominent, opening up gourmand and tropical directions. Combine with citrus oils for sparkle or white florals for lush fruitiness.

missing.title: Galbex®
missing.description: Galbex is a speciality base created by Firmenich to showcase Dynascone when it was first created. Later it was improved upon with the use of Neobutenone Alpha and it remains in that form today. As well as the overdose of Neobutenone, the base contains accessory notes to soften and round out the edges of the base. We highly recommend it for people looking for an easy to use green pineapple note. Galbex blends beautifully with Hedione , Florol , Hivernal Neo , and green materials.

missing.title: Gamma Hexalactone
missing.description: Gamma Hexalactone is one of the more unique amongst the lactones, owing to a floral fruity layer on top of a tonka and tobacco base. It has a very delicate cresylic nuance (vaguely similar to Cyclopidene) in combination with a low key hint of benzyl acetate giving it a ribbon of ylang floralcy through the heart. This makes it a wonderful nuancer for our Signature vanillin. It also has a hint of booziness which is great for a tipsy accord. This is definitely one of the more interesting lactones and a firm favourite at Fraterworks. Blend it with Rum Jungle Essence from V. MANE Fils, Tonka Bean Absolute , Coumarin ( Synthetic or Natural )

missing.title: Geraldehyde
missing.description: When you're looking for an aldehyde which isn't the usual C-10 , C-11 and C-12 , give Geraldehyde a try. Also know as geranyl acetaldehyde, this is a floral meets marine super-powered aldehyde. On its own it is a great way to add sparkle and flash to a citrus fragrance while contributing volume, but it also works as a booster to other aldehydic notes. It's marine quality also makes it a good partner to ozonics like Calone and the surprising sea-moss material Oceanol , also from IFF. When dosed carefully (under 0.1% typically) you can add radiance and lift to a scent. With ylang-ylang you get a wonderful synergy which makes this a great modern material to use in a Chanel No 5 type scent. From our own range this is great with Amazonia and Solafleur . It is also adds an inimitable twist to our highly popular Magnificent Mandarin .

missing.title: Geranyl Acetone
missing.description: Geranyl Acetone (an unsaturated aliphatic ketone) opens with a penetrating freshness that immediately distinguishes it from its close relative, Geranyl Acetate . Where the acetate offers sweet, waxy rose with lavender hints, the acetone brings aldehydic brightness and a unique magnolia cream character. This material captures the elusive scent of magnolia petals—that perfect balance of citrusy freshness, creamy richness, and subtle green that makes the flower so prized yet difficult to recreate authentically. This ketone excels where Geranyl Acetate might feel too sweet or heavy, particularly in modern compositions demanding transparency and lift. Its aldehydic facet provides natural diffusion without the soapy harshness of straight aldehydes, while the green-leafy notes prevent the cloying sweetness that plagues many floral reconstructions. Deploy it at 0.5-3% to transform flat rose accords into living bouquets, or use it as the cornerstone of magnolia compositions where authenticity matters more than intensity. The synergy between Geranyl Acetone and Geranyl Acetate creates magic—combine them in a 1:2 ratio for unprecedented depth in rose accords. The acetate provides body and traditional rosy sweetness while the acetone adds sparkle, freshness, and that crucial magnolia cream note. Together they bridge the gap between vintage floral richness and contemporary transparency. Use this combination to create "rose complexes" that work equally well in fine fragrance and functional products, maintaining character through aggressive bases where single materials fail.

missing.title: Givescone®
missing.description: When is a damascone not a damascone? When it's Givescone! To the untrained nose it would be easy to presume that this sticky and fruity chemical is part of the rose ketone family, but it isn't. As a consequence it can be thrown in your scents with gay abandon. It has no IFRA restriction at all. The author of Perfumery: Techniques in evolution describes it as “a well known chemical that is difficult to describe. It has many nuances of the damascones and damascenone, but is less sharp-metallic and has more of a sweet-apple note. It combines very well with undecavertol [.]” Givescone is used at 0.2% in My Way (2020) by Armani where it enhances the fruitiness of a blend of damascones and raspberry ketone. A larger 0.8% is found in Kurkdjian's Gentle Fluidity Gold (2019) backed up by a massive 38% of sweet musks Helvetolide and Tonalide. “The tall striped tulips stood straight up upon their stalks, like long rows of soldiers, and looked defiantly across the grass at the roses, and said: We are quite as splendid as you are now. The purple butterflies fluttered about with gold dust on their wings, visiting each flower in turn; the little lizards crept out of the crevices of the wall, and lay basking in the white glare; and the pomegranates split and cracked with the heat, and showed their bleeding red hearts.” — Oscar Wilde, The Birthday of the Infanta .

missing.title: Globalide
missing.description: Globalide belongs to the macrocyclic musk family, with a clean, modern character. Its particular quality is warmth and creaminess: a waxy, powdery musk with sandalwood-like facets that sits close to the skin and wraps the wearer rather than projecting outward. There is a soapy, clean-linen quality without the intense metallic "hot iron" bite of its close relative Habanolide. That creamy, soft-focus character makes it especially effective in skin-scent compositions and intimate fragrances where the musk should feel like an extension of the wearer rather than an announcement. It blends naturally with lactonic materials, soft woods like Iso E Super and cashmeran, and floral hearts where it provides a warm, seamless base. Even below one per cent of a formula, its influence on the drydown is substantial. Globalide and Habanolide share the same base molecule but are manufactured differently, and the result is a genuine olfactory distinction. Habanolide is more radiant, metallic, and bright — the "hot iron" pressed-linen character that gives compositions lift and transparency. Globalide is creamier, waxier, more powdery, and more diffuse — it wraps and softens where Habanolide illuminates. The choice depends on whether you want your musk to radiate or to envelop. The individual isomers of Globalide/Habanolide-type musks can be distinguished under suitable GCMS conditions. In our finished-perfume GCMS work, however, these peaks elute very close together and are not resolved clearly enough for us to assign each isomer with confidence. We therefore report them as a combined Globalide/Habanolide-type musk group rather than claiming the exact commercial grade used. With that caveat, this molecule appears in Guerlain Bois d'Armenie (11.4% combined E and Z forms), Dior Vanilla Diorama (9.4%), Chanel Boy (7.2%), Nishane Nefs (5.7%), MFK Universalis (2.5%), Dior Rouge Trafalgar (2.2%), and Henry Jacques Galileo (2.2%). The Chemistry Globalide and Habanolide are closely related musk

missing.title: Globanone®
missing.description: Globanone is an elegant and underrated macrocyclic musk that is solid at room temperature so we offer it here at 50% dilution in DPG or pure. Closely related to the well-known Velvione (the Givaudan copy of the vastly superior Ambretone from Takagasco), globanone is cost effective and an essential musk for perfumers. Globanone offers a fresh, less animalic profile compared to Velvione, while still maintaining elegance. Both musks share a similar behaviour, though Globanone’s affordability makes it the practical choice. Exceptionally stable in detergent powders, it also burns beautifully, making it ideal for agarbati and bakhoor fragrances. NOTE: pure globanone solidifies at low temperatures.

missing.title: Grape Butyrate
missing.description: Grape Butyrate opens with a delicate, airy fruitiness - think fresh grape skin with a tart green-apple edge and a whisper of wine. It sits between ethereal and fleshy, never loud, offering a quiet juiciness that reads as unmistakably natural. The overall impression is of freshly pressed white grape juice touched with tropical pineapple. This is a workhorse nuance material rather than a headline note. Add it to fruity-floral accords to inject convincing freshness without synthetic sharpness, or blend it with methyl anthranilate to build a complete Concord grape effect. Its hydroxyl group gives it better tenacity than most fruit esters - expect around four hours on a blotter - bridging the gap between fleeting citrus top notes and the heavier floral heart. Try it in wine or cognac reconstructions alongside ethyl lactate and damascenone for a rich fermentation effect. In tropical accords, pair it with ethyl butyrate to create a full pineapple-juice impact that neither material achieves alone. Use it at low levels in citrus compositions for a dewy, freshly peeled quality you won't get from terpenes.

missing.title: Grapefruit Base 184062 D
missing.description: Grapefruit Base hits the nose with an immediate sharp citrus burst — zesty, bitter, and unmistakably grapefruit. It captures both the juicy freshness of the flesh and the aromatic bite of the peel. The effect is brighter and cleaner than natural grapefruit oil, without any of the sulphurous off-notes that plague the natural. The real advantage here is performance. Natural grapefruit oil fades fast and develops unpleasant sulphurous undertones as it ages. This base avoids both problems entirely, giving you reliable grapefruit character that lasts.
