Use it as the core of any citrus accord, or add it to floral compositions where you want a sparkling, bitter-fresh lift. Build a full grapefruit accord by combining this base with Methyl Pamplemousse for added juiciness, or pair it with nootkatone for extra depth and persistence. It layers well with bergamot and neroli for a complex hesperidic opening. Try it against pink pepper or cardamom for a modern spicy-citrus contrast. 184062 D vs 015794 R This is Firmenich's 184062 D, not the older 015794 R. Both are synthetic grapefruit bases, but the 184062 D incorporates Firmenich captive molecules not found in the earlier version. The result is a smoother, more stable base with broader application versatility, while the 015794 R is sharper and more raw-peel in character. If you've used the 015794 R before, expect the 184062 D to be more polished and better behaved in formulation — particularly in applications where stability matters.

missing.title: Grenoble Pyrazine
missing.description: Grenoble Pyrazine is intensely walnut-like. It has a distinct "green," oily, and slightly tannic bitterness that smells like the papery skin on a raw peanut or a fresh walnut. It also has a "burnt sugar" or dark caramel undertone that is less "clean" than the related materials Praslin and Torref Pyrazine. Grenoble Pyrazine opens with powerful nut-skin character—that slightly bitter, papery quality of freshly roasted peanuts and walnuts. Unsweetened cocoa facets follow, dry and powdery rather than sweet. A warm peanut butter richness dominates the heart, while savoury corn chip and roasted grain notes add nostalgic edibility. The overall effect is snack-like and comforting. This pyrazine forms naturally during the Maillard reaction when sugars and amino acids meet heat. You'll find it in roasted peanuts, cocoa, coffee, grilled meats, and toasted grains. The high odour strength demands respect—evaluate at 0.1% dilution or less. It anchors gourmand compositions with genuine roasted warmth, particularly where nut or peanut butter effects are needed. Coffee and chocolate accords benefit from its unsweetened cocoa depth. Use Grenoble Pyrazine at 0.02–0.2% in your concentrate. Despite its short substantivity on blotter (under 3 hours), it performs well in finished compositions. It blends beautifully with vanillin, lactones, and coffee materials for realistic gourmand effects. Works in tobacco and leather contexts where savoury warmth adds sophistication. Grenoble, Praslin, and Torref Pyrazines The dimethylpyrazine isomers share family character but differ meaningfully. Grenoble Pyrazine (2,3-dimethyl) emphasises nut-skins and peanut butter—it's the most overtly "nutty" of the three, with pronounced corn chip and walnut facets. Praslin Pyrazine (2,5-dimethyl) leans earthier and more musty, closer to raw cocoa powder with a grassy undertone—better for praline and hazelnut effects. Torref Pyrazine (2,6-dimethyl) is the most intensely roasted, with dark coffee and meaty-beefy

missing.title: Grisalva
missing.description: Grisalva captures the character of natural ambergris with striking fidelity — warm, animalic, and immediately recognisable. Dry leathery facets sit beneath the ambergris body, with a slight metallic edge adding complexity. The overall impression is of deep warmth radiating from the base of a composition. The defining quality here is diffusion — Grisalva projects ambergris character through an entire composition even at trace levels. Over 48 hours on blotter tells you this is a material that defines the drydown. Use it in amber accords, orientals, and woody bases where you want warmth that carries. Pair with ambroxan and labdanum for a complete ambergris accord, or use alone to give woody and floral compositions a warm animalic foundation. The leathery facet strengthens chypre and tobacco blends. Even the smallest additions generate enormous presence — dose in traces and let the diffusion do the work.

missing.title: Guaiyl Acetate
missing.description: Guaiyl Acetate is a lovely soft floral woody material resulting from the acetylation of Guaiacwood oil. It is a perfect material for extending and fixing rose bases (especially tea rose) owing to its complex nuance of rose, spice and wood. Guaiyl Acetate also works as an alternative or supplement to Vetiveryl Acetate which is quite restricted in use under IFRA 51. NOTE: Guaiyl Acetate (also associated with CAS 61789-17-1) is an acetylation of fractions of natural guaiacwood oil and so, like vetiveryl acetate, it derives from a number of alcohols (principally guaiol and bulnesol). Guaiol Acetate (CAS 134-28-1) is the acetylation of the pure guaiol molecule. Guaiyl acetate is more complex, with soft, sweet, spicy and slightly smoky notes in addition to the usual tea rose found in both. Blends very well with Phenyl Ethyl Alcohol , Rose Crystals , and Rhodinol ex Geranium Bourbon as well as all Rose Bases .

missing.title: Guava Base 270237
missing.description: Guava Base 270237 hits you with an unmistakable wave of ripe tropical guava. There's a dry-sweet tartness that reads as realistic rather than candied, balanced by juicy mango-like warmth. Sharp catty undertones give it the same pungent bite found in the real fruit. Even at low levels this base punches through a blend, adding instant tropical recognisability. It works especially well in fruity-floral top notes where you need realistic guava without building the accord from scratch. Think of it as a shortcut to tropical authenticity. Combine with Passion Fruit Base 109223 and peach for layered tropical complexity. Bergamot brightens the guava's tartness beautifully, while cassis base adds complementary catty depth when you blend both. A small addition transforms any fruity accord.

missing.title: Habanolide®
missing.description: Habanolide® is considered a metallic or hot iron musk. It is a macrocyclic musk of the highest quality by Firmenich, indispensable and certainly irreplaceable (though Globalide® by Symrise is frequently touted as such, but that does have its differences). Habanolide® is a radiant musk which adds freshness and vitality. Habanolide® has featured in numerous modern scents. The writers of Scent and Chemistry give by way of example Silver Mist (2006) by Alessandro Gualtieri for Nasomatto, in which it makes up 25% of the fragrance: 250 Habanolide 250 Ethylene Brassylate 125 Scentolide 25 Cashmeran 10 Exaltone

missing.title: Harsingar Attar
missing.description: Of all the attars, Harsingar is the one that most smells like a complete fragrance. This is a blended attar, combining rich Indian Mysore Sandalwood with natural floral extracts and aroma chemicals. Harsingar attar opens with a sweet, intensely floral aroma somewhere between jasmine sambac and orange blossom. A clean, soapy brightness lifts the top before honeyed warmth and gentle animalic depth take over. You get creamy, woody softness from the sandalwood base throughout. Use harsingar attar as an exotic floral heart in your oriental compositions where its jasmine-orange blossom character adds unexpected sophistication. It blends beautifully with oud, rose, and tuberose to create richly layered Indian-inspired accords. The built-in sandalwood base gives you fixative depth from the start. Try it alongside champaca and frangipani for an opulent tropical floral bouquet. Add benzoin or frankincense to push it toward a meditative incense direction. This attar works as a finished perfume by itself, but give it space to interact with other materials and you unlock something extraordinary.

missing.title: Herbac®
missing.description: Herbac offers a powerful, fresh aroma characterised by distinct woody, herbal, and camphoraceous notes, enriched with hints of eucalyptus, mint, and cedar leaf. Its sharp, invigorating scent evokes coniferous freshness, making it ideal for capturing outdoor, nature-inspired impressions. Herbac excels at imparting brightness and lift, particularly in woody and herbal accords, fougère compositions, and masculine fragrances. With good stability across various products, including personal care items and home fragrances, it provides a dynamic, impactful top-to-heart note in diverse scent applications.

missing.title: Herbanate®
missing.description: In Givaudan's own words: “Herbanate has a fruity note with hints of banana, pineapple and blackcurrant. The background is fresh and herbal with a warm spicy element. Herbanate is a versatile material that provides or enhances the natural effect of fragrances, particularly in fruity notes where it gives a juicy tropical fruit effect. It can also be used as a 10% dilution to give a green herbal freshness and blends well with citrus, green and even spicy notes.” Herbanate blends extremely well with agrestical materials such as Clary Sage , Lavender Absolute and Lavender Oil. It offers excellent diffusion in combination with the rose ketones and blends surprisingly well undecavertol and methyl heptine carbonate . Try it with our Daphne base for a very modern and unique mix.

missing.title: Herbavert
missing.description: Herbavert arrives with startling diffusion—a blast of camphoraceous brightness shot through with mentholic coolness that reads as crushed rosemary and eucalyptus leaf. This opening is aggressive, modern, and intensely clean. Within minutes the rubbery edge softens, revealing a gentler herbal-vegetative character. The material's real magic lies in its evolution. As the initial sparkle fades, Herbavert transforms into something unexpectedly delicate: soft apple-blossom, transparent rose nuances, and a clean sweetness that supports fruity-floral hearts beautifully. This two-stage personality makes it invaluable for smoothing the gap between punchy top notes and developing heart accords. Pair it with Verdox for juicy apple realism, or blend with Rose Oxide at equal parts for a sparkling, metallic rosebud effect.

missing.title: Herboxane
missing.description: Herboxane opens with sweet basil and chamomile, fresh and cooling, with a gentle red-pepper spiciness underneath. The overall impression is aromatic and round — green without sharpness. It smells remarkably natural for a synthetic material. Use it as a background ingredient to smooth and round assertive herbal oils like thyme, lavender, and rosemary. It calms their spikier edges and adds body and coherence to green accords. Combined with citrus oils, it brings crisp, natural-smelling greenness that lifts the whole composition. Pair it with lavender and coumarin for classic fougère construction, with bergamot for a herbal-citrus opening, or with clary sage and geranium for rich aromatic heart notes. It also works well with blackcurrant bud materials, where its slight berry facet creates a seamless bridge.

missing.title: Hercolyn® D
missing.description: Firmenich's Hercolyn® D is a high quality deodorised version of hydrogenated pine resin. It is extremely viscous and light amber in colour. This virtually odourless material is a wonderful fixative and blender and finds many uses in fragrances and bases. Its very thick nature makes it excellent for adding body and texture to dilutions. This material has been used successfully in Guerlain's recent efforts to enrich and extend IFRA compliant oakmoss in combination with Mastic Absolute for use in their reformulations of their classic fragrance Mitsouko (1919). Note: Formerly we were selling this under the name Hercolyn® DW.

missing.title: Hexyl Cinnamic Aldehyde
missing.description: An unctuous floral, Hexyl Cinnamic Aldehyde is the key building block to some of the most famous muguet bases and is found in fragrances such as Eau Sauvage (1966), Gabrielle (2017, Chanel — demonstration formula below), Dolce & Gabbana Light Blue (2001), and Tom Ford's Tobacco Vanille (2007). When constructing a jasmine base, this material is preferred over its close relative Amyl Cinnamic Aldehyde, owing to the fact that the hexyl version is sweeter and more floral. Hexyl Cinnamic Aldehyde tempers the harsh character of Benzyl Acetate and other strong jasmine chemicals while providing a light and discreet unisex floral heart note. At room temperature, Hexyl Cinnamic Aldehyde is liquid but at lower temperatures it may solidify. A little heat will return it to a liquid state. Importantly, Hexyl Cinnamic Aldehyde can sour quite quickly so it is recommended that you buy small quantities often, rather than bulk amounts and refrigerate it.

missing.title: Hindinol®
missing.description: Hindinol is one of the most beautiful and radiant of the sandalwood aroma chemicals and somewhat unique in being something of a top note material. Perfumery: Techniques In Evolution speaks highly of the product: “This is […] one of the best sandalwood chemicals, as captivating as as it is extraordinary[.] Most sandalwood chemicals lack a natural top note and we perfumers need to create it; however, when using Hindinol, the natural top note appears and this top note is a dream come true.” While a number of suppliers make this product, the Takasago quality is the nicest and that is what we stock.

missing.title: Hivernal® Neo
missing.description: Named after the man who discovered it in 1994 ( Béat Winter), Hivernal Neo has a similar structure to Lilial but replaces its fatty qualities with fresh and clean notes of white linen and muguet. It is very long lasting and powerful so care should be exercised in its use. From Firmenich perfumer, Harry Frémont: “[T] he freshest and the longest lasting ingredient, although freshness and long-lastingness normally do not coexist. Very monolithic and linear, its modifying power is unequaled with brightness and a humid facet. ” Hivernal Neo blends beautifully with Galbex®, Florol ®, Nympheal ™, Mimosal ™, Celestafleur ™ and all our Muguet bases.

missing.title: Honeyflor 1% DPG
missing.description: We can say with almost total certainty that this is the one of the most potent honey chemicals you will smell and so we sell it at 1% in dilution with DPG. As well as a classic miel note, Honeyflor also exhibits a lovely powderiness and a green hyacinth quality making it perfect for adding unusual nuances and character to floral blends. Honeyflor blends well with Honey Supreme, Miel Blanc (a classic base), Mielarome (also classical) and hyacinth and rose products.

missing.title: Hyacinth Body
missing.description: Hyacinth Body smells of a spring morning — dewy, transparent, leafy-green with an unmistakable hyacinth character. There are clear impressions of nasturtium and sweet pea alongside the hyacinth, plus a subtle mushroom-metallic facet that adds depth. It is fresher and more watery than Hyacinth Body No. 3 , which is more herbal and aggressive by comparison. This material is one of the essential building blocks for green floral accords. It forms the structural core of hyacinth reconstructions and contributes convincingly to lilac, muguet, and sweet pea compositions. Used as a modifier in rose accords, it creates a "rose on the stem" effect — the green, living quality of a freshly cut flower rather than a dried petal. Pair Hyacinth Body with phenylacetaldehyde for hyper-realistic hyacinth, or with galbanum for a sharper green edge. It works beautifully with Hedione for diffusive transparency, and with indole for narcotic white floral depth. Use it at modest levels as a modifier, or push it higher as a structural core in green floral soliflores.

missing.title: Hyacinth Body No. 3
missing.description: Hyacinth Body No 3 opens with an assertive burst of crushed green leaves and sappy stems. This powerful green-floral fusion carries the unmistakable character of hyacinth but with enhanced vegetal depth. The material's exceptional impact allows minute quantities to transform entire compositions. Deploy this acetal when you need aggressive green character without sacrificing floral elegance. Its herbal edge makes it perfect for masculine florals or compositions requiring botanical authenticity. Layer it beneath traditional rose accords to create the impression of roses growing wild among herbs and foliage. Build unexpected contrasts by pairing its vegetal sharpness with creamy white florals like tuberose or gardenia. Use traces in citrus compositions to add mysterious green depth. Combine with galbanum and violet leaf for hyper-realistic stem effects that ground even the most ethereal florals. The No 3 Designation IFF developed multiple Hyacinth Body variants in their quest to capture different facets of the living flower. No 3 offers more pronounced herbal character than the original version (standard Hyacinth Body, CAS 2556-10-7). While No 1 and No 2 appear to have been developmental stages or discontinued variants not commercially available today, No 3 survived as the more assertive, herbaceous alternative perfumers reach for when the original's dewy transparency needs more green muscle.

missing.title: Hydroxyambran
missing.description: Hydroxyambran seems demure at first sniff but it is a wonderful material in the super amber family (though somewhat more woody than ambergris) that is more versatile and longer lasting than most. In fact, Hydroxyambran is so long lasting it works as a fixative for Ambrocenide . It is absolutely synergistic with other amber type materials and is particularly good in combination with Permawood ™, Operanide , Dextro Norlimbanol and Z11 (Ambraketal). Hydroxyambran is a waxy solid at room temperature but it melts easily with a little warmth. Far too few perfumers utilise this very lovely amber wood chemical. It deserves some time in the spotlight. Perfumery: Techniques in Evolution (a series of articles published in Perfumer and Flavorist magazine) sings the praises of Hydroxyambran stating it is "one of the best chemicals I have known and smelled … One of the sublime odours, the best of the best."

missing.title: Indocolore
missing.description: Indocolore gives you the sensual, animalic depth of indole without the two problems that make indole difficult: discolouration and that persistent mothball-naphthalenic edge. What remains is a beautifully floral animalic note — heady jasmine and hyacinth with a feral undertone. It stays colourless in your finished product, which the name makes clear. This material excels wherever you want indolic richness in a transparent composition. White floral accords — jasmine, tuberose, gardenia, orange blossom — all benefit from its depth without the yellow-brown staining that indole causes over time. It lasts exceptionally well on blotter, making it a reliable base-note anchor in floral hearts. Use Indocolore as a direct replacement for indole in any formula where colour matters. Combine it with Hedione and benzyl acetate for a clean jasmine accord, or pair with tuberose absolute for narcotic intensity. It is extremely powerful, so work in heavy dilution — traces are usually enough to bring a floral composition to life.

missing.title: Indolarome
missing.description: _*]:min-w-0"> This material solves indole's biggest problem—it gives you that narcotic white-floral depth without discolouring your formula or overwhelming compositions with harsh mothball notes. The "sparkle" perfumers describe is real: by removing indole's heavy, musty facets, Indolarome lets the radiant floral-animalic core shine through with brilliant diffusion. Use it wherever you need authentic jasmine, tuberose, lily or orange blossom realism—trace amounts transform simple floral sketches into living, breathing flowers with sensual warmth. Blend with hedione for transparent radiance or combine with benzyl acetate to enrich basic fruity-floral notes into complex natural territory. Its civet-like facets build sophisticated animalic accords whilst subtle leather nuances add dry, smoky depth. Handle with precision at trace to moderate levels depending on intensity desired. In tobacco and tea accords it contributes earthy, fermented realism; in oriental compositions it bridges spicy tops to balsamic bases with skin-like intimacy. Pair with ylang-ylang for tropical narcotic florals or use with musks and amber for primal, sensual warmth that lasts.

missing.title: Iraldeine® Beta
missing.description: Iraldeine Beta (Methyl Ionone Beta Coeur) opens with a powdery orris-violet character — clean, slightly woody, with a soft leathery and tobacco depth underneath. A faint creamy-tropical sweetness threads through the heart and base. Use Iraldeine Beta in the heart of orris bouquets, violet-leather accords, classic chypres and modern woody florals. It bridges floral hearts to woody-leather bases without the candy-violet sweetness of other methyl ionones. A small dose deepens iris replicas; larger doses push compositions toward dry tobacco, violet suede and classical leather territory. As used in both Kadine (1911) and L'Heure Bleue (1912) by Guerlain. In L'Heure Bleue it is masterfully blended with Iriseine (Methyl Ionone Alpha Extra), Iraldeine Delta (Isomethyl Ionone Beta), and a little Iralia for polish. The demo formula below demonstrates how truly considered every ingredient was in a classical perfume. From the GCMS Library Iraldeine Beta has been confirmed by GCMS analysis in many landmark fragrances. Quantified examples include Chanel No 5 (1.87%), Replique by Raphael (1.00%), Synarome Cuir HF base (2.09%), Synarome Cuir de Russie base (0.91%), Roja Chypre Extraordinaire (0.43%), Dior Cuir Cannage (0.41%), Detchema by Revillon (0.33%), Histoires de Parfums 1740 Marquis de Sade (0.28%) and Patou 1000 (0.02%). It is also identified in Aromatics Elixir, Twilly d'Hermès, Chanel Le Lion and Comète, Amouage Jubilation XXV and Interlude Black Iris, and several Henry Jacques and Amouage attars. Caveat: GCMS breaks ionone blends into their component parts, so these may be direct add or parts of a mixed isomer material. The Whole Family Iralia ®: Finest and sweetest all round powdery iris / violet chemical. Historic. Iralia® Total : Similar to Iralia, but woodier, less sweet, and less powdery. Isoraldeine™ 70 : Dry, woody, violet-orris methyl ionone. Less floral and less powdery than Isoraldeine 95. Isoraldeine™ 95 : Floral, violet, orris, woody methyl ionone. Smoother a

missing.title: Iraldeine® Delta
missing.description: With subtle nuances of fruit, this is the woody member of the family and is very rare today, being very difficult to obtain. While Iralia is sweet powdery iris and Isoraldeine Cetone Alpha is diffusive floral violet, Isomethyl Ionone Beta is polished wood. This is the famous ionone rediscovered by Edmond Roudnitska discarded in barrels in the stock yard of De Laire during the second world war. With raw materials hard to come by, he decided to turn the "waste" into something wonderful and his Prunol SP was born: a rich and complex floral base with nuances of fruit. It had been previously featured in great perfumes like Styx by Coty (1911). We also sell Iraldeine Beta. Iralia ®: Finest and sweetest all round powdery iris / violet chemical. Historic. Isoraldeine™ Cetone Alpha : Highly purified rare form of Isoraldeine 95. Most floral methyl ionone. Methyl Ionone Gamma Coeur : Cheapest. Floral, violet, soft, powdery. Methyl Ionone Alpha Extra : Bolder, orris, leather, beeswax. Diffusive. Long lasting.

missing.title: Iralia®
missing.description: Iralia ® is the very pinnacle of Firmenich perfection in methyl ionone products. It was first synthesised at the turn of the 20th century alongside Cyclosia ®, the finest quality of hydroxycitronellal which we also stock. Iralia's first use, and perhaps still its finest, was as a 25% overdose in L'Origan (1908) by Coty where it couples with Dianthine , the famed De Laire carnation base. The complete original formula can be found below. Similar products are Isoraldeine ® 70 and 95, Methyl Ionone Gamma Coeur and Methyl Ionone Alpha Extra .

missing.title: Iralia® Total
missing.description: Iralia Total smells like opening a vintage face powder compact — rich violet and orris wrapped in a warm woody veil. A creamy floral heart sits underneath, with a subtle raspberry sweetness that surfaces on the dry-down. François Coty built L'Origan around this very note in 1908. Use Iralia Total as your workhorse violet-orris heart — it gives you the powdery richness of orris butter at a fraction of the cost. It bridges heart and base seamlessly, preventing the abrupt drop-off that plagues lighter florals. Push it to high concentrations where it becomes a dominant structural pillar. Pair Iralia Total with Hedione for a luminous, lifted violet or combine it with vetiver and salicylates for sophisticated leather effects. Try it alongside damascones for convincing rose accords. Its exceptional tenacity — over 200 hours on the strip — means a little carries a composition for days. Iralia Total vs Iralia We also sell Iralia, the classic version. Both share the same CAS number and belong to Firmenich's methyl ionone family, but they're tuned differently. Iralia is the refined, more purely floral version — the most elegant methyl ionone Firmenich makes, with a richer orris character, a softer powdery quality, and a subtle tea-like nuance that makes it the fine fragrance connoisseur's first choice. Iralia Total trades some of that refinement for robustness: a more pronounced woody facet, superior stability in difficult bases, and better substantivity on fabric. Think of Iralia as the delicate artist and Iralia Total as the harder-working, more versatile option that still delivers beautiful violet-orris character across any application.vv

missing.title: Iris Nitrile
missing.description: Iris Nitrile delivers exceptional power and radiance that transforms ordinary iris compositions into memorable creations. This material works at incredibly low concentrations—typically 0.05-0.5%—where its diffusive character amplifies ionones and natural orris. This molecule is excellent for bridging floral hearts to woody bases while maintaining transparency and modern appeal. Apply Iris Nitrile in trace amounts using pre-diluted solutions for accurate dosing. Layer this material with alpha and beta ionones for authentic iris reconstruction. Combine with cedarwood and vetiver to emphasise its woody-rooty facets. The material performs exceptionally in functional products, maintaining stability in soap and shampoo formulations where other iris materials fail.

missing.title: Irone Alpha
missing.description: When Orris Absolute (80% Irones) went past six figures in cost per kilogram, Irone Alpha stepped up to takes it place in most fragrances. While it doesn't have the complexity of Orris Absolute (which is a blend of Irone Alpha, Irone Gamma and Irone Beta), it is incredibly beautiful, powerfully diffusive and radiant. Irone Alpha is sweet and fruity (towards a raspberry note) with woody and seedy nuances and a distinctly iris heart. There is no question at all: no perfume lab is complete without this material. It is pricey but a little goes a long way. Effective from traces so we also offer it at 10% dilution in DPG.

missing.title: Irotyl
missing.description: Irotyl opens dewy and almost misty before settling into dry, powdery orris root with a fruity undercurrent. A grape-like juiciness and faint herbal-carrot nuance set it apart. Light and diffusive, it reads as a modern, airy take on violet root. Forty-four hours on a blotter means this is more than a fleeting top note — it carries the orris quality well into the heart. Pair it with ionones for a believable iris accord, or lean into the grape-like facet for fruity compositions where that juicy quality is unexpected and welcome. Violet leaf absolute and carrot seed oil reinforce the natural orris impression. Heliotropin extends the powdery side. In rose compositions, a small amount of irotyl introduces an iris nuance that gives the heart a sophisticated, three-dimensional quality without requiring expensive orris concrete.

missing.title: Isocyclocitral
missing.description: Isocyclocitral opens with a piercing, almost suffocating green-aldehydic blast that transforms in dilution to reveal photorealistic wet earth and crushed stems. This powerful modifier captures the complete flower shop experience - sappy green foliage, damp soil, and that distinctive cool humidity. Its unique marine-grassy duality revolutionised fresh fragrances in the 1980s. You'll find Isocyclocitral indispensable for cutting through oakmoss sweetness while lifting its top notes. Use sparingly at 0.1-3% where its impact is profound - Bedoukian noted "unusual effects obtained by small quantities cannot be achieved with other known synthetics." Its exceptional synergy with ionones adds dewy freshness to powdery violets. The material excels in creating specific effects: tomato leaf accords, hyacinth compositions, and modernised pine notes for functional products. Combine with Triplal for intensely diffusive aquatic-green effects. React with methyl anthranilate to form woody-orange blossom Schiff bases for unique captive notes. Difference from Citral Though citral and isocyclocitral contain identical atoms, their structural arrangement creates entirely different olfactory profiles. Citral presents pure, linear lemon character - the dominant note in lemongrass oil and citrus compositions. Isocyclocitral delivers no citrus character whatsoever, instead creating complex atmospheric greenness reminiscent of a florist's workspace: crushed stems, humid air, wet earth, and that distinctive metallic coolness. Where citral provides single-note brightness for hesperidic accords, isocyclocitral builds multi-layered environmental effects. This structural difference makes citral ideal for straightforward citrus freshness, while isocyclocitral excels at creating naturalistic green atmospheres with remarkable depth and complexity. The materials serve completely different creative purposes despite their shared formula.

missing.title: Isojasmone B-11
missing.description: Isojasmone B-11 opens with a surprisingly herbal-vegetal facet reminiscent of fresh celery seed, immediately grounding its jasmine character in botanical reality. This distinctive green note prevents the material from reading as purely floral candy. The waxy, petal-like texture creates volume and substance that synthetic jasmine reconstructions desperately need. Unlike cis-jasmone which can feel sharper and more penetrating, isojasmone offers a rounder, fruitier jasmine character that works beautifully as a heart note modifier. Use it at 0.1–1% to add natural jasmine presence to floral bouquets, or blend with quinolines for classic chypre constructions. The 32-hour substantivity on blotter extends to approximately 3 days at working concentrations. Work with Isojasmone B-11 alongside methyl jasmonate and hedione for complex jasmine reconstructions. It blends excellently with undecanolide's fruity lactone character and the clean musk of ethylene brassylate. Ionones and methylionones provide excellent background support.

missing.title: Isomuscone
missing.description: A complex floral and animalic musk (in the deer musk direction), Isomuscone is a very cost effective alternative to other members of the same family such as Muscone Laevo . Coming in crystal form, you simply add the powder to your formula and it will dissolve during resting. Perfumery: Techniques in Evolution (a series of articles published in Perfumer and Flavorist magazine) describe its synergies: “Although I love Isomuscone on its own, mixtures of it with other musks increase its perception. For in- stance, a mixture of Isomuscone with ethylene brassilate [sic] at a ratio of 80/20 is stronger than both chemicals smelled separately. This results from a strong synergy amongst ketones, lactones and dilactones. The same happens when mixing Globanone and Isomuscone. The mixtures of 20 percent Isomuscone + 80 percent Globanone, or the inverse, 20 percent Globanone + 80 percent Isomuscone, are stronger than the chemicals smelled separately. It is very common to see mixtures of Galaxolide, Helvetolide , Habanolide , Muscenone, Ambrettolide and ethylene brassilate. Mixtures of Isomuscone, Habanolide, Velvione [AKA Ambretone ] and Globanone are very, very good — approaching perfection.” Blends well with Aerolide ®, Grojsman Plus , Miraclewood ™ and Veticoeur ™.

missing.title: Isopropyl Quinoline
missing.description: This is isobutyl quinoline on steroids. At trace levels, Isopropyl Quinoline imparts a complex, character-defining signature—metallic, earthy, green-leathery—that endures across every stage of evaporation. Its strength lies not only in tenacity and throw, but in the sheer intensity of its profile. It’s especially valuable in masculine, chypre, and leather compositions, where a touch of sharp verdancy or animalic smoke is needed to lift or ground the structure. Used carefully, it can anchor a base or spark interest in a heart that might otherwise feel flat. We sell it at 10% in DPG because of its strength but we recommend evaluating it at 1% or less to explore the full range. In concentrate, 0.2–2% (in dilution) is usually sufficient—more than that and it can—and will—dominate. Expect high odour strength and excellent stability across most product formats. It blends beautifully with vetiver (especially Haitian or Java mossy types), dry chypre bases, Mousse de Saxe , and tobacco accords like Jean Carles' masterful Fleur de Tabac . Try it with Isobutyl Quinoline for a more dimensional leather, or to build a dark quinoline signature with bite.

missing.title: Isoraldeine™ 70
missing.description: Isoraldeine 70 is the workhorse grade of Givaudan's alpha-isomethyl ionone line — 70% purity, which means roughly 30% of the mixture consists of other methyl ionone isomers. Those additional isomers are not waste; they contribute a woodier, drier, more leathery character that some perfumers actually prefer. This is not a lesser Isoraldeine 95 — it is a different tool. We also sell Methyl Ionone Alpha Extra as the direct equivalent of Isoraldeine 70. Same molecule, same purity tier, same olfactive profile. The additional isomers in both give them more body and more woody backbone than the purer grades. Where Isoraldeine 95 is all violet finesse, Isoraldeine 70 brings violet muscle — it pushes through heavier compositions and holds its own against woods, leathers, and resins. Use it in leather accords where its dry-powdery character enhances suede and hide notes. It is superb in fougères, where it bridges the lavender heart and the coumarin-moss base. And in large-volume productions where budget matters, it delivers serious violet impact for a fraction of what the 95 grade (and even more so the Cetone Alpha variant) costs. The two are not interchangeable — they are complementary.

missing.title: Isoraldeine™ 95
missing.description: Isoraldeine 95 smells of soft, powdery violet with a velvety orris depth and a creamy, almost cosmetic quality. It is gentle and refined — the kind of material that makes everything around it smell more expensive. One of the most widely used materials in all of modern perfumery. Use it to build violet, iris, and orris accords, or add it to virtually any composition for powdery radiance and diffusion. It was a key ingredient in the Grojsman Accord — the legendary combination that underpins Trésor and countless other modern classics. It bridges floral top notes to woody-amber bases like nothing else. We also stock Methyl Ionone Gamma Coeur (IFF), the equivalent of Isoraldeine 95, as well as Isoraldeine Cetone Alpha — the highest-purity variant, a costly treasure with an astonishingly beautiful floral radiance at low doses. For the woodier, more leathery side of this family, see Isoraldeine 70 .

missing.title: Isoraldeine™ Cetone Alpha
missing.description: More commonly known just as Cetone Alpha , this is the perfected methyl ionone surpassing even Iralia ® in quality (and, notably, in price). It first emerged in the mid 1920s as a key material in the Cetonia and Amarante bases of Marius Reboul (1873-1952). This is, effectively, a highly refined version of Isoraldeine 95 . Cetone Alpha quickly became the go-to methyl ionone in Givaudan's internal product range, and, as it became easier to produce in larger volumes, it eventually hit the market as a non-captive material. Compared to Givaudan's Isoraldeine 95 and Iralia ( Firmenich's top product from this family with strong powdery nuances), Cetone Alpha is supremely floral. Used below 5% of a formula Cetone Alpha has an astonishingly beautiful and radiant floralising effect, while higher amounts add a rich iris and violet character. Iralia typifies the early 20th century era of rich powdery fragrances (exemplified by Coty and Guerlain). Its first outing, and perhaps still its finest, was as a 25% overdose in L'Origan (1908) by Coty where it coupled with Dianthine , the famed De Laire carnation base. On the other hand, Cetone Alpha launched the floral and radiant era beginning in the 1930s with Chanel's aldehydic Ivoire (1932) with its Florentine iris and Parma violet heart. Cetone Alpha is to the methyl ionones what Paradisone® is to the methyl jasmonates. Some other members of the family that we sell are Methyl Ionone Gamma Coeur and Methyl Ionone Alpha Extra . And while you wait a couple of days for your latest Fraterworks order to arrive in the post, you may like to read Understanding Ionones .

missing.title: Ivy Dioxolane
missing.description: Ivy Dioxolane (Glycolierral) opens with an abstract impression that can be described as "intense smell of nothing" - this paradox reveals its true genius. The material creates a milky-green aura reminiscent of broken plant stems releasing their sap. This unique ivy-tomato vine character provides naturalistic humidity that transforms synthetic compositions into living gardens. You'll find Ivy Dioxalane invaluable for taming aggressive herbal notes like lavandin , armoise , and tarragon without erasing their character. Use it at 0.5-2% to build authentic fig accords where its inherent milky-green duality eliminates the need for multiple modifiers. Its exceptional stability across pH 2-10.5 makes it perfect for functional fragrances. The material's subtle "sweaty" undertone adds the realism that separates amateur from professional work. Combine with Stemone for photorealistic fig leaves or pair with lemon oils for unexpected roundness. At higher doses (2-8%), it becomes the textural foundation that allows sharp aromatics to coexist harmoniously.

missing.title: Jacintheme
missing.description: Jacintheme blooms with an intensely green, almost sappy floral character — true hyacinth rather than generic white flower. There is a waxy, balsamic quality underneath that gives it body and persistence. The overall impression is of freshly cut hyacinth stems on a cool morning. This base works as a standalone hyacinth core or as a green-floral modifier in larger compositions. Add it to jasmine accords for a leafy green lift, or use it alongside lilac materials for a convincing springtime bouquet. It has real presence in the mid-notes, bridging the gap between fresh green topnotes and heavier floral hearts. Jacintheme pairs beautifully with phenylacetaldehyde for added realism, or with galbanum for a sharper green edge. Try it against a muguet base for a classic lily-hyacinth duo. Keep doses modest — this base has serious throw and can overwhelm lighter neighbours.

missing.title: Jasmal®
missing.description: Jasmal is a jasmine material that smells of the jasmine plant rather than the jasmine flower. It opens oily and herbaceous, with a clear note of tea and a lavender-like edge, and the mushroom is there but kept in check. The jasmine itself sits behind all of this — present, recognisable, but seen through leaves and stems rather than petals. Use Jasmal to add green realism to a jasmine accord without adding sweetness. It is the green end of this family, so it brings leaf, stem and tea where Jessemal brings cream. It behaves like a green lactone: it smooths the rough edges of a floral and gives indolic, narcotic flowers a living, picked-this-morning quality. Use it alone where Jasmonyl’s creaminess is unwanted. It works well with lavender and in tea accords, sits comfortably beside green materials such as galbanum and violet leaf, and lasts well over three hundred hours on a smelling strip. Against Jasmopyrane Forte it is the cleaner cut: the same material with less mushroom and a tidier edge. Understanding the Jasmine Pyrans Jasmal is one of a small family of jasmine materials that are all the same molecule in two forms. One form is green, herbaceous and mushroomy, with a tea note. The other is rich, creamy and petal-like, and lasts longer. Nobody sells either form on its own: every product in the family is a mix of the two, and the proportion is what you are buying. Jasmal (IFF, CAS 18871-14-2) is mostly the green form: herbaceous, with pronounced tea and mushroom notes and an oily, plant-like feel. Jessemal (IFF, CAS 38285-49-3) is mostly the creamy form: the richest, most petal-like and longest-lasting of the group. Jasmonyl (Givaudan, CAS 18871-14-2 and 63270-14-4) is Givaudan’s own balance of the two — green mushroom and creamy petal in one bottle, sitting between Jasmal and Jessemal. Jasmopyrane Forte (Givaudan, CAS 18871-14-2) is Givaudan’s cheaper, rougher cut of the green form: greener and more mushroomy than Jasmal, and slightly more tenacious. Substituting

missing.title: Jasminlactone
missing.description: Not to be confused with the classic Jasmolactone (found in traces in nature in Osmanthus absolute), Jasminlactone (or Creamy Lactone) is essential for realistic replicas of the same. It has prominent peach and apricot skin notes with a celery-like or vegetable undertone. It provides the heavy, waxy petal weight found in natural Tuberose and Jasmine absolutes. It feels thicker and more authentic to the natural oil. Jasminlactone occurs naturally in high abundance in Jasmine grandiflorum and Jasmine sambac, as well as Tuberose, Gardenia, and Peach. It is the key to the waxy scent of real jasmine flowers. It's a costly material, and ours (the highest quality on the market) is manufactured by Firmenich, but a little goes a long way.

missing.title: Jasmolactone® Delta
missing.description: Jasmolactone® Delta by Firmenich (product 965414) is an incredibly powerful lactone with nuances of peach, coconut, cream and jasmine petals. Quantities between 0.1 – 1% make a profound contribution to white floral accords, naturalising and adding radiance. Jasmolactone® Delta blends beautifully with jasmin notes, Hedione ®, the rose ketones, ethyl safranate, and other lactonic chemicals. Also known as 5-hydroxy-7-decenoic acid delta-lactone.

missing.title: Jasmonyl®
missing.description: Jasmonyl hits your nose as oily, waxy jasmine underscored by a pronounced mushroom earthiness. It’s not a clean, polished jasmine — there’s a green, slightly dirty realism here that reads as convincingly natural. That mushroom facet is the signature that makes it instantly recognisable. Use Jasmonyl to add organic, earthy believability to your jasmine accords. Givaudan has balanced the two forms of this molecule so that the green mushroom and the creamy petal arrive together, and that is what makes it read as a flower rather than a note. Where Jasmal gives you the leaf and Jessemal gives you the petal, Jasmonyl gives you the whole bloom in one bottle. Jasmonyl excels where you want jasmine that smells alive, not synthetic. Pair it with indole to push animalic depth further, or with Hedione to brighten its heavier facets. Its waxy texture grounds neroli and orange blossom accords beautifully, it sits naturally with lavender, and it carries unusually well in soap. Understanding the Jasmine Pyrans Jasmonyl is one of a small family of jasmine materials that are all the same molecule in two forms. One form is green, herbaceous and mushroomy, with a tea note. The other is rich, creamy and petal-like, and lasts longer. Nobody sells either form on its own: every product in the family is a mix of the two, and the proportion is what you are buying. Jasmonyl (Givaudan, CAS 18871-14-2 and 63270-14-4) is Givaudan’s own balance of the two — green mushroom and creamy petal in one bottle, sitting between the two IFF materials. Jasmal (IFF, CAS 18871-14-2) is mostly the green form: herbaceous, with pronounced tea and mushroom notes and an oily, plant-like feel. Jessemal (IFF, CAS 38285-49-3) is mostly the creamy form: the richest, most petal-like and longest-lasting of the group. Jasmopyrane Forte (Givaudan, CAS 18871-14-2) is Givaudan’s cheaper, rougher cut of the green form: greener and more mushroomy than Jasmal, and slightly more tenacious. Substituting Jasmonyl with Jasmal or J

missing.title: Javanol®
missing.description: Javanol opens with rich, creamy sandalwood that immediately announces its exceptional quality. Rosy-floral facets emerge alongside subtle milky-lactonic undertones, creating complexity that rivals natural East Indian sandalwood. The clean, powdery character feels refined rather than heavy, while the radiant projection seems almost impossible given its base note weight. This Givaudan molecule represents the pinnacle of sandalwood chemistry. Discovered in 1996, Javanol achieves what many consider the closest synthetic approximation to natural beta-santalol—the principal odour-active component in precious East Indian sandalwood oil. The 400-hour substantivity on blotter translates to extraordinary real-world performance, and its odour threshold makes it approximately 400 times more potent than comparable sandalwood synthetics. Work with Javanol at 0.5–2% of your concentrate—its power means a little goes remarkably far. Even at trace levels of 0.02–0.1%, it functions as a radiance booster that lifts entire compositions. Blend with vetiver, patchouli, rose absolute, Iso E Super, and cashmeran for sophisticated woody accords.

missing.title: Jessemal®
missing.description: Jessemal opens rich, creamy, and unmistakably jasmine. There’s a lactonic smoothness here that feels like actual petals — dense and voluptuous rather than green or airy. A subtle herbaceous note, almost celery-like, sits quietly underneath, adding just enough complexity to keep it interesting. Use Jessemal where you want body. It is the creamy end of this family with only a trace of the green, so it fills out a jasmine, tuberose or white-floral heart without bringing mushroom or earth with it. If a white floral smells thin and sketched rather than fleshy, this is the material that gives it weight. Layer it under indole for animalic depth, or beside Hedione and benzyl acetate for a fuller, more rounded jasmine heart. Its exceptional stability means the jasmine character holds true from application through to dry-down. Understanding the Jasmine Pyrans Jessemal is one of a small family of jasmine materials that are all the same molecule in two forms. One form is green, herbaceous and mushroomy, with a tea note. The other is rich, creamy and petal-like, and lasts longer. Nobody sells either form on its own: every product in the family is a mix of the two, and the proportion is what you are buying. Jessemal (IFF, CAS 38285-49-3) is mostly the creamy form — the richest, most petal-like and longest-lasting of the group. Jasmal (IFF, CAS 18871-14-2) is mostly the green form: herbaceous, with pronounced tea and mushroom notes and an oily, plant-like feel. Jasmonyl (Givaudan, CAS 18871-14-2 and 63270-14-4) is Givaudan’s own balance of the two — Jessemal’s creamy petal with Jasmal’s green-mushroom earthiness in one bottle. Jasmopyrane Forte (Givaudan, CAS 18871-14-2) is Givaudan’s cheaper, rougher cut of the green form: greener and more mushroomy than Jasmal, and slightly more tenacious. Substituting Jessemal with Jasmal or Jasmopyrane Forte will push your formula greener and more mushroomy, losing the creamy lactonic body. Jasmonyl gets you closer, since it carries the creamy

missing.title: Karanal
missing.description: Karanal opens with radiant, powerful woody-amber character—dry, clean, and almost electric in its diffusiveness. Unlike heavier amber materials that sit close to the skin, Karanal projects outward with sharp clarity. Subtle fruity nuances reminiscent of watermelon add unexpected freshness, while the overall effect feels modern and energetic rather than warm and resinous. This spiky woody character transforms florals into architectural statements and gives citrus compositions unprecedented longevity. You'll find Karanal provides the structural spine that connects volatile top notes directly to the base, creating verticality. When combined with macrocyclic musks, it forms the clean-sexy drydown that defined an entire generation of masculine fragrances. Use Karanal at trace levels for invisible lift, or push it to 2% for aggressive woody projection. Mix it with ionones to create masculine florals, or pair with Ambroxan for that endless-freshness effect. Karanal featured prominently in Gucci pour Homme (2003) and Frédéric Malle's Une Rose—both masterworks that showcased its ability to add radiance without heaviness. Sadly, European authorities designated Karanal a substance of very high concern, requiring products containing it to be reformulated by August 2023. Givaudan ceased supply during 2022. While alternatives exist, perfumers mourn the loss of this unique material that could energise compositions like nothing else.

missing.title: Ketoisophorone
missing.description: Ketoisophorone delivers the exact aromatic signature of Buddleia flowers, that elusive butterfly bush scent that combines honeyed sweetness with dusty, woody undertones. This unusual material is deceptively strong—its musty-tea character can dominate at high concentrations. The tobacco leaf facet makes it indispensable for creating authentic cigarette and pipe tobacco accords where it bridges fresh green aspects with cured brown notes. This material is essential for both tea and tobacco bases, owing to its unique ability to capture dried leaf aromatics. Use at 0.01-2% maximum in concentrate—its potency demands restraint. The material excels at adding depth to woody compositions where its musty sweetness prevents flatness, while in florals it contributes an intriguing dusty-honey backdrop reminiscent of late summer gardens. Use ketoisophorone to achieve naturalistic effects impossible with conventional materials. It transforms simple tea accords into complex ceremonial blends, elevates tobacco compositions beyond simple vanilla sweetness, and gives woody bases an unexpected floral lift. Combine with ionones for violet-tobacco sophistication, blend with honey materials for Buddleia recreations, or layer with actual tobacco absolute for unprecedented depth. This is your secret weapon for compositions requiring that specific dried-flower dustiness found in nature but rarely captured in perfume.

missing.title: Koavone®
missing.description: Koavone opens with bright balsamic-pine freshness that quickly reveals its complex woody-violet heart. This sophisticated former IFF captive delivers the powdery elegance of classic methyl ionones while adding warm amber depth impossible to achieve with older materials. The subtle toffee-caramel facet provides unexpected gourmand intrigue. You'll find Koavone invaluable as a modern replacement for methyl ionones, offering superior diffusion and stability. Use it at 1-10% to enhance amber accords where it synergistically amplifies warmth and radiance. At higher levels (up to 30%), it creates powerful aldehydic-pine effects perfect for fresh woody compositions. The material's isomeric complexity creates its unique character - commercial Koavone contains multiple isomers that work synergistically. Build sophisticated violet-orris accords by combining with alpha-ionone and natural orris. Create rich woody structures by pairing with Iso E Super and sandalwood molecules for multi-layered depth.

missing.title: Kohinool®
missing.description: Kohinool opens with quiet, polished warmth — a woody-amber character that reads refined rather than heavy. A distinctly floral quality sets it apart from other amber materials, with dry vetiver-like depth beneath. Subtle raisin sweetness and quiet dryness complete an unusually elegant profile. This is a material you can build entire bases around — few amber chemicals tolerate such generous dosing without distortion. Twenty-four hours on blotter gives you woody-amber warmth that anchors compositions through the full drydown. It works across fine fragrance, soaps, and functional products with equal conviction. Combine with Iso E Super and cedarwood to build transparent woody-amber accords, or layer with labdanum and vetiver for richer oriental depth. The floral facet makes it unusually sympathetic to rose and iris. A backbone material that rewards bold use rather than cautious traces.

missing.title: Kumquat Base 270258
missing.description: Kumquat Base from Firmenich opens with a sparkling, tangy burst — sweeter and more complex than orange, with a distinctive candied-peel quality and fizzy green brightness. The effect is mouth-watering: somewhere between mandarin zest and preserved citrus rind. Firmenich captive molecules add facets you cannot source elsewhere. Kumquat is the only citrus fruit eaten whole — sweet rind over sour flesh — and that sweet-tart contrast defines the note. Use this base to add exotic citrus complexity beyond standard orange, bergamot, or lemon. It lifts fresh compositions and adds a sparkling, piquant twist to florals. Pair kumquat with ginger and pink pepper for an energising opening, or with neroli and jasmine for a sparkling floral heart. It bridges beautifully into woody bases — try it over cedar or vetiver. The name comes from Cantonese: golden orange.

missing.title: Labdamate
missing.description: With gourmand perfumes being all the rage today one can never have too many aromachemicals that trigger thoughts of food. Labdamate (Ethyl hydrocinnamate) is ethereal and sweet, bringing to mind rum, fruit, wines and honey. It also has a floral side reflecting the cinnamic facets of pink rose and hyacinth. Comprising part of labdanum naturally, it is no surprise that this product blends exceedingly well with that material. Labdamate contributes cinnamic sweetness to the masterpiece oriental fragrance Opium Pour Homme (1995) by Jacques Cavallier for Yves Saint Laurent.

missing.title: Lactojasmone
missing.description: This lactone transforms white florals from simple to sumptuous. Its creamy-milky texture adds tangible waxy petal quality that smooths harsh synthetic edges into cohesive luxury. Think of it as the material that gives jasmine and tuberose their velvety depth rather than just their scent. Use it to anchor opulent florals with exceptional staying power—it lasts eight days on a blotter. Add milky accents to sandalwood reconstructions where synthetics alone feel hollow and incomplete. In stone fruit accords it mimics that fleshy, succulent texture you get biting into fresh peach, moving compositions beyond abstract fruitiness into photorealistic territory. Blend with hedione for radiant jasmine diffusion or combine with other lactones for sophisticated peachy-coconut complexity. In gourmand work it provides creamy foundations that soften vanilla and caramel into decadent richness. Watch how it underlines fruity facets in osmanthus whilst adding tropical depth to frangipani—it's a masterful harmoniser across floral families.

missing.title: Lemon Terpenes
missing.description: Lemon Terpenes captures the volatile essence of fresh lemon peel without any fruity sweetness. You'll notice its extremely diffusive, sharp character hits immediately upon application. The material consists of over 75% d-limonene, creating that unmistakable citrus-pine combination. This terpenic fraction proves invaluable for adding explosive lift to citrus accords and sparkling brightness to floral compositions. Use it to amplify bergamot and neroli in cologne formulations or add traces to cut through heavy florals like jasmine. The material works brilliantly with woody notes, creating a fresh-cut timber effect when blended with cedarwood or vetiver . Handle this volatile powerhouse with precision—overdosing quickly turns elegance into harshness. Layer it with folded citrus oils for complete lemon character. Combine with aldehydes and citrus oils to build authentic zesty accords that maintain their sparkle throughout the top note development.

missing.title: Levistamel 25% TEC
missing.description: Levistamel greets you with rich caramelised sugar — not the simple sweetness of vanillin, but something layered and savoury. Green celery and fenugreek notes weave through the caramel, adding a salty, almost curry-like edge. Anise-liquorice warmth and balsamic depth emerge as it develops on skin. This Givaudan lactone is your answer when you want caramel complexity without defaulting to vanillin or ethyl maltol. Herbal and pine compositions gain unexpected warmth from small additions. The celery-fenugreek facet connects it to lovage, immortelle, and maple accords where that savoury-sweet interplay defines the character. Levistamel comes diluted in triethyl citrate for easy handling — the pure material is a solid. Tenacity on blotter reaches several weeks, and stability across soap, shampoo, and detergent is excellent. Blend with sotolon, ethyl maltol, and coumarin for deep gourmand warmth.

missing.title: Lilial
missing.description: Lilial opens with crystalline lily-of-the-valley freshness, its aldehydic sparkle creating immediate lift and radiance. The watery-green transparency reads as morning dew on white petals. This legendary molecule (discovered in the 1960s by IFF) captures muguet's elusive character with extraordinary fidelity and power. Lilial transforms heavy florals into airy bouquets through its unique Schiff base formations. Combine it with hydroxycitronellal for classic muguet or add traces to rose for aldehydic brilliance. Its metallic-clean edge cuts through oriental bases, adding transparency without sacrificing richness. The material's 236-hour substantivity means your compositions maintain fresh character throughout wear. Use it at 0.5-3% in fine fragrance for optimal impact without overwhelming delicacy. Its affinity for phenylethyl alcohol , citronellol , and hedione creates synergies that amplify overall radiance. The variant we sell is a particularly fine “Extra” quality in the Fraterworks® Signature range. NOTE: Over time lilial may oxidise which appears in the form of white crystals or clumps (lysmerylic acid). Remaining liquid can still be used by the oxidised material should be discarded. Lilial may contain a touch of Tocopherol for protection, but storing this material at temperatures below 15°C (59°F) is still advisable. Regulatory: this is banned by the EU but is still permitted by IFRA to 1.4% of your finished product.

missing.title: Lilyflore®
missing.description: Lilyflore® delivers extraordinary volume and structure in muguet compositions. This powerful floral material bridges the gap between Hydroxycitronellal's soft petal character and Lilial's creamy fullness while offering superior tenacity. In addition to being an alternative to the virtually prohibited Lilial and Lyral, Lilyflore® excels due to maintaining integrity where traditional aldehydes can falter. Add Lilyflore® at 0.05-0.3% in your blend to lift muddy florals and add clean radiance. Combine with 0.5% Hedione and a trace of Melonal for solar lily effects. Blend with 1% Iso E Super to create a convincing muguet-stem accord. Use with caution—this material dominates easily and turns plastic-sweet when overdosed. It's beautiful… until it's not.

missing.title: Lyral®
missing.description: Banned in the EU and restricted to 0.2% by IFRA for the rest of the us, Lyral remains one of the most profoundly beautiful white floral chemicals. It gave life to Aventus illustrating its amazing ability to floralise masculines without adding a feminine touch, and without it the masterpiece Chanel fragrance Coco (1986) wouldn't be possible. As Europe strips bare its greatest works of modern fragrance art in honour of health and safety regulators, we can at least be happy to know that thousands of bottles of now-vintage perfume are still floating around on eBay to allow us to enjoy the beauty of this material. And thankfully most non-European perfumers are still free to use this in commercial scents. And of course, if you are perfuming for your own pleasure or gifts, you may continue to use this glorious aroma chemical.

missing.title: Madranol
missing.description: MADRANOL® has a clean, sweet, powdery violet scent with nuances reminiscent of orris root, violet leaves, and faint raspberry or berry undertones. It is significantly less woody and less dry than the better-known methyl ionones. Compared to beta-ionone, it is more floral and less austere, which makes it especially useful for modernised violet accords where a lighter, fruitier tone is preferred over classical austerity. Its diffusiveness is moderate, with very good tenacity, making it well-suited for use in mid to base notes. Usage MADRANOL® elevates compositions with its refined powdery-floral character. Modern perfumers utilise it at 0.5-2% for sophisticated violet signatures. It delivers exceptional tenacity while maintaining transparency throughout development. Use MADRANOL® in conjunction with ionone derivatives for dimensional violet accords. Dose at higher concentrations (2-4%) in soaps for substantivity. Pair with green galbanum notes or heliotropin to create classical yet contemporary floral foundations. Applications Violet accords (paired with ionones, methyl heptine carbonate , or methyl ionone gamma ) Orris reconstructions (especially in combination with irone-type materials) Floral-powdery blends , such as heliotrope , mimosa , or aldehydic florals Soft berry or lipstick notes (when dosed subtly) Retro-modern feminines , especially in the 1950s–70s French tradition Its low harshness and gentle, slightly waxy sweetness make it ideal for high-end cosmetic applications as well, including fine soaps and lipsticks.

missing.title: Majantol®
missing.description: Majantol is a vibrant synthetic aroma chemical, providing a transparent and intensely floral Lily of the Valley note. This material is valued for its ability to impart a fresh, clean, and uplifting floral character to fragrances and is particularly valuable these days as more and more muguet materials are put on the chopping block of EU compliance. Use at 1-5% concentration for balanced floral heart notes. Combine with Hedione ® for enhanced diffusion and radiance. This material exhibits excellent stability across most product bases and exceptional substantivity on fabrics, making you successful in both fine fragrance and functional applications like detergents and softeners.

missing.title: Mandarin Aldehyde Total 10 TEC
missing.description: Mandarin Aldehyde was first discovered in orange skins in the 1940s. It is a wonderful chemical to use when needing an aldehydic boost to citrus and green fragrances. Mandarin Aldehyde is only available as a diluted product owing to its great strength. Even at 10% it conveys the most intense odour of Vietnamese mint, coriander and mandarin peels. The total version is a blend of isomers and makes for a very cost-effective citrus bomb.

missing.title: Maritima
missing.description: _*]:min-w-0"> Maritima opens with an intense burst of cold sea spray and metallic ocean air. This powerful marine pyridine captures the minerality of oyster shells and wet rocks at low tide. You'll recognise its distinctive character—that peculiar freshness after a storm at sea. _*]:min-w-0"> This material transforms aquatic accords from abstract freshness into photorealistic seascapes. Use it at 0.1% to add wet texture to white florals or green notes. At higher levels, it creates powerful marine effects that dominate compositions. Pair with Calone and Floralozone for complex oceanic accords that capture both the sparkle and depth of the sea. And for naturalness of course you mustn't forget Dimethyl Sulfide . _*]:min-w-0"> Maritima works brilliantly with aldehydes to amplify its metallic freshness. Combine with rose oxide for striking metallic-marine effects. Add traces to citrus compositions for a mineralic edge that cuts through sweetness and adds textural wetness.

missing.title: Mayol®
missing.description: Mayol is a clean and bright floral ingredient with a fresh scent that closely resembles lily of the valley. It adds a natural, smooth quality to fragrances and blends beautifully with jasmine, lilac, and tuberose. Its light and airy character also lifts citrus notes like bergamot while softening woody bases for a balanced effect. Mayol is versatile, working well in both fine perfumes and functional products like soaps and detergents. Its floral freshness is long-lasting, making it a valuable tool for creating soft, elegant compositions. Mayol's versatility can be seen where 2% modifies 9.5% lyral in Tom Ford's Tuscan Leather . It is also found in his Ombre Leather and Amouage's Opus XIV where a modest 0.05% contributes a light floral undertone.

missing.title: Melon Oliffac
missing.description: Melon Oliffac opens with bright, sparkling freshness - think ripe honeydew just sliced open on a warm morning. The juicy, fleshy sweetness sits over a clean green-rind character that keeps the note from ever becoming cloying. A subtle waxy-floral undertone adds body and realism that isolated melon chemicals simply cannot match. This IFF specialty base works as both a featured theme and a background modifier depending on dosage. At trace levels, it adds a dewy, fresh-cut quality to floral bouquets without being identifiable as melon. Overdose it and it becomes a full-blown fruity statement - ideal for summer scents and aqua-floral constructions. It excels at bridging volatile citrus top notes with heavier floral absolutes, adding moisture and transparency that dry aromachemicals struggle to provide.

missing.title: Melozone®
missing.description: This material is unbelievably underated. It is perhaps the most naturalising and radiant of all the green aroma chemicals yet it is so often overlooked. It has a dense earthiness absent from other similar products and a complexity that would make you believe you were smelling a blend rather than a single molecule. Traces can completely transform a mixture contributing fresh air and mildly aldehydic qualities. This material blends well with Melonal , Cis 3 Hexenol and its Acetate , Verdantol ™, Amazonia ™, Triplal , Floralozone , Calone Plus , Liffarome and Helional .

missing.title: Mesifuran
missing.description: Mesifuran opens with sweet burnt sugar and a distinctive musty earthiness — mushroom, raw potato, and a savoury warmth that initially reads more umami than gourmand. Coffee and nutty undertones add complexity. It occurs naturally in strawberry, raspberry, mango, and pineapple. Use Mesifuran to add that elusive cooked-fruit quality — the warmth of strawberry jam rather than fresh strawberry. It deepens and rounds fruit accords, particularly berry, tropical, and dried fruit compositions. A trace amount transforms a flat fruity note into something utterly convincing. Blend with the closely related strawberry furanone and gamma-decalactone for rich strawberry constructions. Try it in coffee and chocolate accords where the musty-caramellic facet adds authenticity. Over sixteen days' tenacity on blotter makes this one of the most persistent materials in your palette.

missing.title: Metal Oxazole
missing.description: METAL OXAZOLE (AKA Sclarene) opens with an immediate dry woody impact that's distinctly different from typical wood notes—there's something almost mineral-like in its presentation. This sclareol derivative doesn't smell of clary sage but rather presents a fascinating herbal-metallic character reminiscent of heated metal or steam rising from hot iron. The camphor facet adds coolness without menthol's sharpness, while earthy-green undertones ground the composition. What makes this material unique is its ability to suggest temperature—it smells warm yet cool, dry yet moist, creating an almost synesthetic experience. At 80% in DPG, this Givaudan specialty delivers consistent, powerful effects. We also offer a further dilution of 10% but note that when purchasing the 100% pure you are receiving the Givaudan standard 80% as it is the only form in which they manufacture it. Use Metal Oxazole at 0.1-1% for standard applications, though it can be overdosed for unique signature effects. Its primary value lies in enhancement rather than standalone character—use it to add metallic warmth to Ambrofix and other ambergris materials, creating more complex amber accords. As a "musk booster," it amplifies musky notes without contributing its own musk character, adding substantivity and fixation through different mechanisms. In modern masculine fragrances like Hermès H24, it provides the distinctive herbal-metallic signature that defines contemporary perfumery. The material excels at creating industrial coolness—that elusive quality of steam, hot metal, or mineral water that makes fragrances smell futuristic. Needless to say it is outstanding when combined with the hot metallic blend of Habanolide and Aldambre. Throw in a hint of cinnamon for a glittering combination. Metal Oxazole occupies a unique position in the sclareol-to-ambergris pathway. While sclareol provides clary sage character and Ambrofix delivers pure ambergris effects, Metal Oxazole offers something entirely different—

missing.title: Methyl Cyclogeranate
missing.description: _*]:min-w-0 gap-3"> _*]:min-w-0 gap-3"> Methyl cyclogeranate belongs to the same family as damascone alpha and delivers a similar luminous, fruity-rosy radiance — but without the sensitisation issues that increasingly restrict the damascones. This is the unrestricted alternative that gives you the same palette of effects. The character is lighter and more transparent than damascone itself. Where damascone alpha punches hard with a jammy plum-rose impact, methyl cyclogeranate suggests it. The apple facet is clean and ripe, the rose dewy rather than heavy, and a faint camphoraceous undertone keeps it from tipping into sweetness. It functions as a top-heart material rather than a heart-base, lifting compositions upward. _*]:min-w-0 gap-3"> Think of methyl cyclogeranate as your regulatory pressure valve. Wherever IFRA limits force you to ration damascones, this material fills the gap with its own fruity-floral signature. Try it alongside linalool and linalyl acetate to brighten citrus-herbal accords, or blend it with Ambrox for a contemporary fruity-amber contrast.

missing.title: Methyl Myristate
missing.description: Methyl myristate is barely there on the blotter—a whisper of waxy petals, faint honey, and the unmistakable fatty-smooth character of orris butter. This is not a material you smell and immediately identify; it is a material you notice when it is missing. That quiet, lipid-rich smoothness is the backbone of what makes natural iris smell so luxurious. Use methyl myristate to bring waxy realism to orris and iris accords built on ionones and methylionones. It rounds out mimosa, cassie, and tuberose bases with a fatty-floral body that reads as natural and expensive. In powder compositions alongside musks, it provides that soft, skin-like smoothness that separates flat from three-dimensional. Methyl myristate is the same fatty ester that constitutes much of orris butter's waxy body, so you are effectively adding the structural backbone of real iris without the price tag.

missing.title: Methyl Tuberate
missing.description: Methyl tuberate captures the waxy, lactonic heart of tuberose with remarkable precision. This powerful modifier brings an authentic white floral signature that lifts tuberose and gardenia accords beyond what absolutes achieve alone. You'll notice its metallic edge cuts through heavy florals whilst the creamy lactone body adds dimensional depth. Use this material to build the fleshy, fruity core of tuberose compositions alongside gamma decalactone and benzyl alcohol. It works brilliantly with fruity lactones to provide lift and airiness to otherwise dense white floral structures. Keep dosages around 0.5-1% in your concentrate—its strength means a little delivers substantial impact without overwhelming more delicate floral notes. Pair methyl tuberate with methyl anthranilate to amplify exotic white floral character. Benzyl salicylate softens its metallic facets whilst hydroxycitronellal extends its muguet-like freshness. This lactone excels when you need authentic tuberose tonality without the indolic heaviness that can dominate a composition.

missing.title: Microcare PEHG
missing.description: Microcare PEHG is a ready-to-use liquid preservative blend of phenoxyethanol and ethylhexylglycerin in a 90:10 ratio. It barely smells of anything — just the faintest rose-like hint from the phenoxyethanol, which vanishes entirely at working concentrations. Add it to any formula that contains water. If your product contains water — body sprays, room mists, toners, anything with an aqueous phase — it needs a preservative. Microcare PEHG gives you broad-spectrum protection against bacteria, yeasts, and moulds in a single, easy-to-use liquid. It is paraben-free, formaldehyde-free, and approved for use globally. Add it during the cool-down phase at half to one percent of your finished product. Phenoxyethanol also acts as a mild fragrance fixative, so it does double duty.

missing.title: Milk Lactone
missing.description: Milk Lactone (so-called as it is really an acid), is an intriguing material which, while clearly milky, exhibits an unusual but rather natural green quality. A hint of cheese and floralcy completes it. Use this to add a peach-skin effect to a fruity base or to enhance a lovely Gardenia base such as our Gardenia J. Ellis . This fine aroma chemical should not be confused with the product sold by some vendors as Milk Lactone Super or Milk Lactone (Mixture) which is really just a base built around Delta Dodecalactone. Milk Lactone blends with all the other lactones as well as green chemicals Stemone , Triplal , and Liffarome . This also finds use as an extender for rose absolute when combined with Phenoxanol.

missing.title: Mimosal™
missing.description: The latest muguet floral to hit the markets, Mimosal™ is designed to fill, at least partially, the gap left in the market with the banning of Lilial and Lyral. Mimosal is powerfully aldehydic bearing soft powdery floral notes with a watery aspect. It is novel in having something of a dual personality — crossing between muguet and Mimosa. Mimosal brings a clean, fresh long lasting muguet note for floral fragrances and is so elegant it could be considered a perfume in its own right. From Firmenich: “Intense green muguet note with a soft anisic facet and fresh cyclamen undertone. Mimosal is really performing and offers an impressive clean and long-lasting effect. It brings a fresh and soft muguet signature to floral accords. Mimosal is part of Firmenich's Beyond Muguet 2018.” Mimosal blends beautifully with Gardenia J. Ellis , Cyclamen des Alpes , Sandexol , all our Muguet bases , Dreamwood ™, Florol, and Hivernal® Neo.

missing.title: Mintonat
missing.description: Mintonat is not a straightforward mint material. It opens minty and fresh, yes, but immediately reveals floral-lavender depth, a warm spicy-clove facet, and a green herbal quality that makes it far more interesting and versatile than menthol or carvone. It smells like a herb garden rather than a peppermint sweet. Use it to boost freshness and vivacity across a wide range of compositions. It has a particular affinity for lavender, where it amplifies and rounds the herbal character beautifully. In fougères, it unites the aromatic top with the coumarin-oakmoss base in a way that feels seamless and natural. A little goes a long way. Pair it with lavender and coumarin for classic fougère construction, with bergamot and dihydromyrcenol for modern aromatic freshness, or with geranium for a herbal-floral heart. It fades quickly on paper but clings well to skin and fabric — judge it in wear, not on a blotter.

missing.title: Mirabelle Base 002000 F
missing.description: Mirabelle de Nancy is a type of yellow mirabelle plum tree that has scented blossoms — a rarity for fruit trees. Firmenich's Mirabelle base takes that delicate scent and builds a fantasy chord around it, of lactones, fruit, spices and florals. Mirabelle Base is unusual on first sniff, with its powerful lactones dominating the opening, shortly followed by the classic plum aroma chemicals and finally a balsamic cinnamon dry down which is very beautiful. In its own, the odour is quite reminiscent of the fruity character of Visa by Piguet. Blend it with Lactone Storm to add character, and with Prunella (Firmenich's classic plum base) to add radiance and top note power. You may not reach for this as frequently as Prunella, but it is definitely worth keeping in the arsenal.

missing.title: MMB
missing.description: MMB (Methoxymethyl Butanol) is a new product from Kuraray designed as a general purpose diluent to be used with air fresheners (reed diffusers, plugins, pump sprays etc). MMB has excellent solubility properties, exceeding those of most classic diluents, and a low odour. This is a must have material because solvents like DPG, TEC and IPM are not suitable for use in reed diffusers. MMB can be combined with alcohol to increase its evaporation rate, or with water to decrease it. It can also safely be combined with Isopar-M, Dowanol DPM and Dowanol TPM which are the more traditional types of diluent used for reeds. With a flash point over 70 Celsius degrees, it can be safely uses in products that need international air shipping without the fear of triggering dangerous goods costs. Check out our demonstration formula below to see MMB in use. This is our excellent and highly accurate replica of Ernesto by Cire Trudon.

missing.title: Muguet Aldehyde
missing.description: Muguet Aldehyde opens with a burst of aldehydic freshness that captures the elusive scent of lily-of-the-valley petals covered in morning dew. Its distinctive ozone character provides a cold, metallic sharpness reminiscent of fresh air after rain. The material combines a rosy-citrus heart with an almost aquatic transparency. You'll find this aldehyde transforms heavy floral accords by introducing ventilation and lift where traditional muguet materials feel flat. It bridges the gap between aggressive marine molecules and soft florals seamlessly, making unisex fragrances sing with its gender-neutral freshness. At 0.1-1% in your concentrate, it provides the diffusive power that projects off skin during the first four hours. Combine it with Florol to recreate the volume once provided by restricted materials. Layer it over patchouli for the legendary Mellis accord that vibrates with sweet-woody harmony. Trace amounts will modernise rose compositions by highlighting their lemony morning aspects rather than their heavier afternoon sweetness.

missing.title: Muguissimo™
missing.description: Muguissimo opens with a fresh, clean burst of lily-of-the-valley—bright and aldehydic but never harsh, with an immediate watery transparency. Beneath the muguet sits a soft cyclamen facet and subtle anisic sweetness. The overall effect is elegant, modern, and unmistakably floral.
