This is Firmenich's newest addition to their Beyond Muguet collection, released publicly in 2022 after years as a captive ingredient. What makes Muguissimo special is its linearity—it brings that fresh, clean muguet character from top note all the way through to the drydown, maintaining consistency throughout the life of a fragrance. Use it in white floral compositions, fresh feminine accords, and anywhere you need transparent lily-of-the-valley without the regulatory concerns of older muguet aldehydes. Despite being classified as a base note by volatility, it reads as fresh and transparent throughout. Dose it where you would use hydroxycitronellal or other muguet aldehydes. Pair it with Hedione, linalool, and other white floral materials for luminous bouquets, or use it in aquatic compositions where its watery facet enhances freshness.

missing.title: Muscarome
missing.description: A warm, powdery musk with buckskin softness — Muscarome J5 is a classical reconstruction of Tonkin deer musk 5% tincture. The smell is sensual and animalic, with creamy ambery-balsamic warmth and a subtle leathery edge. It is built around musk ketone and a supporting cast of musky-animalic materials. Use Muscarome J5 to give orientals, fougères, chypres and leather bases a classical animalic warmth without the cost of natural musk tincture. A small amount rounds the base and adds powdery skin depth; larger doses push into full deer-musk territory. It fixes light materials around it and extends the dry-down. Pair with sublimolide and Civettone Base for a rounded, refined musk accord, or push it alongside castoreum and costus Oliffac for a more openly animalic base. A trace under cedar or oud pulls them into skin territory. In chypres it revives a dusty oakmoss-labdanum backbone. Among the three classical deer musk reconstructions on the market, Muscarome J5 is the softest and most powdery, with a buckskin-smooth character and balsamic-ambery sweetness. Tonquitone (IFF) reads sharper and more openly animalic, with a pronounced civet-urinous edge and sweet caramel-vanilla facets. Shangralide Oliffac (IFF) sits between them — dirtier and more leathery than Muscarome J5, but less fierce than Tonquitone's direct deer-musk character.

missing.title: Muscenone®
missing.description: Muscenone is perhaps the nicest of the musk chemicals and certainly one of the most profound in its ability to add radiance, blending and fixation to a fragrance. This musk has the ability to put people at ease and to induce comfort, so much so that casinos famously spray it through their air conditioning ducts to keep clients gambling longer. Muscenone can be used in trace to overdose. According to Arctander: “Delicate, but extremely tenacious musky odor, upon dilution developing more woody notes, not quite as soft and velvety as those of the Muscone , perhaps equal in power, but inferior in beauty.” And Perfumery: Techniques in Evolution (a series of articles published in Perfumer and Flavorist magazine) says: “If habanolide is radiant, floral and musky with metallic notes, muscenone is animal, strongly musk tonkin, and plays a role in [replicating] the natural product’s odor, perhaps, more important[ly] than muscone . […] Muscenone smells of the most animal-like part of deer musk powder or musk absolute, if made. All of these unsaturated macro cyclic musks are incredibly strong and accords we made in the past mixed cresols with exaltolide or muscone and are now much finer and more elegant when using muscenone or chemically related products. It is being widely used in fragrances such as Bulgari for Men.” Muscenone even finds its uses in the world of ouds and attars; the wonderful tonkin musk note of Ajmal's Areej Al Shouk is owed largely to this chemical in combination with a touch of Muscone Laevo.

missing.title: Musk Ambrette
missing.description: Musk Ambrette is the fruitiest of the nitro musks and the classical musk that blends best with floral notes. It has an astonishing power to tame and beautify large quantities of coumarin and tonka bean and so became something of a work horse (often in concert with Musk Xylene ) in the fougère fragrances of the past. Edmond Roudnitska loved it so much that when he created Eau Sauvage for Dior (which contains no musks at all), he had a special version made with 10% Musk Ambrette. It was his private signature fragrance for the remainder of his life. Its most famous overdose was in the original Brut where it was used at 13% by Karl Mann for Fabergé in 1964. It is, however, effective at very small amounts. It blends beautifully with the other classic nitro musks which we also stock: Musk Xylene and Musk Ketone . IMPORTANT: Musk Xylene and Musk Ambrette are prohibited from fragrance use in most countries. At Fraterworks we do not use either of these musks in any of our products. We sell the musks solely so that fragrance aficionados can have access to all the materials of classical perfumery. This should not be used in production cosmetics or fragrances unless you are certain your target market allows it. NOTE: We package all high odour or high risk materials individually in separate heat sealed aluminium bags to mitigate any risk of cross-contamination.

missing.title: Musk R1
missing.description: Musk R1 opens with creamy, powdery softness that immediately evokes warm, clean skin. This macrocyclic lactone delivers the quintessential white musk character modern perfumery demands. Its lactonic sweetness brings an intimate, sensual dimension that transforms compositions. This material excels at creating that coveted "your skin but better" effect in fragrances. You'll find it indispensable for contemporary clean compositions where it adds depth without heaviness. Its exceptional substantivity ensures your creations maintain their intimate warmth for days on fabric. Combine Musk R1 with florals to enhance their creamy facets, or use it in amber bases for added sensuality. Layer it with other musks like Habanolide for complex skin effects. Small additions transform aldehydic compositions, rounding harsh edges while maintaining transparency.

missing.title: Musk Xylene
missing.description: Musk Xylene (or Musk Xylol) is the gentlemen's "shaving musk". Because of its soapy and fatty qualities, it was frequently found as part of classic fougère type fragrances and men's colognes in general. Perhaps its most famous overdose was in Canoe created by Jean Carles for Dana (see our demo named " Kayak " below for the formula of this classic fougère fragrance). It is, however, effective at very small amounts. It blends beautifully with the other classic nitro musks which we also stock: Musk Ambrette and Musk Ketone . Musk Xylene is a crystalline powder which you can add directly to your juice by weight as it will dissolve in the blend. IMPORTANT: Musk Xylene and Musk Ambrette are prohibited from fragrance use in most countries. At Fraterworks we do not use either of these musks in any of our products. We sell the musks solely so that fragrance aficionados can have access to all the materials of classical perfumery. This should not be used in production cosmetics or fragrances unless you are certain your target market allows it. NOTE: We package all high odour or high risk materials individually in separate heat sealed aluminium bags to mitigate any risk of cross-contamination.

missing.title: Myrac Aldehyde
missing.description: At full strength myrac aldehyde is waxy and overwhelming, but at working dilution it opens into something fresh, clean, and faintly floral — like standing outdoors on a bright morning. The citrus character is more orange than lemon, with an ozonic, marine quality underneath. It smells very different at 10% than it does neat. It extends citrus top notes well into the heart of a composition, maintaining orange-like brightness alongside materials that would otherwise be left without citrus support. In muguet accords it contributes a clean, green brightness. In marine compositions the ozonic facet adds outdoor realism. Bergamot, lemon oil, and hydroxycitronellal are natural companions on the citrus-floral side. For marine accords, hedione and dihydromyrcenol amplify the clean-air quality. Cedarwood and Iso E Super in the base give its brightness a woody foundation to rest upon.

missing.title: Myroxide
missing.description: Myroxide is an astonishingly powerful chemical. It opens with sweet, metallic freshness — herbal and immediately aromatic, like the best facets of lavender and clary sage distilled into a single material. Warm opoponax resinousness emerges underneath, adding unexpected depth. Fruity pear and tarragon accents round out a remarkably complex profile. Think of this as ocimene refined for fine perfumery — all the aromatic freshness and diffusion, none of the terpenic harshness. Even small additions give tremendous lift and volume to fougères, lavender compositions, and spicy accords. It brings unexpected brightness to citrus and oakmoss work too. Apply sparingly in citrus colognes where 0.3% increases brightness dramatically without smelling chemical. Combine with hedione for clean, diffusive floral-citrus topnotes or pair with oakmoss and coumarin for contemporary fougère structures. Works exceptionally well with coranol, vetiver, and aldehydes to accentuate woody-green facets. Avoid overdosing - this material's high power means even small amounts transform a composition's topnote character completely.

missing.title: Mysore Acetate
missing.description: Mysore Acetate has a clean, soft sandalwood character with an unusual violet-floral accent that sets it apart from every other sandalwood material. There is subtle amber warmth and a light tropical-fruit nuance in the background. It reads as transparent and woody rather than creamy or milky. The violet facet is what makes Mysore Acetate special — it bridges woody and floral notes in a way other sandalwood synthetics cannot. Use it to add woody depth to iris and violet accords, or floral dimension to sandalwood bases. It lasts well over a week on a blotter. Pair Mysore Acetate with ionones to amplify the violet-wood effect, or blend it alongside Javanol and Sandalore for a full sandalwood accord. The name references Mysore sandalwood — the Indian benchmark — and that is the quality it aims to evoke. Also sold under Symrise's trade name Sandelione.

missing.title: Nectarate
missing.description: Nectarate opens with pleasant, immediately recognisable peach and nectarine character—ripe, juicy, and naturalistic. The woody-balsamic undertone adds sophistication that prevents the fruit from becoming confectionery, while subtle green facets provide freshness. It delivers stone fruit realism that simpler peach materials cannot match. Use Nectarate to modernise rose and jasmine accords where it softens metallic edges while adding dewy freshness, to build realistic stone fruit accords in fruity-florals, or to add juicy lift to tropical and gourmand compositions. It amplifies the fruitiness of other molecules beautifully when blended with materials like Fructalate or ethyl 2-methyl butyrate. This material excels where others fail. Layer it with ethyl butyrate for seamless top-heart transition. Partner with ionones for sophisticated violet-peach lipstick accords.

missing.title: Nectarol 184139 D
missing.description: Nectarol smells convincingly of real honey — thick, waxy, and sweet with a slightly phenolic edge that keeps it from becoming saccharine. There is a piercing, almost wine-like depth beneath the sweetness. This is not a simple sugar-sweet honey; it has genuine complexity and bite. What sets Nectarol apart is how clean it reads in compositions. Firmenich designed it to push floral strength without dirtying the blend, and it does exactly that. Add it to rose or jasmine accords to bring warmth and richness, or use it as the heart of an oriental where you need honey without animalic heaviness. Build an amber accord around Nectarol by pairing it with benzoin and labdanum for a golden, nectarous warmth. It also works beautifully with tobacco absolute and tonka for a sophisticated gourmand facet. Dose carefully — the phenolic edge can become sharp if overdone, but at the right level it adds irresistible depth.

missing.title: Nectaryl
missing.description: Nectaryl opens with luscious nectarine character—ripe, juicy, and effortlessly natural. The peach-apricot facets add stone fruit depth, while creamy lactonic undertones evoke custard and coconut warmth. This is summer fruit rendered with sophistication: not candy-sweet but elegantly ripe, with the complexity of fruit fresh from the tree. This Givaudan chemical delivers what gamma-undecalactone promises but with far greater naturalism and tenacity. The material has 380-hour substantivity making it valuable across fine fragrance and functional applications alike; Nectaryl persists through the entire fragrance journey, anchoring fruity accords that would otherwise evaporate. Blend with Javanol for an unexpected peach-sandalwood accord, or layer with other lactones for tropical creaminess.

missing.title: Neo Patchouli
missing.description: It's like a mix of Apo Patchone, cloves, camphor, patchouli and Iso E Super. What a marvel and a wonderful material that almost no one knows about! Use it in traces as an alternative to all of the above, or in overdose for a truly novel approach to leather, earthy and even gourmand fragrances. A hidden jewel of perfumery, Neo Patchouli brings a polished, modern twist to classic woody and spicy themes. Its ultra-slow evaporation and deep, sweet-amber warmth create remarkable fixation, sophistication, and enduring presence in any composition.

missing.title: Neobutenone® Alpha
missing.description: Firmenich's Neobutenone® Alpha is the supreme expression of greenness in modern fragrances. At mere traces Neobutenone Alpha adds a modernity impossible to achieve with other materials. This is the Paradisone of green materials. Closely related — but vastly superior — to dynascone® (also known as galbascone). Neobutenone Alpha features in Aventus and many other fragrances were traces add an inimitable green fruity top note. This really is an essential material. Due to the high cost and strength we offer it here pure and in dilution at 10% in DPG.

missing.title: Neofolione
missing.description: Neofolione hits you with vivid green — crushed violet leaves, sliced green apple, a flash of cucumber. There is a metallic, almost aldehydic brightness to it that cuts through any composition. It is powerful, so measure carefully. This is the modern replacement for the now-restricted methyl heptine carbonate, and it has become a standard building block for violet accords. Use it alongside ionones and methyl ionones to construct realistic violet, or add it to green florals for that sharp, leafy opening that makes a fragrance feel alive and immediate. Pair it with alpha-ionone and methyl ionones for classic violet, with violet leaf absolute for depth, or with cassis and nonadienol for a contemporary green-fruity effect. It fades within about sixteen hours, so layer it over longer-lasting heart and base materials.

missing.title: Nerolidol
missing.description: Nerolidol opens with an understated elegance—a whisper rather than a shout. This sesquiterpene alcohol presents faint woody-floral notes that seem to hover just at the edge of perception, like "an aura of light or a cool breeze." The initial impression is deceptively mild: soft rose petals, fresh apple skin, and delicate muguet float above a woody base. Yet this subtle character masks exceptional staying power—what starts as barely perceptible evolves into a persistent presence that can last over 280 hours on a blotter, quietly supporting and enhancing everything around it. Deploy Nerolidol at 0.5-3% when you need sophisticated structural support without obvious character modification. Its true genius lies in functional excellence: as a blender, it seamlessly links disparate notes, smoothing harsh transitions between top and base; as a fixative, it anchors volatile materials while adding its own substantive trace. Use it to build delicate florals like muguet, honeysuckle, and peony where heavy fixatives would overwhelm. In woody-vanillic accords, it provides an "airy side" that prevents density. Its ability to enhance skin penetration makes it valuable in functional fragrances. Despite the similar names, Nerolidol and Nerol are fundamentally different materials with distinct roles in perfumery. The key difference lies in their molecular structure: Nerol is a C10 monoterpene alcohol (rose-fresh, citrusy, lighter), while Nerolidol is a C15 sesquiterpene alcohol (woody-floral, tenacious, heavier). Nerol provides bright, fresh rose with seashore wetness and moderate tenacity; Nerolidol offers subtle woody-floral depth with exceptional longevity. Nerol functions as a vibrant top-to-middle note in rose and citrus accords; Nerolidol serves as an invisible base note, fixative, and blender. The extra isoprene unit in Nerolidol's structure dramatically reduces volatility, transforming a fresh floral material into a sophisticated structural element. Choose Nerol for immediate

missing.title: Nerolin Bromelia
missing.description: Nerolin Bromelia opens with a soft acacia, wattle and neroli character that's distinctly more refined than its methyl ether cousin. You'll discover a mild yet tenacious orange blossom fragrance with grape and strawberry nuances emerging at lighter concentrations. This crystalline material melts easily at body temperature, releasing its characteristic powdery-floral sweetness that persists for hours. Use Nerolin Bromelia frequently with oranger crystals, methyl anthranilate and petitgrain to build convincing orange blossom accords. Its exceptional alkali stability makes it irreplaceable in fine soaps where other florals decompose. The drydown remains fresher compared to oranger crystals' honeyed warmth, providing the dry petal-like quality that grounds volatile citrus notes. Bromelia vs Yara Yara vs Fragarol The nerolin family comprises three beta-naphthyl ethers that share orange blossom character but differ meaningfully in personality. Yara Yara (methyl ether) is the most intense and industrial—powerfully diffusive with a harsh, pronounced naphthyl (mothball) edge that dominates functional fragrances where sheer impact matters. Its 400-hour substantivity and rock-bottom cost make it a workhorse for soaps and detergents. Bromelia (ethyl ether) is softer and rounder, retaining the orange blossom character but with less harshness and better alcohol solubility—easier to blend into refined compositions while still offering 400-hour tenacity. Fragarol (isobutyl ether) is the fruitiest of the three, with pronounced strawberry and berry facets alongside its floral character. Its lower substantivity (116 hours) and higher functional usage (up to 10%) make it more versatile for fine fragrance applications where that fruity-floral quality adds value. Choose Yara Yara for maximum power at minimum cost, Bromelia for balanced orange blossom character with finesse, and Fragarol when you want the nerolin signature with added fruity sweetness.

missing.title: Nerolin Fragarol
missing.description: The strawberry note hits first — sweet, ripe, unmistakable. Underneath sits a warm orange blossom character, musky and slightly powdery, that gives this material far more depth than a simple fruit note. The crystals melt close to room temperature, making them easy to work with as a liquid. That 116-hour persistence on a blotter is remarkable for something that smells this fresh and fruity. It works as both a heart note and a genuine fixative, holding your composition together long after brighter top notes have faded. In berry and orange blossom accords the dual character is especially valuable. Methyl anthranilate and neroli oil both complement its orange blossom side. For the strawberry facet, fruity lactones and ethyl maltol help build a convincing berry accord around it. White musks in the base extend the musky drydown into something genuinely long-lasting and skin-like. Yara Yara, Bromelia, Fragarol Three materials share the nerolin name but smell quite different. Nerolin Yara Yara is the most intense — a strong, somewhat harsh orange blossom note with a pronounced naphthyl character, historically popular in soaps. Nerolin Bromelia is softer and rounder, with a cleaner orange blossom quality better suited to fine fragrance. Nerolin Fragarol is the fruitiest of the three — the strawberry and berry facets set it apart, and it is the most versatile for modern perfumery work.

missing.title: Nerolin Yara Yara
missing.description: Intensely orange blossom with strong naphthalenic (mothball) nuances. Very useful for industrial or functional fragrances but also a wonderfully powerful neroli note to boost oranger crystals which are heavily restricted by IFRA. Blends extremely well with methyl anthranilate, oranger crystals, citrus products (orange blossom, neroli, petitgrain, citrus oil) and rose alcohols. We also stock Nerolin Bromelia and Nerolin Fragarol .

missing.title: Norlimbanol®
missing.description: Norlimbanol® is the classic Firmenich version of Timberol. It is a racemic blend and so is softer and easier to work with than the highly purified Norlimbanol® Dextro which we also stock; this racemic version is also much more affordable. Like the dextro form, Norlimbanol — in traces — boosts the woody and ambery notes of a fragrance, with an impact from top to bottom. This is the hedione of wood materials. It is indispensible and every perfumer should have it even if they already have Norlimbanol® Dextro. Nolimbanol® blends beautifully with Sandexol® , Ambre Royal , Ambrexol™ and Royal Leather . NOTE: We package all high odour or high risk materials individually in separate heat sealed aluminium bags to mitigate any risk of cross-contamination.

missing.title: Norlimbanol® Dextro
missing.description: Firmenich's Norlimbanol® Dextro is the purest form of the desirable dextro isomer of norlimbanol (timberol) on the market. It has a radiance and power that is unequalled. In traces this boosts the woody and ambery notes of a fragrance, with an impact from top to bottom. This dextro product is to norlimbanol, what paradisone is to hedione. This is the supreme quality. Nolimbanol® Dextro blends beautifully with Sandexol® , Ambre Royal , Ambrexol™ and Royal Leather . NOTE: We package all high odour or high risk materials individually in separate heat sealed aluminium bags to mitigate any risk of cross-contamination.

missing.title: Nutty Furan
missing.description: Nutty Furan opens with an intense, musty nuttiness — roasted hazelnuts and toasted almonds layered with sweet hay-coumarin warmth. A coconut-milky softness emerges underneath, giving the material a genuinely edible quality. The overall impression is warm, roasted, and deeply comforting. This is a concentrated material — a trace transforms vanilla and tonka compositions into praline-gourmand territory. It adds toasted depth to tobacco and coffee accords, and that hay-coumarin facet gives it versatility beyond pure gourmand. Pair it with vanillin, coumarin, and cocoa absolute for dark confectionery effects. Use Nutty Furan at microdose levels — its strength is remarkable. It occurs naturally in coffee, black tea, roasted filberts, and raisins, all foods defined by that same toasted character. Blend with ethyl maltol, benzoin, and tonka for a warm praline accord that smells genuinely baked.

missing.title: Nutty Pyrazine
missing.description: It may be called Nutty Pyrazine but on first whiff it is decidedly hot buttered popcorn. What a delightful chemical when used correctly. It features in our own Frater fragrance Menagerie and is often used to create a nutty scent or as part of a broader gourmand blend. Essential for recreations of coffee and, of course, nuts and popcorn, this chemical is powerful so we sell it at 1% in DPG . If you want pure, we can accommodate you, just drop us a line. Even at 1% so we recommend further dilution. Nutty Pyrazine blends beautifully with Filbertone , Orbitone, Nutmeg Absolute , Birch Tar , gourmand and wood chemicals. NOTE: We package all high odour or high risk materials individually in separate heat sealed aluminium bags to mitigate any risk of cross-contamination.

missing.title: Oakmossarome
missing.description: Oakmossarome, a Synarome base, opens with a clean, mossy-woody impression that feels polished and refined. There's a gentle sweetness here—not gourmand, but balsamic and resinous, like warm amber. Soft leathery undertones emerge in the dry-down, lending the kind of furry, animalic depth that once defined classic cuir fragrances. This Synarome specialty base acts as a powerful harmoniser, smoothing transitions between heart and base notes. You can use it as the structural backbone of a chypre or fougère, or at trace levels to add green depth and fixation to white florals. Pair it with bergamot, labdanum and patchouli for a modern chypre skeleton, or combine it with lavender and coumarin for a classic masculine dry-down. Think of Oakmossarome as the refined sibling of traditional oakmoss - all the structural power, none of the heavy seaweed-mushroom baggage. Try it alongside Isobutyl Quinoline or Ambrarome for dark leather accords, or blend with Helional or Algenone to build contemporary marine chypres. Its great tenacity makes it a serious fixative weapon.

missing.title: Oakwood Base, Ventos
missing.description: Oakwood Base, Ventos smells like the inside of a spirits cellar. Dark, rich oak wood meets cognac and whisky-barrel booze, threaded with woodsmoke, sweet vanilla and a nutty chestnut warmth. A balsamic sweetness rounds the whole thing off. Because of the sweetness, it is an excellent base to add a touch of smoke without dominating as easily as you can with Birch and Cade. A touch will ground woody, leather and oriental accords in aged-barrel warmth, and it turns sweet gourmand ideas boozy, lending cognac, rum and whisky effects an authentic woody backbone.

missing.title: Octinoxate
missing.description: Octinoxate is sunscreen for your perfume, not a scent material. This colourless, low-viscosity liquid absorbs UVB radiation (280–320 nm) before it can break down fragrance molecules. At typical use levels, it contributes no detectable odour to a composition. Use Octinoxate wherever UV-sensitive ingredients need shielding — citrus oils, aldehydes, and terpenes are the first casualties of light exposure. It's miscible with most fragrance oils and doubles as a co-solvent, dissolving other oil-soluble additives with ease. Simply stir it into your oil phase. One critical caveat: Octinoxate and Avobenzone destabilise each other under UV light unless a photostabiliser is also present. Add Oxynex ST at just 0.5% to quench this reaction and protect both filters. For UVB-only protection, pair Octinoxate with 2-Ethylhexyl Salicylate instead. Octinoxate vs Avobenzone Octinoxate and Avobenzone protect against different portions of the UV spectrum. Octinoxate absorbs UVB (280–320 nm) — the shorter-wavelength radiation that degrades terpenes, aldehydes, and other volatile components. Avobenzone absorbs UVA (320–400 nm) — the longer-wavelength light responsible for yellowing liquids and breaking down vanillin. Octinoxate is a pourable liquid that incorporates instantly; Avobenzone is a crystalline powder requiring heat (80–85°C) and a co-solvent to dissolve. Octinoxate itself can dissolve up to 26% Avobenzone by weight, making it a useful carrier for the powder. However, the two destabilise each other through photocyclisation unless a photostabiliser like Oxynex ST is included as a third ingredient. With Oxynex ST present (just 0.5% of the finished formula), the combination provides excellent broad-spectrum UV protection for your fragrances.

missing.title: Okoumal
missing.description: Okoumal smells of warm, dry wood wrapped in soft amber and snuff. It is not loud — in fact, some people cannot smell it at all in isolation. But add it to a composition and the effect is unmistakable: warmth, volume, and richness appear from nowhere. This is one of those rare materials that works by stealth. Use it at low doses to fill out woody and amber bases, adding body and expensive-smelling roundness. It lasts over 420 hours on a blotter — well over a month — making it one of the most tenacious fixatives available. Evaluate it in blends rather than on its own. Pair it with cedarwood for rich woody depth, with patchouli and vetiver for dark, earthy warmth, or with sandalwood materials for a smooth, enveloping base. A little goes a long way — start at trace levels and build up until you feel its effect on the composition's body.

missing.title: Olibanol
missing.description: The very purest heart of olibanum, Olibanol from Robertet is a perfect natural isolate that can be used anywhere a clean incense note is needed. It is a co-distillation on natural triethyl citrate making it very easy to use. When comparing it to our other beautiful Olibanum Coeur MD , the Olibanol is fresher and more vibrant but less complex. They are both very compatible with one another and you should certainly have both. This is a pure and natural material and complies with ISO 9235.

missing.title: Olibanum Coeur MD
missing.description: Under the beating desert sun the frankincense tree exudes its sweet gum so revered it was offered as one of the Magi's gifts to Christ. For millennia this precious resin has been used in religious sacraments and ceremonies and blended with sweet oils to make fragrances for royal courts. If heaven were scented, this would be that scent. Olibanum Coeur begins as pure olibanum resin and through the mastery of modern molecular science is distilled to its purest heart. This is the most sublime extraction of the Frankincense tree on the market today. It can be used one for one anywhere olibanum gum, resinoid and absolute are used. This is a pure and natural material and complies with ISO 9235. It is a viscous liquid but pourable at room temperature.

missing.title: Onestolide®
missing.description: Onestolide (high purity Dihydroambrettolide) opens with a sophisticated sweet muskiness that immediately distinguishes itself through its balsamic richness and distinctive animalic undertones. This macrocyclic lactone presents a fascinating duality—simultaneously clean and animalic—creating depth without heaviness. The crystalline, vibrant quality particularly characteristic of Synarome's 98% grade adds luminosity to its inherent warmth. Use Onestolide when you need exceptional fixation combined with character. Its remarkable diffusion enhances delicate florals without overpowering them, while its animalic facets create sensual depth in amber accords. This material excels at bridging modern clean aesthetics with classical warmth, making it indispensable for contemporary oriental compositions. Combine with Aerolide ®, Exaltolide or ethylene brassylate for complex musk accords. It harmonises beautifully with methylionones, vetiver derivatives, and aldehydes, while lending crucial support to labdanum and vanilla in amber bases. Dihydroambrettolide vs Ambrettolide The key distinction between Dihydroambrettolide and its unsaturated cousin Ambrettolide lies in their fundamental olfactive characters. While Ambrettolide presents pronounced floral and fruity facets with red fruit sweetness reminiscent of ambrette seeds, Dihydroambrettolide shifts the balance toward animalic warmth and balsamic depth. Where Ambrettolide might lift a composition with botanical muskiness, Dihydroambrettolide grounds it with sensual warmth, making it the preferred choice for amber fragrances and compositions requiring direct, less "botanical" musk character.

missing.title: Operanide
missing.description: First discovered in 2001 by the same IFF chemist that discovered AmberXtreme, Operanide is one of the most perfect modern amber molecules with a creamy quality nuanced by moss, soft woods and gourmand facets. It is an incredibly diffusive and radiant material which joins the likes of Amber Xtreme, Ambrocenide , Amberketal and others in the radiant amber family, though usable in far greater amounts as it is considerably easier to control. Until recently a captive of IFF. A simple blend of Operanide and Amber Xtreme results in an accord more elegant, more radiant and more beautiful than either chemical singularly. To that you can add profound fixative qualities with a touch of Z11® MIP (preferable to the HD version). Even a small amount of Operanide adds a lovely creaminess and naturalises blends astonishingly well. It adds varnish to wood materials. In addition, Operanide blends beautifully with Ambrocenide , Musks Zenolide and Edenolide, tonka materials (for example Florex and Coumarone ), everything patchouli (especially Clearwood ®), Vetiverol and Vetiveryl Acetate , the Rose Ketones (with olfactorily similar chemicals such as Ethyl Safranate) and the ozonic / marine family (Cascalone, Calone, Maritima, Floralzone, etc).

missing.title: Orange Flower Ether
missing.description: Orange Flower Ether opens with an immediate burst of bitter citrus reminiscent of fresh grapefruit peel, yet softened by subtle floral whispers that prevent it from being aggressively sharp. This sophisticated duality makes it indispensable for contemporary perfumery where clean, bright openings are paramount. Its unique position between pure citrus materials and true orange blossom extracts provides perfumers with precise control over their top note architecture. Deploy this material at 2-5% when you need to inject life into tired citrus accords or create seamless transitions from citrus tops to floral hearts. Its particular genius lies in enhancing natural neroli without the heaviness of orange blossom absolute —think of it as neroli's sparkling cousin who arrives early to every party. Combine it with natural bergamot to amplify its Earl Grey facets, or layer it with pink grapefruit for a photorealistic pomelo effect that maintains stability where natural oils fail. The practical applications for Orange Flower Ether extend far beyond traditional cologne structures into modern clean beauty and functional fragrances. Its exceptional stability in soaps and acidic products makes it your go-to for maintaining citrus-floral character in challenging bases. Use it to build contemporary "white shirt" accords by combining with hedione and white musks, or create addictive fresh-fruity openings by pairing with rhubarb and cassis bases.

missing.title: Orcinyl 3
missing.description: This crystalline captures the essential phenolic and leathery facets of traditional oakmoss absolute. It has impressive tenacity and provides reliable structure and longevity to sophisticated compositions. Use orcinyl at 0.05-1% concentration in formulations with Evernyl for complete oakmoss effects. This material creates excellent synergy with patchouli, vetiver, and labdanum notes. Apply in chypre and fougère bases requiring compliant mossy character. Owing to the high cost and strength, we are offering this diluted to 10% or pure.

missing.title: Orivone®
missing.description: Orivone imparts a distinctive floral-woody aroma characterised by prominent iris-like and powdery notes, enriched with subtle camphoraceous and earthy undertones. Its sophisticated scent effectively mimics the prized orris root, making it invaluable for crafting elegant iris accords economically. Orivone is highly valued for enhancing floral compositions, notably violet and iris-centric fragrances, and lending depth to powdery, woody blends. Its powerful diffusivity and cost-effectiveness also make it ideal for use in functional products like soaps, lotions, and detergents.

missing.title: Osyrol
missing.description: Osyrol is a very light sandalwood chemical (one of a myriad). It is extremely versatile as it can be used in very high doses as a canvas chemical. It is sweet and clean and has floral nuances and it blends extremely well with most of the sandalwood family. It is used to good effect in Coco (Chanel, 1984) with Sandalore and Mysore Sandalwood , and the original M7 (2002) by YLS at 1%. It also features in Allure Homme by Chanel (0.3%), Burberry Women at a huge 9%, 1.25% of J'Adore by Dior, and Pardon by Nasomatto.

missing.title: Oud Oliffac
missing.description: This IFF oud base opens with fruity sweetness, a touch of dank earth, and the whisper of a medicinal note. This is followed by balsams, spices (particularly cinnamon) and a quiet animalic growl. This is almost like a refined version of the classic Firmenich Oud Synth . Unlike Oud Synth, this IFF speciality is less vetiver forward. The blending is impeccable. This is one of the most polite (but not tame) oud bases and one I heartily recommend. If you are new to oud, this is a good start. Blend it with red berry aromachemicals like dulcinyl , rasberry ketone, and raspberry glycidate , or with our highly popular Raspberry Ripple base . To bring out the spiced notes I recommend Firmenich's Pretty Oud .

missing.title: Oudhbois
missing.description: Oudhbois is a speciality product (sold by some retailers as Oudamide). It is a woody aroma chemical with nuances of grapefruit (nootkatone type) and oud and a whisper of animal. It blends beautifully with other woody materials such as Cedrol crystals, Aetoxylon Oil , Orbitone ® and Iso E Super ™. Use it to make a dark fantasy base of gnarled wood or as an alternative to the common woods that are overdosed in most modern fragrances. This product is found in a few significant fragrances such as Marc-Antoine Barrois's 2019 Ganymede (formula below) and Tom Ford's Santal Blush and Plum Japonais , however widespread adoption is still yet to occur. Be the first!

missing.title: Oxynex® ST
missing.description: Oxynex® ST is an essential stabiliser, safeguarding fragrance integrity against light and oxidation . It ensures your perfumes and cosmetics remain true and vibrant . Use it alone in your finished product or with Solgard ® for added protection. Oxynex® is the commercial name for Diethylhexyl Syringylidenemalonate in Fractionated Coconut Oil (FCO). This oil base ensures DESM’s solubility and modifies its texture and consistency . Due to the FCO, Oxynex® ST also acts as an emollient, offering a light conditioning skin-feel upon perfume application. Oxynex® ST is a synthetic molecule derived from Syringa Aldehyde and no natural form exists. If you already use our Solgard® technology, you may still want to add a touch of Oxynex® ST because it has a powerful synergy with Avobenzone which is a key material in that best seller. Use it at just 0.2 – 0.5% of your finished perfume. Use Case: Eau de Parfum 200 Fragrance Compound 788 Perfumer's Alcohol 8 Solgard® E 4 Oxynex® ST In the formula above you can omit the Solgard® but keep the Oxynex® quantity the same. If you are using our Deluxe Perfumer's Alcohol , omit the Solgard® from the formula above.

missing.title: Oxyoctaline Formate
missing.description: Oxyoctaline Formate opens with a distinctive moist woodiness — not the dry, static cedar of most woody molecules, but something that feels alive, like freshly sawn timber still wet with sap. An incense-like dryness settles in quickly, powdery and dusty, with a refined amber warmth that recalls good frankincense without the sharp resinous bite. Givaudan developed this as a blender, and that is where it truly excels. It fills the space between transparent woody notes and heavy amber bases, creating seamless transitions that make compositions feel more expensive and more coherent. Use it in sandalwood accords where its moist character adds realism, or drop it into oud compositions where its resinous quality supports the raw-wood facets without adding sweetness. Think of it as the mortar between bricks. It does not call attention to itself, but remove it and the structure feels hollow. Pair it with Iso E Super for a modern woody foundation, or combine with labdanum and olibanum for an amber accord that smells like it grew rather than being assembled.

missing.title: Pamplefleur®
missing.description: Pamplefleur opens with a tart, zesty burst of grapefruit peel tempered by a sharp rhubarb bite. Unlike fleeting citrus terpenes, this material carries dry, earthy vetiver undertones. The effect sits somewhere between fresh-cut peel and sun-warmed root vegetables. This phenyl-substituted alcohol solves the age-old citrus problem: longevity. Where Methyl Pamplemousse flashes brightly and fades, Pamplefleur persists through the heart and into the base. Layer both materials together for a linear grapefruit effect that carries from opening spray to final drydown. Its animalic warmth also makes it unexpectedly effective for lifting jasmine accords. Think of Pamplefleur as your citrus anchor rather than your citrus sparkle. Blend it with Iso E Super for clean, modern woody-citrus effects found in sport and blue fragrances. Pair with Paradisamide for tropical guava-grapefruit combinations. Use restraint—overdose pushes it toward rubbery synthetic territory, but at trace levels it adds convincing rind realism to any fruit accord.

missing.title: Pamplocoeur
missing.description: Pamplocoeur opens with a bright, fizzy grapefruit burst that feels almost effervescent on the blotter. There is a distinct sweetness here - think pink pomelo flesh rather than bitter rind. A soft floral shimmer sits underneath, giving the whole impression an airy, sparkling quality that natural grapefruit oil simply cannot sustain. This is Firmenich's answer to the instability problem that plagues natural grapefruit oil. Where the natural decays into sulphurous off-notes, Pamplocoeur holds its juicy, tart character throughout the life of your product. Pair it with Hedione to boost its radiance and sillage, or add Oxane to push the profile toward tropical passionfruit and blackcurrant. It works brilliantly as a freshener in floral hearts - a few percent into jasmine or rose prevents heaviness without adding obvious citrus. Think beyond straightforward grapefruit accords. Combine Pamplocoeur with Methyl Pamplemousse to build convincing yuzu reconstructions. Blend it into woody compositions alongside Iso E Super and vetiver for a bitter-fresh contrast that reads as sophisticated and modern.

missing.title: Pandanol
missing.description: If you have ever buried your nose in chrysanthemums, you already know this molecule. Sharp, green, and penetrating, with a metallic floral brightness and rosy-jasmine facets underneath. It is the main component of kewda oil and essentially is the chrysanthemum note in perfumery. What surprises is the tenacity. Pandanol smells like a fleeting top note but persists for nearly ninety hours on a blotter — a genuinely unusual combination of ethereal character and lasting power. On dilution the sharpness softens into something grassy and warm, almost pungent, with more rose showing through. A trace in heavy floral accords cuts through the opacity and weight. Indispensable for kewda ( it comprises up to 80% of the natural material from Pandanus fascicularis ) and chrysanthemum recreations, it also lifts jasmine and hyacinth compositions with its penetrating green radiance. Phenylethyl alcohol, hedione, and galbanum are its most natural companions.

missing.title: Para Cresyl Caprylate
missing.description: Para Cresyl Caprylate is the gentle member of the cresyl family. But don't be fooled! While it has a much smaller impact on top notes, it has a wonderfully long dry down and modifying effect. A delicately fecal animalic with traces of hay, ylang-ylang, narcissus and jasmine, this has a surprisingly broad range of applications, from florals to oud recreations. Para Cresyl Caprylate was sometimes used in overdose in honeysuckle and animalic accords, but in smaller amounts (typically under 0.1%) it adds texture and naturalness to florals. This is a material that all perfumers should stock. It may have fewer applications than classic Para Cresol but it is invaluable nonetheless.

missing.title: Para Cresyl Methyl Ether
missing.description: Para cresyl methyl ether hits you with an immediate phenolic punch that rapidly unfurls into something unmistakably ylang-ylang. Beneath that sweet floral attack, you catch powdery, nutty facets and a faint camphoraceous edge. On a strip, it softens into a greener, almost marigold-like drydown. This is one of those materials whose true magic only reveals itself inside a blend. A trace amount lifts narcissus, jasmine, and ylang accords from pleasant to convincing, lending the phenolic-animalic undertow that makes real flowers smell alive. It bridges the gap between clean florals and the darker, cresylic facets found in narcissus absolute, tuberose, and champaca, without the heaviness of para cresol itself. Work with it at low levels in a 10% dilution to keep control. Pair it with indole and para cresyl phenyl acetate for a narcissus heart, or stir it into ylang reconstructions alongside benzyl acetate and isoeugenol. In leather accords, it reinforces the phenolic backbone beautifully. Always evaluate in dilution first—neat, the camphoraceous top note can mislead your nose about what this material truly contributes.

missing.title: Parmantheme
missing.description: Parmantheme opens with an unmistakable blast of Parma violet — green, leafy, almost cucumber-fresh on top, then quickly powdery and sweet. The ionone backbone gives it terrific projection. In dilution, it becomes beautifully soft and cosmetic. This is a complete violet accord in a bottle. The green-waxy topnotes come from nonadienol and nonadienal components, while a generous ionone core provides the classic powdery body that defines violet in perfumery. Use it as a starting point for any violet-forward composition, or add traces to floral bouquets for an elegant powdery lift. Parmantheme rewards restraint — try it at low levels in a chypre for subtle violet warmth, or push it harder in a standalone soliflore. Pair it with orris butter for added realism, or with musks and sandalwood for a vintage powdery effect. It dominates easily, so build around it rather than layering it in.

missing.title: Parmentier Pyrazine
missing.description: Parmentier Pyrazine opens with unmistakable roasted character—nutty, coffee-like, and immediately evocative of foods transformed by heat. The burnt woody facets add complexity, while earthy potato notes provide the distinctive quality that earned this material its name (after Antoine-Augustin Parmentier, the French agronomist who championed the potato). Toasted cocoa and savoury broth undertones complete a profile that smells genuinely edible. Work with Parmentier Pyrazine at high dilution—evaluate at 0.1% or less to appreciate its nuances without overwhelming your nose. Use it alongside other pyrazines like Grenoble, Praslin, and Torref to build complex roasted accords. The earthy-potato facet distinguishes it from purely nutty pyrazines, making it valuable in compositions where root vegetable warmth or cooked-food authenticity is desired. Excellent in gourmand, tobacco, and leather contexts. This pyrazine is named after Antoine-Augustin Parmentier (1737–1813) who convinced the French to add potatoes to their diet by various clever marketing tricks such as having King Louis XVI wear potato flowers in his buttonhole. Some Clever Uses The Synthetic Oudh Base Real Oudh oil has a "rot" and "fermented" quality that is very hard to fake. A trace of Parmentier Pyrazine combined with Castoreum and Cypriol creates an incredibly realistic "barnyard" Oudh effect. The earthy/potato note mimics the rotting wood of the Agar tree perfectly. The "Dark" Chocolate Most chocolate accords smell like cheap Easter eggs (too much Vanillin and Isobutavan). Parmentier Pyrazine adds the bitterness. It mimics the smell of the cocoa nib roasting in the drum. It turns a "Milk Chocolate" accord into "70% Dark Chocolate". And of course a touch of civet absolute takes the blend in a ganache direction. The Coffee Illusion If you are making a coffee base, Torref Pyrazine gives you the smell of the dry beans. Parmentier gives you the smell of the hot liquid espresso. It provides the "wet grounds" no

missing.title: Passifloran 1% DPG
missing.description: Unbelievably potent, we sell this at a usable 1% in DPG (previously at 0.1% so check your dose carefully). Passifloran is catty, buchu-like, tropical, fruity, sulphurous and vegetative. It is a profoundly good material for adding naturalness to fruit accords or even in traces as a passionfruit note in a fragrance. Perfumery: Techniques in Evolution (a series of articles published in Perfumer and Flavorist magazine) calls this “one of the best tropical fruit ingredients every synthesized.” Passifloran blends beautifully with Oxane, Magnificent Mandarin, Pomelo Grandis, Citrus oils and fruit notes. NOTE: We package all high odour or high risk materials individually in separate heat sealed aluminium bags to mitigate any risk of cross-contamination.

missing.title: Passion Fruit Base 109223
missing.description: Passion Fruit Base 109223 GEB opens like a spoonful of fresh tropical fruit puree. You get soft, rounded smoothness leaning toward kiwifruit, mango, and creamy peach rather than sharp passion fruit. Everything sits in a gentle milky haze that makes the impression plush and almost edible. This base builds tropical accords instantly without sourcing a dozen individual components. It excels in modern fruity feminines where you want creamy, rounded fruit rather than sharp acidity. Dose carefully though; the full impact develops over a week and will sneak up on you. Layer it with peach and apricot for stone fruit richness, or brighten with bergamot and lychee for a sparkling tropical opening. Add Oxane or Passifloran in traces to push the character toward authentic passion fruit tartness. At higher levels the kiwifruit facet becomes more pronounced.

missing.title: Pastry Carbaldehyde
missing.description: Pastry Carbaldehyde (5-Methyl Furfural) opens with soft caramellic warmth that's gentler and more refined than furfural's harsh character. This extraordinarily powerful material captures the essence of heated sugars transforming into rich caramel, with prominent bready-brown notes of fresh pastry crust. The spicy roasted grain character carries subtle almond-cherry facets nuttier than benzaldehyde, adding unexpected depth. You'll find Pastry Carbaldehyde invaluable for creating authentic caramelised effects in gourmand compositions. Use at 0.01-0.2% maximum where it provides the crucial "heated sugar" foundation beneath coffee, chocolate, and brown sugar accords. The material excels in tobacco themes where its roasted sweetness enhances leaf character, and in autumn concepts evoking harvest warmth. The compound bridges sweet and savoury territories brilliantly - think maple bacon, roasted nuts, or rum-soaked fruitcake. Combine with coffee Arabica CO2 for enhanced roasted depth, maltol for sweeter caramel effects, or almond pyrazine for nuttier facets. Its natural occurrence in coffee, roast beef, and baked goods explains its authentic culinary warmth that synthetic sweeteners cannot replicate. Difference from Furfural While both are furan aldehydes born from sugar caramelisation, Pastry Carbaldehyde offers crucial advantages. Furfural brings harsh, bitter secondary notes and faces severe IFRA restrictions (0.001% skin contact). Pastry Carbaldehyde's methyl group creates a softer, more refined caramel without furfural's harshness, plus subtle almond-cherry nuances furfural lacks. With usage up to 0.2% - that's 200 times more freedom than furfural - it's the practical choice for modern perfumery. Where furfural delivers burnt toast with bitter edges, Pastry Carbaldehyde provides warm croissant with caramel glaze.

missing.title: Patchone
missing.description: Patchone has a dry, woody, distinctly patchouli-like character with a camphoraceous bite and subtle leathery warmth. It reads as the stripped-back, structural side of patchouli — the woody earthiness without the sweet, fruity top notes. A balsamic, pine-like quality rounds out the profile and keeps it from feeling too austere. Use patchone as a patchouli modifier or replacement in your woody, oriental, and chypre compositions. It dries down floral notes effectively, adding structure and earthy depth. Combine it with richer patchouli materials to extend and sharpen the woody base of your accords. Blend with patchouli oil and vetiver for a deep, earthy woody foundation. Try it alongside cedarwood and Iso E Super for a modern transparent woody base. Pair with rose and violet materials where its drying effect creates elegant contrast between floral sweetness and woody depth.

missing.title: Patchoulol Crystals PA99
missing.description: Patchoulol (patchouli alcohol) is the "coeur" element of patchouli oil. After trials and tests of products from all the major suppliers, the Ventos patchoulol comes out miles ahead. It has absolutely no off notes. Small amounts can sweeten patchouli oil, while large overdoses can add a wonderfully novel new woody earthy character to a fragrance. This product is 100% natural according to ISO 9235 standards and can be used in all natural perfumes.

missing.title: Patchoulyl Acetate
missing.description: A speciality of Ventos, Patchouli Oil Acetylated is a real treasure for those who love patchouli. It has a more intense and definitely sweeter profile than regular patchouli oil. Its blends with the rose ketones are astonishingly good and it can be used with no limits under IFRA. It can't be stressed enough that this is perhaps the most elegant of all the patchouli extracts and one we highly recommend.

missing.title: PEG 60 HCO
missing.description: PEG-60 hydrogenated castor oil is a non-ionic solubiliser that dissolves fragrance oils cleanly into water. The result is a crystal-clear solution — no cloudiness, no separation, no residue. It is essentially odourless, so your fragrance reads exactly as you intended. The critical technique is premixing: blend PEG-60 HCO with your fragrance oil first at a 3:1 to 5:1 ratio, then add this premix slowly to water. Skipping this step produces cloudy, unstable solutions. Use it in room sprays, body mists, linen sprays, water-based perfumes, and micellar waters. It arrives as a white wax that melts around 35°C — warm it gently to liquefy before measuring. Unlike polysorbate 20, it produces virtually no foam and has no detectable odour of its own. Always use distilled water and always add a preservative to water-based formulations. This can also be used in regular alcohol fragrances as a texture enhancer. Fraterworks makes no guarantees as to the suitability of this material for any purposes beyond its minor use in alcoholic fine fragrances.

missing.title: Peomosa
missing.description: Peomosa opens with an impressively natural wet-petal aroma that captures flowers still glistening with morning dew. This distinctive green-cortex character immediately distinguishes it from traditional rose alcohols. You'll notice how it creates spatial dimension in florals, adding the waxy texture of real petals. This material excels at bridging harsh top notes to creamy bases while maintaining transparency. Use it at 1-3% to add peony's characteristic dusty-powdery sweetness to any floral bouquet. A green freshness and subtle wet-earthy quality give this material its distinctive transparent, watery character that feels like petals just after rain. Combine Peomosa with rose oxide for wet-petal realism, or blend with ionones for cosmetic powder effects. It has excellent compatibility with syringa aldehyde. Its medium strength allows generous dosing without overwhelming compositions. Apply it strategically when you need florals to feel alive rather than dried.

missing.title: Peranat
missing.description: Peranat delivers one of the most convincingly natural pear notes available. The aroma is clean, sweet, and unmistakably pear-like, with subtle floral undertones that hint at jasmine and a faint woody-orris quality in the drydown. It reads as genuinely fruity rather than synthetic or candy-like. Use peranat to add realistic pear character to your fresh and fruity-floral compositions. It pairs naturally with white florals — freesia, lily of the valley, peony — where its clean fruitiness brightens the heart. Combined with bergamot it creates sparkling citrus-fruit openings that feel contemporary and sophisticated. Blend with other pear materials for a layered, multidimensional fruit effect. Try it alongside sandalwood and cedarwood where its fruity sweetness creates an elegant contrast against warm wood. Pair with hedione and muguet bases for the kind of fresh fruity-floral accords that typify modern feminine perfumery.

missing.title: Phenoxanol®
missing.description: Phenoxanol stands in for rose absolute when rose absolute is too costly to use in large doses. It is a rich and long lasting heart note with similarities to Phenyl Ethyl Alcohol. Cécile Zarokian uses it in a megadose in her Rose Aqor (2021) attar for Amouage (formula below) to contribute the main rose note in addition to a selection of high powered synthetics and it is also a key rose note in Gris by Dior. Phenoxanol has a strong yet refined character which allows for the creation of fragrances with remarkable radiance and persistence. It is one of those chemicals that contributes a highly appealing quality to perfumes and certainly should be exploited far more often because of it.

missing.title: Phenyl Ethyl Cinnamate
missing.description: Phenethyl Cinnamate presents a distinctive olfactory profile, characterised by rich, balsamic warmth, complemented by sweet, rosy nuances, subtle spicy undertones, and gentle hints of honey, vanilla, and green foliage. This complex, multifaceted aroma provides depth and enduring warmth, making it a prized ingredient within the perfumer's palette. Phenethyl Cinnamate serves prominently as a base note and effective fixative, enhancing the longevity and richness of floral and oriental fragrances. It excels in harmonising compositions, imparting volume and body, while specifically boosting the persistence and presence of delicate floral notes such as rose, lilac, and gardenia.

missing.title: Phenyl Ethyl Pivalate
missing.description: Phenyl Ethyl Pivalate opens with immediate distinction from typical rose esters—this isn't grandmother's rose. Tea-rose delicacy mingles with unexpected berry fruitiness. The bulky pivalate group creates unique dewy freshness, as if rose petals were sprinkled with morning moisture and crushed berries. This ester's structural complexity delivers multifaceted performance where simpler esters provide single notes. Deploy it for contemporary rose interpretations that demand more than honeyed sweetness. The material bridges floral and fruity families effortlessly, creating accords that feel both sophisticated and accessible—perfect for modern consumers seeking familiar-yet-distinctive signatures. Work with this treasure at 0.5-3% to exploit its exceptional stability in alkaline conditions. Where phenyl ethyl acetate degrades in soap, pivalate persists brilliantly. Combine with Peonile for ultra-modern rosewater effects, or pair with aquatic molecules for innovative marine-floral fusions. The 40-hour substantivity ensures your rose blooms from top through heart.

missing.title: Phenyl Ethyl Propionate
missing.description: Phenyl Ethyl Propionate opens with immediate sweet floralcy—not just any rose, but the rich, velvety character of red rose petals warmed by sunlight. This primary floral impression quickly reveals sophisticated complexity: deep fruity notes suggesting berries and stone fruits merge with distinct honeyed sweetness. The material's warmth comes not from spice but from its inherent balsamic-herbaceous undertones, creating a naturalistic depth that prevents it from reading as simple or one-dimensional. Phenyl Ethyl Propionate is excellent at 0.5-20% when you need to add warmth and sweetness to floral compositions without sacrificing sophistication. Its remarkable blending properties make it invaluable for smoothing transitions between notes—use it to bridge sharp florals with rich base notes seamlessly. In rose accords, it amplifies and enriches rather than dominates, adding the fruity-honeyed facets that transform a basic rose into something luxurious. For Oriental compositions, its balsamic warmth and moderate tenacity provide essential support through the heart notes. Making Sense of Esters Understanding the differences between phenyl ethyl esters transforms your formulation approach entirely. The propionate (C3) delivers warm, fruity-honeyed rose with excellent balance and moderate tenacity. The acetate (C2) presents brighter, more volatile rose with green-fresh facets ideal for top notes. The formate (C1) offers sharp, fresh rose with aldehydic brightness but fleeting presence. The butyrate (C4) extends into deeper, almost animalic territory with plum-like fruitiness and longer persistence. The tiglate brings unique green-herbal complexity with distinctive hay-like nuances perfect for natural effects. Chain length directly impacts volatility and character: shorter chains (formate, acetate) favour brightness and diffusion; medium chains (propionate) achieve optimal balance; longer chains (butyrate) emphasise depth and tenacity. Choose propionate for versatile warmth,

missing.title: Phenyl Ethyl Tiglate
missing.description: Dark, green, herbal and floral, Phenyl Ethyl Tiglate is like smelling a preserved and polished dark red rose. It is a wonderful nuancer for rose bases and also works extremely well in hyacinth compositions owing to its green and balsamic qualities. Phenyl Ethyl Tiglate blends very well with Amazonia ™ and chemicals Cascalone and Calone Plus . Use it to add nuance to our lovely rose bases or blend it with Pineapple Supreme or Pear Belle .

missing.title: Phenyl Propyl Cinnamate
missing.description: Phenyl propyl cinnamate smells of soft roses wrapped in warm balsam, with a delicate apricot sweetness underneath. It is mild at first impression but builds in richness over time. This is one of those materials that defines the character of classic oriental perfumery. It occurs naturally in Peru balsam, storax, and benzoin — the great balsamic resins — and carries their warm, enveloping quality in a pure, controllable form. Use it as a fixative in oriental and rose bases, where it adds tenacity and a sweet, rosy depth that lasts over 400 hours on a blotter. Pair it with ionones and methyl ionones for rich floral compositions, with benzoin and labdanum for full oriental warmth, or with mimosa absolute for a sweet, powdery, golden effect. Work from dilution — a small amount transforms a formula's base without announcing its presence.

missing.title: Piconia
missing.description: Piconia is a diffusive and lively chemical that is not at all as widespread as it should be! Think of it as a patchouli and pipe tobacco radiant with dank vetiver elements. It is earthy, forest-like, fresh and has an interesting power in both top and base notes. A touch of Piconia can really give lift to a scent. Piconia is usually used pure and while you can use a fairly hefty dose, it is more commonly seen in the 0.1-2% range. Piconia may contain a trace of butylated hydroxytoluene as a preservative. That is added by IFF directly and not Fraterworks. Fortifying chemicals in this way is common in the industry and should pose no problems. Piconia is synthesised from the same starting material (isolongiopolene) as some other great chemicals, notably Symroxane , Ysamber, Ambermax and Folenox. Piconia blends marvellously with Ethyl Linalool , Linalool , Coranol , Dihyhdromyrcenol , Dimetol, Citrus and green bases like Amazonia and Verdantol . And of course it is a masterful modifier of patchouli naturals and members of the Clearwood family.

missing.title: Pinoacetaldehyde
missing.description: Pinoacetaldehyde greets you with a bracing burst of oceanic freshness wrapped around a clean pine heart. The marine character emerges almost immediately watery, ozonic, evocative of windswept shores - yet anchored by soft balsamic undertones. There's nothing synthetic about its transparency; it reads natural and luminous on the blotter. This aldehyde excels at bridging disparate worlds in your formulations. Pair it with cascalone or calone to amplify aquatic accords without losing warmth or blend it into fougères alongside lavender and oakmoss for unexpected coastal dimension. It performs admirably in shampoos, fine fragrances, and antiperspirants alike, offering six hours of substantivity with strong top-note impact. Think of pinoacetaldehyde when you need to conjure a forest overlooking the sea. Try it with fir balsam absolute and traces of seaweed materials for masculine marine compositions or add it to Christmas fragrances where its piney facet can sing. Working dosages up to 3% give you room to explore before the aldehydic character dominates.

missing.title: Pistachio Thiazole
missing.description: This material opens with the unmistakable scent of fresh pistachios – green, vibrant, almost creamy. At 0.1% dilution, you get pure nut clarity. Its power rivals the strongest pyrazines but offers unique savoury depth. Use pistachio thiazole when you need authentic nut character in gourmand fragrances. Combine it with cocoa absolute for realistic praline effects or blend with coffee CO2 for espresso depth. This thiazole bridges sweet and savoury worlds, turning flat chocolate accords three-dimensional, hence its sometimes name of Chocolate Thiazole. Start with 0.01% in your trials – this material dominates quickly. The green facet persists through drydown, unusual for such volatile notes. Mix pre-diluted stock to maintain control over its exceptional diffusion. This material is available pure on request.

missing.title: Plicatone
missing.description: Plicatone is a lovely synthetic from Firmenich which has a light herbal top note reminiscent of artemisia and myrtle with side notes of cedarwood. It also has a hint of fruity rose ketone. It's dual nature makes it ideal to link wood base notes with herbal top notes. A trace is used in Calvin Klein's Defy (2021), while 0.2% is found in Valentino Uomo (2014) though it is perhaps more famously known for its inclusion in the great Fixobois base of Firmenich.

missing.title: Poirenate
missing.description: It's not overripe or underripe: poirenate is a pear at its most perfect stage of ripeness. Even better, it is more of a classical pear note, so it is not saccharine sweet like the genetically manipulated varieties sold in supermarkets today. This makes it far more useful for building a pear note as you don't have to fight stickiness. The balanced quality of this aroma chemical makes it useful in non-fruit contexts also. It can add freshness and an aquatic sense to fruit notes, and it can temper the harshness of green notes in florals like hyacinth and lilac . For pear texture and fruity realism, pair Poirenate with a touch of safraleine and Pear Ester. Ethyl-2-methyl butyrate will take it in the direction of overripe, and a higher dose of safraleine and a touch of cis-3-hexenol will unripen it.

missing.title: Polysantol®
missing.description: Strong and profoundly beautiful, Polysantol is perhaps the most useful sandalwood chemical we have today. It works in traces to add a true to life radiant sandalwood note that is beloved by all and in overdose it can add interesting effects. But do bear in mind that it is restricted by IFRA 51 to a maximum of 1.1% of your finished product. Polysantol is, like Javanol® from Givaudan, incredible in its power. At 0.85% it makes up the entire Sandalwood note of Creed's Original Santal and first appeared in Samsara by Guerlain in a 9.5% overdose.

missing.title: Praslin Pyrazine
missing.description: Praslin Pyrazine (named after the 17th century Marshal du Plessis-Praslin who invented the toffee-nut candy) opens with that unmistakable roasted nut character—think freshly made praline or warm peanuts. The cocoa facet follows immediately, rich and slightly powdery. An earthy, musty undertone grounds the material, adding depth. This pyrazine forms naturally during the Maillard reaction when sugars and proteins meet heat—the same chemistry that creates the irresistible aromas of roasted coffee, fresh bread, and chocolate. It is naturally present in cocoa products, roasted peanuts, potato crisps, and roasted barley. In perfumery, it anchors gourmand compositions with genuine roasted warmth that synthetics so often find difficult to replicate. Use Praslin Pyrazine sparingly—up to 0.1% in fragrance concentrate. It works beautifully with vanilla, lactones, and other chocolate materials to build convincing praline and hazelnut effects. The powdery quality pairs well with iris and violet notes for sophisticated gourmand-floral hybrids. Combine it with unctuous Coconut Pure Jungle Essence (CO2) for a toasted coconut note. Praslin Pyrazine vs Torref Pyrazine Both share the chocolate-nutty pyrazine family character, but their differences matter for formulation. Praslin Pyrazine (2,5-dimethyl Pyrazine) leans more musty, earthy, and powdery—closer to raw cocoa powder and roasted peanuts with a grassy undertone. Torref Pyrazine (2,6-dimethyl Pyrazine) is more intensely roasted, with pronounced coffee and meaty-beefy notes alongside its chocolate character—think dark-roasted coffee beans or caramelised meat. Praslin works better for praline, hazelnut, and milk chocolate effects; Torref excels in coffee accords, dark chocolate, and compositions needing that deep torréfié (roasted) quality. Many perfumers use them together, though this can add complexity that overwhelms simpler compositions. When forced to choose, Praslin Pyrazine offers broader versatility across gourmand applica

missing.title: Precyclemone B
missing.description: Precyclemone B (Aldemone) opens with a radiant ozone-aldehydic character that evokes crisp outdoor air and sea spray. Its clean, almost ethereal quality combines sharp citrus brightness with a smooth marine freshness. You'll notice the muguet undertones emerge as the material develops, lending an unexpected floral softness to the otherwise bracing profile. This material transforms masculine fragrances with its exceptional diffusion and tenacity. Use it at low concentrations in floral or woody bases—typically around 0.1%—though citrus compositions can accommodate higher levels approaching 2%. It blends beautifully with dihydromyrcenol, calone, and ambroxan to build classic aquatic accords, whilst patchouli, rose, pepper, and gardenia benefit from its uplifting brightness. Pair it with florhydral and citrus oils to accentuate its aldehydic grapefruit facets. Consider Precyclemone B when you need a booster that lifts compositions without dominating them. It defined the fresh wave of 1990s masculines and remains essential for creating that distinctive Cool Water-style freshness. Work carefully with dilution—its power reveals itself best when you resist the temptation to overdose, letting its radiant character enhance rather than overwhelm your accord.

missing.title: Pyroprunat
missing.description: This Symrise aroma chemical is primarily plummy with a dried fruit, peach skin and floral quality. It is naturally fruity and not sugar-sweet making it a nice material to put alongside more saccharine fruit bases or products. The classic blend of rose and violet is great enhanced by Pyroprunat as it pairs extremely well with the damascones and ionones. Much fun could be had playing around with the original YSL Paris form to create something new and more appealing to a younger generation that craves more edible scents.

missing.title: Raspberry Glycidate
missing.description: First let's deal with the naming conventions. Like strawberry glycidate, this chemical is often known under a false name. Strawberry Glycidate: Aldehyde C-16 (so-called); Ethyl 3-methyl-3-phenylglycidate Raspberry Glycidate: Aldehyde C-20 (so-called); Ethyl 3-(4-methylphenyl)glycidate Despite the molecular similarities, the scents (and power) are quite different. Raspberry Glycidate delivers an intense sweet, ripe berry impression with a distinct iris and rose-like florality that sets it apart from its weaker strawberry cousin. Broader fruity facets emerge — bold grape, tutti-frutti, banana, and a soft warmth that reads almost amber-like. The overall effect is sweeter and more complex than C-16, with a considerably bolder presence. In fact, this could well be a contender for unexplored power-notes. In addition to its fruit note, a clear affinity with ionones and methyl ionones is clear. Use Raspberry Glycidate in berry accords, red fruit compositions, and anywhere you need fruity sweetness that endures. It nuances rose, orris, and violet notes with convincing berry realism. At over three hundred hours on blotter, this is one of the most persistent fruity materials available.

missing.title: Rhubofix
missing.description: Rhubofix opens with crisp green rhubarb and bright grapefruit, then develops into a dry, woody core with vetiver-like facets and spicy warmth. It has real verticality — presence from top through heart to base. This is the structural, long-lasting member of Firmenich's rhubarb family. Where Rhuboflor is floral, fruity, and powdery, Rhubofix is woody, spicy, and dry. Rhuboflor gives rhubarb an orris-like softness; Rhubofix gives it a vetiver-like backbone with grapefruit sparkle. Rhubofix also lasts twice as long — four days on a blotter versus Rhuboflor's two. Use both together for a complete rhubarb picture, or choose one depending on the direction you want. Pair it with vetiver and cedarwood to amplify its woody side, with bergamot and grapefruit for citrus-green freshness, or with pink pepper and cardamom for spicy warmth. It also creates interesting effects with salicylates, especially when sweetened with heliotropin. Always evaluate well diluted.

missing.title: Rhumacetal
missing.description: Rhumacetal delivers that unmistakable boozy rum character—refined alcohol warmth without harsh solvent notes. The tobacco facet emerges alongside, adding a dry, slightly smoky complexity. Woody undertones ground the composition, evoking aged oak barrels and fine spirits. This acetal serves as a cornerstone material for building convincing rum accords in perfumery. Some perfumers describe it as the best pure alcohol aromachemical available, providing a concentrated hit of refined spirits character. The tobacco fixative effect makes it valuable beyond simple gourmand applications—try it in oriental compositions where that aged, sophisticated warmth enhances the overall blend. Combine Rhumacetal with MANE's incredible Rum Jungle Essence , rum ether, vanillin , oakwood materials, and Peru balsam for dark rum effects. It pairs beautifully with woods like cedar and sandalwood, and enriches gourmand notes of vanilla, chocolate, and caramel. The material can seem underwhelming against very powerful notes, so balance carefully.

missing.title: Riotous Red™
missing.description: The Fraterworks® Perfumer's Palette™ is a range of dyes that can be used alone or in combination with each other to add vibrance and colour to your perfumes or cosmetic products. Our proprietary blend of FD&C and D&C colours are sold in liquid form. Perfumer's Palette colours contain preservatives and distilled water which is perfectly safe for alcoholic perfumes in the quantities needed for colouration. Typical use is from 0.01–0.5% of finished product. This product complies with the current BP / Ph Eur Preservative Efficacy Test Criteria A for Topical products. The PET Certificate can be downloaded below. At these low levels, staining of clothing or skin is minimal to none but you should always test your finished product against white cloth or paper. Riotous Red contains FD&C Red 4 (Ci 14700). According to the New Zealand cosmetics group standard, this product should not be used in hair dye products but is permitted otherwise.

missing.title: Romandolide®
missing.description: Romandolide opens with a remarkably clean, delicate musk character that immediately distinguishes itself from heavier polycyclic musks. This alicyclic musk delivers subtle fruity-berry top notes that dance above its core musky heart, creating an effect both fresh and substantial. Soft ambrette-like nuances add sophistication without the animalic edge of natural ambrette, while gentle balsamic facets emerge as it develops. What sets Romandolide apart is its ability to maintain delicacy while building exceptional volume on the drydown—it whispers initially but grows to fill space with its clean, modern presence. Use Romandolide at 5-20% when you need a modern musk with universal perception—unlike some musks, everyone can smell it. As an alicyclic musk, it bridges the gap between light top-note musks and heavy base musks, offering the clean character of the former with the tenacity approaching the latter. Use it as a direct replacement for polycyclic musks like Galaxolide where you need similar performance with a cleaner, less fruity profile. In floral compositions, it provides invisible support without the sweetness that can overwhelm delicate petals. For oriental fragrances, its balsamic facets and sandalwood-like drydown create sophisticated depth without heaviness. The structural innovation of Romandolide places it perfectly between traditional musk families. Unlike macrocyclic musks (like Muscenone) with their animalic depth, or polycyclic musks (like Galaxolide) with their sweet-fruity character, Romandolide offers clean delicacy with surprising tenacity. Where Helvetolide—its alicyclic cousin—leans fruity and ambrette-like with less persistence, Romandolide provides superior volume and drydown performance while maintaining transparency. Its camphoraceous undertone adds an interesting cool facet absent in sweeter musks. Choose Galaxolide for sweet, fruity musk effects; select Helvetolide for light, fruity-ambrette notes; choose Romandolide when you need clean, vo

missing.title: Romascone
missing.description: Romascone delivers a unique aromatic signature defined by distinct rosemary and thujonic qualities. Its true value lies in its potent, damascone-like radiance, providing exceptional lift and diffusion. Perfumers leverage this molecule to build modern accords that require vibrant, red fruity-rose effects with a novel herbal twist. Combine Romascone with aldehydes C-11 Undecylenic and C-12 MNA to amplify radiance and diffusion. This material excels in fine fragrances where its dual character fully develops. Add armoise oil to enhance the thujonic aspect. Blends beautifully with Artemal . Use Romascone strategically to augment restricted rose ketones in your formulas. Since IFRA limits rose ketones to 0.043% combined, add Romascone at 0.05-0.3% to restore the missing radiance. This material acts as a force multiplier—its fruity-damascone character harmonises with trace damascones while contributing its own distinctive freshness.

missing.title: Rose Crystals
missing.description: Rose acetate has a lovely soft scent akin to that of the scent of a deep red rose floating across a great distance. It has facets that are powdery, sweet (almost gourmand) and floral. While it is a nice material in its own right, its true power comes to light when blended with phenyl ethyl alcohol (PEA) as part of a rose accord.
