Rose crystals have an astonishing ability to add an almost three dimensional effect to PEA, imparting a naturalness and an inimitable quality that is extremely appealing. For any perfumer serious about making good rose bases or sophisticated rose notes, this is an essential material. Rose crystals are a fine white powder which can be simply added to your blends into which it will quite happily dissolve.

missing.title: Rose Oxide
missing.description: Rose Oxide (Racemic) opens with an almost aggressive metallic freshness that cuts through compositions like a blade. This sharp, gassy-green character delivers the unmistakable scent of rose stems being snapped in half. You'll recognise its penetrating quality immediately—that bright, almost electrical sensation that makes roses feel alive rather than preserved. This material transforms predictable rose reconstructions into dynamic, three-dimensional experiences. Use it when you need compositions to project powerfully from the bottle, creating that crucial first impression. Combine Rose Oxide with traditional rose alcohols like citronellol and geraniol to build complexity, or pair it with black pepper for unexpected vibrancy that modern perfumery demands. Deploy Rose Oxide with extreme restraint—overdosing creates harsh, unpleasant effects that dominate rather than enhance. Working concentrations rarely exceed 1% in your concentrate, with trace amounts often sufficient for remarkable transformation. Its poor tenacity makes it purely a top-note material, disappearing within hours but leaving behind space for your heart notes to bloom. We also stock Rose Oxide High Cis and Rose Oxide Laevo . Rose Oxide Variations Rose Oxide comes in three commercially significant forms, each offering distinct olfactory profiles and potency levels. Racemic Rose Oxide (this product) contains approximately seventy-five percent cis isomers mixed with trans forms, delivering strong rose-geranium character with pronounced metallic-green edges and good diffusion. High Cis Rose Oxide elevates cis content above ninety percent, resulting in cleaner, brighter red rose character with significantly reduced metallic sting—it's easier to dose and exceptionally diffusive. Laevo Rose Oxide isolates the pure minus-cis isomer, offering unmatched potency (one-hundred times stronger than racemic) with softer, more radiant floral character, enhanced greenness, and sublime diffusion—though its extreme stren

missing.title: Rose Oxide HC
missing.description: Rose Oxide has the most value in three forms: Racemic (cis isomer ~ 75%), [Racemic] High Cis (cis isomer ~ 90+%) and Laevo . The latter is the finest, containing only the purest odour quality and is incredibly powerful with an odour threshold of 0.5 ppb (racemic is 50 ppb). Of the lower cost racemic types, Rose Oxide High Cis has a beautiful scent of red roses and geranium and lacks the metallic sting of the 75% cis version. It is far easier to dose than the laevo material owing to its considerably lower strength, and is extremely diffusive. Rose Oxide High Cis is used far more often in commercial fragrances due to the affordability. This product blends extremely well with the regular rose materials ( Phenyl Ethyl Alcohol , Geraniol , Citronellol and Nerol ) and with the less common Peomosa. It is lovely when combined with Black Pepper.

missing.title: Rose Oxide Laevo
missing.description: Rose Oxide has the most value in three forms: Racemic (cis isomer ~ 75%), [Racemic] High Cis (cis isomer ~ 98%) and Laevo. The latter is the finest, being of the purest odour quality and incredibly powerful with an odour threshhold of 0.5 ppb (racemic is 50 ppb). Racemic rose oxide (regular and high cis) has a beautiful scent of red roses and geranium, while Laevo Rose Oxide has that same scent but with added greenness and a radiance that has to be experienced to be truly appreciated. The merest whisper of Rose Oxide Laevo can convert a lovely rose or geranium accord into something sublime. This product is many times more expensive than the others for very good reason. Due to the high cost and strength we sell this product pure and diluted to 10% in DPG.

missing.title: Rosethyl
missing.description: Rosethyl delivers a beautifully natural Rose de Mai character — green, earthy, and spicy with honeyed warmth. You get tea rose and peony facets that read as convincingly natural rather than synthetic. The tenacity is excellent, lasting well over two days on a blotter, making it unusually persistent for a rose-type material. Use rosethyl as a core building block in your rose and peony accords. It adds the green, earthy authenticity that phenylethyl alcohol and citronellol alone cannot deliver. In ylang ylang compositions it contributes a natural rosy quality that enhances and refines the floral heart. Pair with rose absolute, geraniol, and damascone for the most complete rose accord possible. Try it alongside hedione for a fresh, radiant rose-peony effect. Blend with citrus and green notes where a natural rose character needs to emerge gradually from a sparkling opening.

missing.title: Rosyrane Super
missing.description: Rosyrane Super hits you with immediate, expansive rose — bright, green-edged, and remarkably diffusive from the first moment. A geranium-like freshness and distinctive metallic sharpness give it realism that simple rose alcohols cannot match. This is rose with presence, not delicacy. But be warned, it will absolutely take over everything you add it to so the lightest touch is needed. Seventy-two hours on blotter gives you rose persistence that outlasts most floral materials. Use it as the core of rose and geranium accords where diffusion needs to carry through functional bases. In fine fragrance, lower doses let the metallic-green edge add complexity without overwhelming. Blend with citronellol and geraniol for naturalistic rose, or pair with linalool and methylionones for green-floral bouquets. The metallic facet makes it particularly effective alongside hedione in modern transparent florals. Start at traces and build — the diffusion here is considerable.

missing.title: Rum Ether
missing.description: Rum Ether (Ethyl Oxyhydrate) has been discontinued but fortunately Firmenich makes this base which is excellent in its own right and can be used as a one for one replacer. On first sniff you can have no doubt that this is a boozy material, with caramellic and buttery notes. It also has a distinct fruity quality: primarily pineapple but also some shades of banana — fresh, not overly ripened. It is also aldehydic. While this is an obvious pick for alcoholic top notes, it works extremely well with labdanum (particularly the light variety or as a sweetener for the more volatile Cistus Oil ). It would be a wonderful addition to our demo formula for Bertrand Duchaufour's Or du Serail (for Naomi Goodsir) which we've added below for completeness sake. It's aldehydic facets make it a great partner to Aldalia (Chuit Naef & Cie) or Jean Carles' classic Aldehone . If you are looking for a rum note which is easy to use and won't overwhelm, while lasting a little longer than the very ethereal Rum CO2 extract we sell, this is it.

missing.title: Safraleine®
missing.description: While Safranal is the closest material to Saffron in terms of odour, it is highly restricted and so we rely on the very elegant and luxurious Safraleine from Givaudan which has no limits at all. Safraleine is usually used in small doses (below 0.5%) as it is very potent, but in some contexts it can work in overdose. Safraleine smells of saffron, herbs and leather with phenolic nuances and hints of tobacco and wood. It is a hugely versatile material that works wonders in leather bases or can simply provide a necessary saffron note much loved in Middle Eastern perfumery. This is a wonderful blender and booster of our highly popular Saffron Attar FW Base.

missing.title: Sakura Salicylate
missing.description: Sakura Salicylate smells of soft, pink petals — sweet, powdery, gently fruity, with a faint berry nuance and a warm, solar glow underneath. Takasago named it after the Japanese cherry blossom, and the connection is genuine: it captures the delicate, ephemeral quality of sakura without being literal about it. Use it as a direct substitute for benzyl salicylate where allergen labelling is a concern — it shares the same fixative and blending properties but brings a more distinct, more beautiful floral character. It gives compositions cohesion and bloom, softening sharp edges and adding a powdery radiance to rose, muguet, and peony accords. Pair it with linalool and rose materials for a classic cherry blossom accord, with hedione for airy, transparent florals, or with berry notes and aquatic materials for contemporary compositions. It projects well without shouting, and works best in lighter, fresher fragrances where its delicate character can breathe.

missing.title: Salicynile®
missing.description: Salicynile has a luminous, sun-drenched quality — warm white flowers, orchid petals, with a fruity breath of banana and pear floating underneath. There is a subtle metallic freshness and a hint of something marine. The overall impression is solar, radiant, and extraordinarily persistent. Salicynile gives you the warm, solar quality of materials like hexyl salicylate — but roughly five times stronger and vastly more stable. It lasts close to 200 hours on a blotter. Use it in white floral accords, orchid reconstructions, and anywhere you want fruity-floral radiance that refuses to fade. A little goes a very long way — evaluate Salicynile well diluted, where its floral complexity unfolds. At higher doses the fruity facets dominate. Pair it with Hedione for maximum solar radiance, or with ylang ylang to amplify its natural orchid-banana character.

missing.title: Sandalwood 77125 B
missing.description: Sandalwood 77125 B opens with a surprisingly bold sandalwood hit, faster and more immediate than natural Mysore oil. The heart is rich and creamy with deep milky warmth and subtle ambery-leathery complexity. It captures the precious-wood quality of true sandalwood with great fidelity. This base gives you instant sandalwood impact wherever you need woody warmth. In oriental hearts its creaminess wraps beautifully around spice and amber, while its bold opening projects more than natural oil ever could. The trade-off is slightly less tenacity, so layer with fixatives for lasting power. Pair with Dartanol and Hindinol to reinforce the creamy sandalwood core, or combine with vetiver and cedar for woody-masculine structures. It supports white florals surprisingly well, adding milky warmth beneath jasmine and tuberose. Rose absolute makes a particularly beautiful partner here.

missing.title: Sandela® 85 IPM
missing.description: Sandela is perhaps the most important of all the sandalwood aroma chemicals. It is very light in odour strength but it is extremely long lasting, sweet and pleasing to pretty much everyone. Sandela's odour profile is creamy, nutty and sweet. It is a beautiful material to work with and every perfumer should be using it. Sandela can be used in an overdose as the main Sandalwood chemical in a blend (and it is not IFRA restricted so you really can go crazy with it) or in very small amounts for its fixative properties. Note that it may be difficult to smell initially if you haven't used it before, but in time you will develop the ability to smell it (much like Galaxolide and other very heavy molecules). Because Sandela is very viscous, Givaudan sells it with a 15% addition of IPM.

missing.title: Sarriette Base 199618
missing.description: Sarriette Base 199618 is a Firmenich aromatic herbal specialty of extraordinary potency. The opening is dry and thyme-like with a sharp, piercing green edge, settling into vegetal pepper notes and cool spearmint. It smells like wild savory growing on a sun-baked Mediterranean hillside, intensified tenfold. This base transforms fougeres and aromatic compositions with a raw, wild herbal character that polished lavender and rosemary alone cannot achieve. Use it to add untamed Mediterranean intensity to your accords. It reinforces and lifts other herbal notes, making them feel more vivid and natural. Dilute well before blending — this is extraordinarily powerful and a single drop changes a composition. Pair with lavender, oakmoss, and coumarin for classic fougere construction. Try it alongside pine, juniper, and cedarwood for wild forest accords that smell genuinely alive.

missing.title: Sclareolate®
missing.description: Sclareolate opens with crystalline freshness that sits between linalool and linalyl acetate, capturing the aromatic brightness of clary sage within a white floral framework. This transparency makes it invaluable when you need clean radiance without heaviness. Its diffusive nature lifts entire compositions while maintaining remarkable stability across all media. This material excels at bridging citrus tops with floral hearts, particularly in lavender-cologne structures where its aromatic facets enhance naturalness. Use it to modernise classic fougères or add sparkle to white floral bouquets. In functional fragrances, Sclareolate maintains its character through aggressive bases where traditional florals might distort or disappear entirely. Deploy Sclareolate from trace amounts for subtle refinement up to 10% for pronounced fresh-floral impact. It partners brilliantly with bergamot and lavender in masculine structures, while in feminine accords it amplifies lily-of-the-valley and freesia notes. Consider it your go-to for adding contemporary freshness to any composition requiring both immediate appeal and lasting radiance.

missing.title: Shangralide Oliffac
missing.description: Shangralide Oliffac hits you first with a feral, leathery punch - almost aggressive neat, with a phenolic bite that recalls wet animal hide. Give it time and that rawness melts into a honeyed, skin-warm sweetness. The dry-down is creamy, powdery, and astonishingly long-lived on paper and skin alike. This IFF specialty base is built on a Galaxolide skeleton but bears almost no resemblance to standard white musks. Trace amounts of phenylacetic acid and other animalic modifiers give it a convincingly "biological" character that rounds sharp indoles in jasmine and tuberose, softens synthetic edges in woody accords, and anchors leather compositions with raw-skin realism. Layer it with macrocyclic musks like Ambrettolide for a musk cocktail that has both volume and radiance. Try Shangralide at low doses to add a living, breathing quality to florals and ambers. Push it higher in leather and oud accords where you want unmistakable animalic grit. Remember that this material transforms radically on dilution — what smells aggressive in the bottle becomes seductive and intimate below one percent. For a truer-to-nature deer musk base, we recommend Tonkin Intense or Nearly Deer which are built around laevo muscone, the key musk molecule in deer musk, rather than the cheaper Galaxolide and white musks in other third party bases.

missing.title: Silvanone® Supra
missing.description: Silvanone Supra opens with a soft, sweet powderiness - warm skin dusted with talc, underscored by a gentle animalic presence that recalls vintage nitromusks without their harshness. There is a milky, almost lactonic quality beneath the powder. The effect is intimate, enveloping, and unmistakably musky. This Givaudan macrocyclic musk is a blend of cyclohexadecanolide and cyclopentadecanone (Exaltone), combining the powdery sweetness of a macrocyclic lactone with the animalic warmth of a macrocyclic ketone. Use it in orientals and ambers where you need musk that radiates rather than merely sits. It brings a living, skin-like warmth to white florals and adds powdery depth to spicy carnation accords. Silvanone Supra is extraordinarily tenacious—it will last months on a blotter. You can dose it generously, up to twenty percent in your concentrate, without distortion. Pair it with woody-amber bases for rich oriental foundations, with Hedione and jasmine for radiant white florals, or layer it with other musks to build complex, multifaceted skin accords.

missing.title: Silvial®
missing.description: Silvial opens with a bright floral burst that feels clean and watery, followed by a subtle sparkle that hints at citrus zest. This powerful muguet material delivers crystalline lily of the valley freshness without the heavy sweetness of older alternatives. You'll find its marine quality and aldehydic touch particularly valuable when modernising classic floral structures. At low levels Silvial refreshes top notes and adds a watery floral sheen, perfect for modern colognes. Push it into the mid-range and it becomes the star of a muguet accord, often paired with traces of hydroxycitronellal or rose oxide for added petal realism. The material blends beautifully with lilac materials, rose alcohols, styrax and methylionones . Its aldehydic character provides exceptional lift to dense orientals whilst the marine facet brings contemporary freshness to woody bases. Use Silvial between 1-15% in fine fragrance, capping around 5% to prevent sharpness. Reserve higher dosages up to 20% for functional products where bloom after dilution is vital. The material shows excellent tenacity at one week on blotter with good substantivity both damp and dry. Combine with other modern muguet materials like Nympheal or Hivernal® Neo to build complex lily accords that replace restricted aldehydes.

missing.title: Sinensal Natural ex Orange
missing.description: Sinensal is what gives orange oil its deep, juicy richness — isolated here from the peel in its natural form. The aroma is sweet, full-bodied orange with a powdery, mandarin-like quality. This smells like the heart of a ripe orange, concentrated and intensified far beyond standard orange oil. Use sinensal to extend your orange top notes deep into the heart of a composition. Where standard orange oil fades in minutes, this natural isolate persists for hours — remarkable staying power for a citrus material. It adds depth and juiciness to citrus accords that synthetic alternatives cannot match. Pair with bergamot and neroli for a rich, natural hesperidic accord. Try it alongside blood orange and nootkatone for the most complete citrus spectrum possible. Blend with petitgrain and orange flower absolute to build orange blossom compositions rooted in authentic orange character.

missing.title: Skatole 1% DPG
missing.description: Skatole is undoubtedly one of the strongest and most repellent chemicals the perfumer has to work with, nevertheless it remains an indispensable item for many reasons. Traces of skatole can impart a sense of true naturalness to a floral bouquet (impossible to achieve with any other material), while a touch in excess can create the illusion of dying flowers wilting as they gracefully expire. In high doses skatole contributes a distinctly animal quality which can, as if by magic, be tamed by high doses of natural sandalwood oil with which it has an inimitable synergy. Skatole is frequently found as the chief component in civet compounds. Skatole can be a useful booster for indole where an excess of that related aromachemical can introduce an unwanted naphtholenic character. Skatole, like indole, can be highly discolouring which should be borne in mind when using it in fragrances demanding little to no colour. We supply skatole in a 1% solution with DPG but we recommend diluting it further to 0.1% or even 0.01% for most practical needs. NOTE: We package all high odour or high risk materials individually in separate heat sealed aluminium bags to mitigate any risk of cross-contamination.

missing.title: Sotolone
missing.description: Sotolone is an incredibly powerful sweet material commonly used in flavours but absolutely wonderful for modern gourmand fragrances. Depending on the dose sotolone fluctuates between the penetrating scent of sugar and the exotic and spiced warmth of fenugreek. A truly remarkable sweetener that blends beautifully with members of the maltol family and other sweet "edibles" such as strawberry and maple furanone. This material is so powerful and long-lasting that we are offering it at 10% and 1% dilution in DPG and we highly recommend diluting it further to 0.1% or even 0.01%, both levels at which it still performs well.

missing.title: Special Order Items
missing.description: Sometimes you need a material that isn't listed for sale but we have stock in our warehouse. Contact us to confirm availability and pricing and use this product to add the necessary value to your cart. For a $40 special order, add two $20 items to your cart. For a $100 add a $100 item. If you need to pay $120 add a $100 item and a $20 item. When checking out be sure to tell us in the order notes what the special order is to pay for.

missing.title: Spirambrene
missing.description: Spirambrene is a woody and elegant amber material with extremely good diffusion. It ranks amongst the very best of the woody chemicals (with Dextro Norlimbanol, Cedroxyde, Orbitone and others). It is rare to find in small traces but really should be part of every perfumer's palette. Perfumery: Techniques in Evolution (a series of articles published in Perfumer and Flavorist magazine) discusses the chemical: “Spirambrene is a nice, strong chemical with a closeness to boisambrene forte, norlimbanol, cedroxyde and cedramber. It is somewhat more seaweed-like than the above and imparts important velvety nuances to woody notes. Again, I believe it is a chemical that has a bright future in our industry. It is being widely used in fragrances such as Kenzo for Men (0.8%), Eden, Gio (0.85%) and Agua Fresca (0.3%) by Adolfo Dominguez, among many others.” Givaudan describes it thus: “Spirambrene blends well with sparkling, green, spicy and aldehydic top notes. It is an interesting complement in woody accords for providing a diffusive ambery effect. Due to its high impact, it produces unique and original effects when combined with other woody elements.” Featured in such fragrances as Duro by Nasomato (0.3%), Enigma by Roja Dove (0.4%), Black Agar Givco (1%), Himalaya by Creed (0.55%), Blends beautifully with Dextro Norlimbanol, Muscenone, Muscone Laevo, Exaltolide and all the amber chemicals.

missing.title: Spirogalbanone
missing.description: Spirogalbanone is pure green, and plenty of it. It smells like a freshly snapped flower stem: sharp, cool and sappy, with the clean bite of galbanum. A juicy green-pineapple facet keeps it bright and fresh rather than bitter or resinous. Use it to build a green galbanum signature that holds. Where galbanum oil and other green materials flash and fade, this one keeps its sharp, sappy freshness deep into the drydown, anchoring the green of a composition. It lends green florals and chypres a crisp, natural stem realism. Because it lingers, it doubles as a quiet fixative for greenery: add a trace under violet leaf, cis-3-hexenol or other fast green notes to stop them vanishing. Blend it with Florhydral for a fresh cut-flower, flower-shop accord. A little goes a long way, so dose with restraint.

missing.title: Squalane
missing.description: Squalane is a completely odourless, colourless carrier oil that adds nothing to the scent of your composition. It absorbs into skin quickly, leaving a silky, non-greasy finish rather than the oily residue of heavier carriers. This makes it ideal for perfume oils and roll-on fragrances. Your skin produces squalene naturally as part of its own sebum — squalane is the stabilised version, hydrogenated to prevent oxidation. This means it absorbs readily and feels familiar on skin rather than sitting on the surface. It will not go rancid, turn yellow, or develop off-notes over time. Use squalane anywhere you would use jojoba or fractionated coconut oil, but with a lighter feel and longer shelf life. It is non-comedogenic and suitable for face-safe formulations. This olive-derived version is identical in every functional way to sugarcane squalane.

missing.title: Starfleur™ 40
missing.description: Starfleur smells like a handful of fresh spring flowers: lily of the valley and freesia, clean and see-through, with a cool green edge. A soft citrus brightness lifts the top. It reads natural and dewy, the floralcy transparent rather than heavy or soapy. Use it to build fresh muguet, freesia and lily accords with real body and lift. It gives white florals a modern, watery transparency and a natural, just-picked feel. Pair it with hydroxycitronellal, citronellol and a trace of indole to round out a full lily-of-the-valley.

missing.title: Strawberiff
missing.description: In high dilution, Strawberiff reads as jammy ripe strawberry with a sour, slightly sweaty edge and a faint woody undertone. Concentrated, the sweaty-acidic side dominates and the fruity note retreats so care is needed. Use it in trace amounts to add realism to strawberry, raspberry, blackcurrant and tropical fruit accords. It supplies the fermented-jam character that pure fruity materials cannot achieve alone. It also bridges fruity tops to gourmand bases by adding a sweaty, lactic-fruit nuance. Pair with strawberry glycidate, gamma undecalactone and beta damascenone for a complete strawberry accord. A trace under blackcurrant or passionfruit lifts the natural ripeness without adding sugar. Dose extremely low — one drop too many and the whole composition turns rancid.

missing.title: Sublimolide™
missing.description: Sublimolide™ is the V. MANE Fils produced version of Scentolide, the high cis version of Ambrettolide which is considered to be the supreme form of that musk. In comparison to the more fruity Ambrettolide by IFF which we sell, Sublimolide has a scent closer to true ambrette seeds and a stronger power. Sublimolide is the superior option but they are sufficiently different to justify owning both and using Sublimolide as a special treat. Sublimolide's super power in a perfume is a marvellous ability to elevate the senses of the wearer. To draw us closer to the achingly distant call of the sublime. In MANE's own words: “ SUBLIMOLIDE is a captivating macrocyclic musk whose structure and scent mirror the natural Ambrettolide found in ambrette seed, a plant from the hibiscus family. Rather subtle at the top, its musky note begins with a soft, understated introduction, only to bloom into a lavish and warm embrace, adorned with fruity nuances and powdery floral undertones. SUBLIMOLIDE is very long-lasting and has an impressive volume and sillage, exalting the top notes along the way. This musk can be used in vegan formulas.”

missing.title: Sulfurol (Milky)
missing.description: Sulfurol delivers extraordinary dairy effects with remarkable authenticity. This specialised lactonic material creates realistic milk, cream, and condensed milk impressions at concentrations of 0.2-0.8%. Perfumers integrate this powerhouse when constructing high-impact gourmand accords requiring genuine dairy dimensions. This material pairs exceptionally with vanillin , coumarin , and benzyl salicylate . The impact of sulfurol may not be immediately obvious so be cautious and wait at least 24 hours between additions. Owing to its strength we are offering it at 10% in DPG or pure.

missing.title: Symroxane
missing.description: Symroxane opens bright, almost conifer-green and faintly earthy, then settles into velvety dry wood: vetiver root, old timber and a peppery spice, with dried apricot and a thread of tobacco leaf running through it. A soft amber warmth sits underneath. It is complex without ever being loud. It has a family resemblance to Cashmeran , with a more pronounced woody side and less of that wet-concrete opening. Blend it with Ambrocenide and Timbersilk for a powerful modern wood, or with damascones, patchouli and vanilla for a warm, fruity-woody oriental. Piconia , Ysamber K and Ambermax share its starting material. Our 212 VIP demo formula uses Symroxane at 5.5%, alongside Iso E Super, Habanolide and Cashmeran in its woody-amber base. You can read an interesting article about it here .

missing.title: Syringa Aldehyde 50% PEA
missing.description: Syringa aldehyde opens with a strong, sweet floral-green burst—immediately recognisable as the honeyed, powdery heart of lilac blossom. It shares the phenylacetaldehyde family's floral-green intensity but arrives with less pungency and more warmth. Beneath the floral top, a soft animalic facet and mimosa-like sweetness give it a living, breathing quality. This is one of the essential building blocks for lilac accords, where it provides the warm, honeyed-floral depth that hydroxycitronellal and terpineol alone cannot achieve. Use it in hyacinth bases for green-floral impact, in rose accords for added freshness, and in mimosa compositions where its powdery sweetness enhances the honeyed character. It also brings a gentle animalic warmth to white florals—think indolic without the indole. Syringa Aldehyde vs Phenyl Acetaldehyde These two aldehydes are easy to confuse, but they occupy very different olfactory spaces. Phenyl acetaldehyde is the powerhouse of the two—an overwhelmingly intense green-floral hyacinth note with harsh, almost aggressive pungency at full strength that softens into honeyed, chocolatey sweetness on extreme dilution. It is the sharpest and greenest of the three, and demands careful dosing at fractions of a percent. Syringa aldehyde sits in the middle: it is structurally a phenylacetaldehyde with a methyl group added to the para position of the ring, which softens the harshness dramatically. The result is warmer, more honeyed, and more powdery—recognisably floral-green but without the aggressive bite, making it far easier to work with in lilac and mimosa accords.

missing.title: Syringol
missing.description: Syringol is what makes wood smoke smell like wood smoke. Its character is intensely smoky and phenolic — charred hardwood, bacon, bonfire — but with a sweet, powdery, almost vanillic warmth underneath that keeps it from turning medicinal. Where guaiacol (its single-methoxy relative) can feel harsh and cough-syrup-like, syringol stays rounded and balsamic. That sweetness makes it far more versatile than raw phenolic smoke materials. In leather accords it provides authentic smokiness without the medicinal edge that can spoil the effect. Tobacco compositions gain a genuine charred-leaf quality. Incense and frankincense accords become more convincingly burnt. Even whisky-inspired gourmand fragrances benefit from a trace. At 356 hours on a blotter it outlasts almost anything you pair it with. Birch tar oil, cade oil, and labdanum reinforce the leather-smoke direction. Patchouli and vetiver add earthy depth. Vanillin and coffee absolute take it toward smoky-gourmand territory.

missing.title: Syvertal
missing.description: Syvertal hits your nose with remarkable intensity—a wet, dewy greenness that captures freshly cut stems and vegetative sap. The radish-like character brings crisp bite while subtle gardenia and chrysanthemum tones soften the edges. A faint metallic shimmer runs through the profile, adding dimension without harshness. This material excels at creating moisture effects in floral compositions where you need that fresh-cut flower impression. Use it in gardenia accords to capture stem and leaf alongside bloom, or work it into chrysanthemum reconstructions where its natural affinity shines. It strengthens citrus compositions with green depth that mimics peel oils without using them. Apply Syvertal at low levels—its strength is considerable and a light hand rewards you with dewy freshness. Pair it with aldehydes to amplify its metallic sparkle, or combine with ionones in violet-gardenia blends. Work it into fougère bases for crisp green impact or layer with vetiver for earthy wetness.

missing.title: Tabanon
missing.description: Tabanon captures the essence of warm, aged tobacco leaf — sweet, nutty, and unmistakable. Dry acorn and nut-skin facets give it a distinctive warmth unlike any other tobacco material. Fruity-plum undertones and a soft leathery quality add quiet complexity beneath the surface. Diffusion is the defining quality here — even at traces, Tabanon radiates tobacco warmth through an entire composition. Use it as a heart-to-base connector in orientals, leathers, and woody-amber blends. It defines the drydown of some of the most celebrated niche tobacco fragrances. Pair with labdanum and benzoin for rich oriental tobacco, or blend with oud and leather materials for smoky depth. The fruity-plum facet makes it surprisingly sympathetic to damascones and osmanthus. Start with the smallest additions — this is one of perfumery's most potent materials, and overdosing flattens a composition.

missing.title: Tamisone
missing.description: Tamison is an intense and powerful herbal green chemical with an obvious thujonic character and nuances of tropical fruit. It also exhibits a lovely green note not dissimilar to the highly restricted Methyl Octine Carbonate and Methyl Heptine Carbonate . Tamisone blends incredibly well with super ambers such as Z11 ™, Boisiris ® and Hydroxyambran , aroma chemicals like Iso E Super , Orbitone® T , Plicatone and Coranol , and with numerous naturals such as Davana , Clary Sage , and Frankincense . Firmenich was the last major manufacturer in the industry to make and sell Tamisone but they discontinued manufacturing in 2023 citing manufacturing difficulties. As a result, Fraterworks is working with a third party chemical manufacturer to return the product to market. Once you try it you'll definitely understand why this could not be allowed to vanish from perfumery organs around the world. Tamisone is a rare chemical and there is very little information available. It is not restricted at all by IFRA or the EU. The RIFM Fragrance Safety Assessment (version 031618, 17 April 2018) “ concludes that this material is safe under the limits described in this safety assessment.” [ Download ]

missing.title: TCD Alcohol DM
missing.description: TCD Alcohol DM is used for its woody, ambery, and slightly musky profile. Its molecular structure provides excellent diffusion and fixation, making it a suitable addition to chypres, modern ambers, and high-end woody accords. This material is particularly valued for its ability to enhance depth and structure, seamlessly integrating with Iso E Super, Ambroxan , Vertofix , and musks . Due to its stability, TCD Alcohol performs well across different formulations, from alcoholic perfumes to personal care applications. Its low volatility and high substantivity make it an effective fixative, ensuring long-lasting impact in fragrance compositions. NOTE: Our supplier, Ventos, has used incorrect data in its paperwork (supplied on by us). They wrongly refer to this material by the CAS 26896-48-0 (HHCB, Muscomer) when it is 26160-83-8 ( Tricyclodecanedimethanol).

missing.title: Terrasol
missing.description: Terrasol (2-Ethyl Fenchol) is perhaps the most true to life damp earth chemical next to geosmin which is literally the chemical that causes the scent of rain. On first sniff pure, Terrasol has a slightly camphoraceous scent - almost a blend of camphor, menthol, eucalyptus and ethyl salicylate. However, in dilution and in use, that gives way to pure petrichor and decaying leaves. Use this to naturalise fragrances that are high in synthetics. With floral blends, Terrasol will root the flower in the earth. Touches of green materials give you the complete garden — soil, flower, foliage. Another very clever use is to blend this with synthetic woods, or even dry woods like cedar, to dampen them down. Blended right this can contributed a cool effect by association (think autumn forests and winter wood piles). The material is long lasting so it will sit alongside your naturals quite comfortably matching longevity.

missing.title: Tetrahydrogeraniol
missing.description: Tetrahydrogeraniol opens with an immediate waxy quality that sets it apart from every other rose material in your palette. Where geraniol sparkles with citrus-bright sweetness and fresh green vitality, this fully hydrogenated cousin brings gravitas—a rose viewed through frosted glass, softened and abstracted into something more textural than literal. The "tetrahydro" modification strips away geraniol's reactive double bonds, and with them goes much of the bright citronella edge and sweet floral lift, leaving behind a fascinating skeleton of waxy rose with unexpected soapy-clean nuances. In fact you can see this facet clearly exploited in our Amrita demonstration formula below. This material excels where geraniol fails catastrophically—in the harsh alkaline environments of bar soaps, liquid detergents, and industrial cleaners where pH levels would normally decompose traditional rose alcohols into unrecognisable fragments. Deploy tetrahydrogeraniol at 0.5-5% in functional products to maintain authentic floral character through aggressive bases. Its remarkable stability extends beyond mere survival; it actively contributes to the perception of cleanliness through its inherent soapy-waxy character. This synaesthetic quality makes it invaluable for creating "clean laundry" accords and fresh textile impressions that feel authentic rather than imposed. The chemical transformation from geraniol to tetrahydro geraniol reveals perfumery's hidden architecture. By saturating all double bonds through hydrogenation, we trade volatility for stability, brightness for depth, and ephemeral beauty for enduring presence. The resulting material offers unique creative possibilities: combine it with traditional geraniol and citronellol to create rose accords with both sparkle and tenacity, or use it solo in functional products where other florals dare not venture. Its subtle minty-fresh undertones open surprising applications in masculine grooming products, while its waxy texture enhances

missing.title: Theobromal
missing.description: Also known as Syringaldehyde, this should not be confused with Syringa Aldehyde , which is a completely unrelated material. Theobromal smells of dark chocolate, soft smoke, and warm leather, with a grape-wine quality underneath and a whisper of vanilla. It is mild — you will not notice it immediately — but it lasts over 400 hours on a blotter. Think of it as vanillin stripped of its obvious sweetness and given depth. Where vanillin is straightforwardly creamy and sweet, theobromal adds smoky, leathery, chocolatey dimensions that feel more grown-up and more interesting. Use it to build sophisticated amber and oriental bases, or add trace amounts to chocolate and tobacco accords for realism. Pair it with vanillin for a smoky-vanilla effect, with labdanum and castoreum for full leather, or with benzoin and styrax for incense depth. It is a crystalline powder — dissolve in warm ethanol before use. One of perfumery's best-kept secrets for balsamic fixation.

missing.title: Thesaron®
missing.description: Thesaron (Ethyl Tetrahydrosafranate) opens with crisp fruity-floral character—rosy, fresh, and immediately appealing. Peach and berry facets provide juicy richness, while subtle amber warmth adds depth without heaviness. Woody-herbaceous undertones keep the profile grounded, preventing it from becoming overly sweet. The overall effect is modern, diffusive, and remarkably versatile. This Takasago product is classified as 100% bio-based, appealing to formulators seeking renewable ingredients. The 24-hour substantivity on blotter ensures your fruity-floral effect persists well into the heart and base of compositions. Excellent stability in everything from fine fragrances to functional products including bleach applications. Work with Thesaron at up to 15% of your concentrate—the medium odour strength and forgiving nature make it easy to blend. Use it in peach, apple, and berry compositions where crisp fruitiness needs rosy support, or in floral accords seeking fruity freshness. The amber undertone works beautifully in oriental and woody contexts where fruit notes add modern appeal. Good substantivity on wet fabric and hair makes it valuable for personal care applications. Thesaron vs Ethyl Safranate These two esters share similar names because Thesaron is ethyl tetrahydrosafranate—but their olfactory profiles differ significantly. Ethyl Safranate (CAS 35044-59-8) is intensely spicy and saffron-like, with powerful damascone-rose character, apple cider facets, and woody depth; its 164-hour substantivity and high odour strength make it a demanding material that requires careful dosing at 5% maximum. Thesaron is softer, fruitier, and more approachable—peach and berry notes dominate over spice, and the amber warmth replaces Ethyl Safranate's saffron edge. Use Ethyl Safranate when you want bold saffron-spice or damascone effects; reach for Thesaron when you need gentler fruity-rose character that blends easily without dominating. They complement each other beautifully in com

missing.title: Thiocineole 0.1% DPG
missing.description: Utterly intense, this grapefruit chemical will blow you away. Pure it has the most distinct odour of burnt rubber but when diluted its mimicry of bitter grapefruit skins is astonishing. Traces are all you need to impart a very realistic and powerful grapefruit note to your blends. further dilution to 0.01% is recommended but in the right context this material can even be overdosed. Thiocineole, in addition to grapefruit, has nuances of apricot, papaya, passionfruit and other tropical fruits, as well as a seedy and vegetative nuance. A hint of mint is also apparent. This is truely a remarkable and interesting material. NOTE: We package all high odour or high risk materials individually in separate heat sealed aluminium bags to mitigate any risk of cross-contamination.

missing.title: Thujopsene Ex Cedar Wood
missing.description: Far too infrequently used by perfumers, thujopsene is a wonderful cedarwood note extracted from the heart of real cedar oil (typically it makes up 25% of the natural oil). It blends well with Iso E Super and other wood materials to provide a unique and distinctly modern wood quality. Thujopsene exhibits the clean scent of freshly sharpened pencils. If you're sick of fragrances overloaded with the same cedar chemicals (such as Iso E Super), try blending those materials with this special natural or simply use this pure instead. Priced incredibly well and in plentiful supply, this is a must-have. Best of all it is not under any form of restriction by IFRA or the EU and is not scheduled to be restricted in any way under IFRA 51.

missing.title: Timberide®
missing.description: This radiant base opens with an immediate sensation of penetrating woody dryness — think sun-bleached driftwood. The effect is both brutal and refined—sharp enough to cut through any composition yet smooth enough for sophisticated wear. You'll recognise its signature "icy dagger" quality piercing through from top to base. Composed around large doses of such materials as Ysamber® K, Ambrocenide and Timberol , this is a treasure trove of well-blended power molecules. Reach for Timberide when building modern masculines that demand both power and polish. Its unique architecture amplifies citrus freshness while anchoring volatile notes with tenacious woody structure. This base transforms simple accords into radiating auras that project metres from the skin—essential for contemporary "beast mode" creations. Deploy Timberide at 0.5-5% to create that coveted halo effect in your fragrances. It excels when paired with bergamot and grapefruit for vibrant woody-citrus structures. Combine with modern musks and sandalwood molecules like Javanol for compositions that seem to glow from within—the hallmark of today's luxury powerhouses.

missing.title: Tomato Thiazole
missing.description: _*]:min-w-0 gap-3"> _*]:min-w-0 gap-3"> _*]:min-w-0 gap-3"> _*]:min-w-0 gap-3"> Tomato thiazole hits the nose with an unmistakable burst of crushed tomato vine - green, earthy, and startlingly lifelike. In concentration it reads sharp and sulphurous, but proper dilution unlocks a warm, herbaceous vegetal character. Work exclusively from a 1% or 0.1% dilution; the neat material is far too powerful to dose accurately. This is one of perfumery's true high-impact molecules, with a detection threshold around 3.5 parts per billion in water. Pair it with cis-3-hexenol to soften the metallic edges and bridge it into naturalistic leaf accords. Blend with galbanum and basil oil for full greenhouse realism, or add traces to citrus compositions to enhance the zesty peel effect and banish any candy-like sweetness.

missing.title: Tonquitone
missing.description: IFF's Tonquitone opens with unmistakable animalic warmth — the rich, slightly urinous musk character of natural Tonkin deer musk, faithfully reconstructed. Ambergris-like depth sits beneath the animalic surface. Sweet caramel-vanilla facets and dry-woody undertones emerge as the base develops on skin. This IFF base built entirely on macrocyclic musks gives you a true animalic backbone without the cost and variability of natural musk tincture. It fixes and enriches leather, chypre, oriental, and fougère accords at trace levels. Even small additions lend convincing skin-like presence to any composition. Blend with castoreum and indole to amplify the animalic facets, or combine with ambroxan and sandalwood for softer skin-musk warmth. Push the dose and pronounced civet character emerges.

missing.title: Torref Pyrazine
missing.description: Torref Pyrazine hits with unmistakable dark-roast intensity—think freshly ground espresso beans or chocolate pushed to the edge of caramelisation. The meaty, almost beefy undertone adds savoury complexity that distinguishes this from sweeter gourmand materials. An ethereal cocoa quality weaves through, rich and deeply satisfying. This pyrazine forms naturally during the Maillard reaction at higher temperatures, which explains its more intensely torréfié (roasted) character. You'll find it in dark-roasted coffee, toasted bread, grilled meat, roasted nuts, and fermented foods like malt and beer. The French torréfié—meaning roasted or kiln-dried—perfectly captures its essential quality: deep, smoky, and almost burnt without becoming acrid. Use Torref Pyrazine at medium strength—evaluate at 10% dilution before committing to your formula. It excels in coffee accords, dark chocolate compositions, and tobacco bases needing authentic roasted depth. The meaty facet also makes it valuable in unexpected contexts: leather compositions and certain animalic accords benefit from its savoury warmth. Torref Pyrazine vs Praslin Pyrazine Both share the chocolate-nutty pyrazine family character, but their differences matter for formulation. Torref Pyrazine (2,6-dimethyl Pyrazine) is more intensely roasted, with pronounced coffee and meaty-beefy notes alongside its chocolate character—think dark-roasted coffee beans or caramelised meat. Praslin Pyrazine (2,5-dimethyl Pyrazine) leans more musty, earthy, and powdery—closer to raw cocoa powder and roasted peanuts with a grassy undertone. Torref excels in coffee accords, dark chocolate, and compositions needing that deep torréfié quality; Praslin works better for praline, hazelnut, and milk chocolate effects. Many perfumers use them together, though this can add complexity that overwhelms simpler compositions. When you need that dark, smoky roasted intensity, Torref Pyrazine is the definitive choice. Torref Pyrazine is a solid at room tempe

missing.title: Trans-2,Cis-6-Nonadienol
missing.description: This material delivers the authentic watery-green signature of natural violet leaf and cucumber at remarkably low concentrations. Work with pre-diluted solutions (we recommend 1%) due to extreme potency that overwhelms neat evaluation. The alcohol form provides softer, more floral character compared to its aggressive aldehyde counterpart, making it ideal for sophisticated green accords. You achieve remarkable effects using trace amounts below 0.1% to add dewy naturalness to white florals like muguet and lily. Combine with cis-3-hexenol for initial green snap, then let this material provide sustained watery depth. Aldehyde-Alcohol Synergies Trans-2,Cis-6-Nonadienol (alcohol) offers a softer, more floral profile compared to iTrans-2,Cis-6-Nonadienal's (aldehyde) sharp, aggressive character. The alcohol is fractionally more floral than the aldehyde. Perfumers often combine both: the aldehyde provides initial punch while the alcohol lends sustained, rounded body to violet leaf accords. Together with nonadienal, nonadienol creates the complete nostalgic odour of violet gardens. The alcohol's moderate tenacity bridges top notes into the heart, while the aldehyde's extreme diffusivity creates immediate impact. Balance these complementary materials to achieve dimensional green effects impossible with either alone. We also stock Trans-2,Cis-6-Nonadienal which we sell at 1% dilution.

missing.title: Traseolide
missing.description: Traseolide opens with an enveloping musk quality reminiscent of expensive fabric against skin – soft, warm, and immediately comforting. Unlike sharper polycyclic musks, this material carries a distinctive sandalwood-like creaminess throughout its development. The combination creates an effect that's neither purely musky nor woody, but occupies a unique space between these categories. This material excels at smoothing compositional rough edges. Sharp aldehydes become rounded, aggressive woods gain sophistication, and disparate notes merge seamlessly. The optimal usage at 10% provides this harmonizing effect while maintaining transparency – the composition improves without the musk becoming dominant. Consider this the perfumer's equivalent of a soft-focus lens. Traseolide's interaction with sandalwood molecules creates particularly successful accords. The material enhances creamy, milky aspects while contributing its own textural richness. Exceptional stability in alkaline conditions makes this indispensable for functional applications. When extreme longevity matters – think fine fragrance base notes or premium laundry products – Traseolide delivers consistent performance across challenging conditions. See our demonstration formula for Amrita, our smells-like version of the official Mysore Sandalwood Soap from Karnataka, to see Traseolide in action in a Sandalwood context.

missing.title: Triethyl Citrate, Natural (TEC)
missing.description: Triethyl citrate is a wonderful natural (US & EU) diluent for perfumery. It is naturally extracted with pure food grade alcohol from citric acid from citrus fruit. Triethyl Citrate (TEC) has no odour and allows for dilutions of natural materials that maintain an ISO 9235 standard. TEC is particularly good as a diluent for rose materials and bases and it is widely used in the fragrance industry in both synthetic and natural versions. TEC has excellent solubility in alcohol as well as fractionated coconut oil. It also solubilises in jojoba oil but may cause slight cloudiness. Always perform a small test to ensure compatibility as solubility can vary from medium to medium and depends upon the overall blend of materials in play.

missing.title: Trifernal
missing.description: Trifernal hits the nose with striking green intensity — bitter foliage, crushed stems, and the raw vegetal bite of freshly torn leaves. It smells unmistakably natural despite being synthetic. This is among the most powerful green materials available, effective at vanishingly small concentrations. This material excels in floral compositions built around lilac, hyacinth, violet, and muguet — adding the green backbone that makes those accords smell alive. It works equally well in aromatic and cologne creations. Combine with other green notes for layered botanical freshness. Use Trifernal at trace levels — its power demands careful dosing. Pair with galbanum and violet leaf for intensely realistic green accords. Blend into citrus compositions where a bitter herbal edge adds welcome complexity and natural character.

missing.title: Trimofix®
missing.description: With radiant nuances of earthy vetiver, subtle smoky tobacco , and a touch of musky softness, Trimofix adds depth and sophistication to fragrance. It can be used in traces as a fixative or in overdose (but keep in mind its 2.4% IFRA restriction). It can be seen as somewhat similar in profile to Ambraketal ( Z11 ) but with a shorter lifespan and intensity. However, its complexity and ability to lift woody compositions make it a highly useful ingredient. Trimofix blends well with Vetiver oils, Iso E Super ™, Vertofix , and other woody synthetics and has a synergy with galbanum related materials like Dynascone, Neobutenone Alpha and Allyl Amyl Glycyolate . Trimofix's popularity can be attested to by the large number of perfumes in which it is to be found: Green Irish Tweed , 1.8% in The One (Dolce & Gabbana, 2008), Nasomatto Duro (2007), Baccarat Rouge 540 , Amouage Memoir Men, Bleu de Chanel (2010), Balade Sauvage (Dior), Opium for Men, By the Fireplace (Maison Martin Margiela) and many many more.

missing.title: Trisamber
missing.description: Trisamber is a powerful, dry, dusty woody-amber with an unusually velvety texture. Where most synthetic ambers at this strength feel harsh or chemical, trisamber stays smooth and elegant. Subtle animalic and musky facets give it a primitive, naturalistic quality. It persists for days on a blotter. Use trisamber to build deep amber and dry wood accords in your orientals, chypres, and masculine compositions. It sits between the explosive power of AmberXtreme and the softer creaminess of Operanide — powerful enough to anchor any base, smooth enough to blend without fighting. It adds warmth and sensuality at remarkably low doses. Blend with sandalwood and labdanum for classic amber accords. Try it alongside Iso E Super and cashmeran for a modern, transparent woody-amber heart. Pair with vetiver and patchouli where its dry, dusty character reinforces the earthy base without adding sweetness.

missing.title: Troenan
missing.description: Troenan captures that unmistakable privet hedge in bloom—warm, honeyed yet distinctly green. The scent opens with broken twig freshness before blooming into a gorgeous floral heart. Subtle mushroom and metallic facets add complexity that keeps this material fascinating on the blotter. This material shines in white floral compositions where you need naturalistic green depth. It works beautifully in jasmine accords, lending that spring-garden authenticity. It also proves invaluable in lavender reconstructions for functional products, where its herbal-spicy character provides support and lift but it is equally at home in fine fragrance. Pair Troenan with lily of the valley materials to build convincing privet effects. Its excellent stability in bases makes it reliable across applications. The 24-hour substantivity at full strength means it anchors green-floral hearts without fading too quickly—a genuine workhorse for fresh compositions.

missing.title: Tropicalia™
missing.description: Tropicalia bursts forth with the intensity of a tropical storm, capturing juicy mango, jackfruit, melon, and guava in a single molecule of extraordinary power. This newly liberated captive from IFF delivers what others merely suggest—true tropical environment memory. The unexpected mint facet cuts through sweetness like fresh leaves crushed underfoot, while white floral undertones add sophisticated opulence that elevates simple fruit into complex paradise. Use Tropicalia when you need tropical fruit that transcends cliché beach cocktails. Its exceptional strength means trace amounts transform compositions—use in dilution for signature effects or pure for singular fruit explosions. The material's animalic castoreum effect in chypre accords reveals its versatility beyond fruit, supporting leather and oud with unexpected warmth while bringing naturality to vanilla bases . This high-impact ingredient maintains intensity from top through heart with medium base persistence. Combine Tropicalia with Aprifloren for amplified fruit juiciness, layer with Isobutyl Quinoline for leather-tropical hybrids, or blend with Floralozone and Methyl Ionone Gamma for contemporary white florals with tropical twist. Released from captivity in 2024, this molecule represents IFF's answer to competitive tropical materials—more complex than typical passion fruit chemicals, more natural than synthetic mango bases, and powerful enough to define entire compositions at minimal dosage. Tropicalia is very powerful and so we sell it at 10% dilution for every day use as well as pure for those making larger blends or wishing to experiment with overdosing. You may wish to split your 10% and make a further 1% dilution depending on your needs.

missing.title: Ultravanil
missing.description: Ultravanil is a big comfy bowl of warm custard. In addition to its bold vanilla qualities, this material has a discreet caramel edge and a clear phenolic depth with woody and spicy undertones. Four hundred hours on blotter makes this one of the most tenacious vanilla materials available. Use it to boost vanillin and ethyl vanillin in any composition — even traces add remarkable depth and longevity to vanilla accords. The phenolic backbone gives it staying power that lighter vanilla notes simply lack. Pair with vanillin and ethyl vanillin as a booster, or use alongside benzoin and labdanum for dark oriental richness. The smoky-spiced warmth strengthens gourmand and tobacco compositions beautifully. Sold pure and diluted in DPG — dose in traces and build upward, as the potency is exceptional. It is worth noting that Givaudan sells this "pure" as an 80% concentrate, with the other 20% being DPG. We offer it further diluted to 10% (a total of 8% actual ultravanil) for price and strength reasons.

missing.title: Valencene
missing.description: _*]:min-w-0 gap-3"> _*]:min-w-0 gap-3"> _*]:min-w-0 gap-3"> _*]:min-w-0 gap-3"> Valencene takes its name from Valencia oranges, where it occurs naturally. The aroma is sweet, juicy citrus — unmistakably orange — with a subtle grapefruit edge and gentle woody warmth underneath. Unlike most citrus materials that vanish in minutes, valencene persists for hours, carrying its fresh orange character deep into a composition. Use valencene to extend and deepen citrus accords that would otherwise fade too quickly. It bridges your bright top notes into the heart, maintaining fresh orange character where standard citrus oils have long gone. Pair it with nootkatone for a complete orange-to-grapefruit citrus spectrum. Blend with bergamot and mandarin for rich, layered citrus openings. Try it alongside cedarwood and amyris where its woody undertones create a natural bridge to your base. Add to fresh masculine compositions where long-lasting citrus impact matters.

missing.title: Vanitrope
missing.description: Most perfumers default to vanillin or ethyl vanillin without a second thought. Vanitrope asks you to reconsider. Roughly twenty times vanillin's strength, it carries a heliotrope-violet dimension neither of those workhorses possess — plus tobacco warmth, a woody-spicy edge, and a powdery finish that belongs in a different league. That potency changes how you work. Derive no more than half your vanilla character from vanitrope, filling the rest with ethyl vanillin or vanillin for balance. The heliotrope dimension gives you a vanilla accord of genuine complexity. And unlike vanillin, it won't yellow your formulations. Ethyl vanillin is its best partner — the two boost each other in ways neither achieves alone. Heliotropin reinforces that violet-powder facet in the background. In tobacco accords, vanitrope's smoky warmth fits better than vanillin, which can flatten the complexity you're trying to build.

missing.title: Velberry™
missing.description: Velberry™ is a soft sweet chemical with a red fruit character. It has some similarities to raspberry ketone but with interesting whisky and green facets. This can be a particularly useful material when an alternative is needed to the classic (but discolouring) vanillin and heliotropin. Velberry adds volume and body to a scent and can be used in very large doses (particularly in functional fragrances). The price is incredibly good and has virtually no regulatory barriers to widespread use. In BASF's own words: “The gourmand character combines soft, powdery notes with freshness and red fruits. Showing good stability in all applications, the top note material has an excellent blooming effect.” In this interesting interview from Perfumer and Flavorist (sponsored by BASF,) Ralf Pelzer, director of new business development, BASF Aroma Ingredients, and Tony Dallimore, perfumery director of Phoenix Fragrances LTD., discuss the ingredient’s development, applications, profile and more.

missing.title: Veratraldehyde
missing.description: Veratraldehyde is a crystalline aroma chemical with a soft powdery vanilla custard quality. It is a really good alternative to vanillin (though it suffers from the same discolouration problems in soaps) or can be used to add nuance and interest to the same. In the age of the gourmand, this material absolutely cannot go unnoticed and we highly recommend it for all perfumers. If you are unfamiliar with the use of crystallines in perfume, take a look at our little primer: How To Weigh A Powder .

missing.title: Verdol
missing.description: Verdol hits with bracing camphoraceous freshness — clean, minty, and immediately arresting. A woody-pine body emerges beneath the minty impact, grounding the material in forest depth. Earthy patchouli undertones complete a profile that moves from bright aromatic top to dark, rooted base. Use it in patchouli accords where it amplifies earthy-woody depth while adding bracing lift. It excels equally in pine-forest compositions and dark, brooding woody-amber blends. Pair with ambery and oud materials to add unexpected radiant lift to dark compositions. Blend into weathered, elemental accords for brooding atmospheric depth.

missing.title: Verdone
missing.description: Verdone opens with an immediate cooling rush - think white camphor with bright mint leaves and clean medicinal clarity. This alicyclic ketone combines dry woody structure with herbal sharpness, creating a backbone that elevates top notes without weighing them down. The initial impact is intense and crystalline, delivering a sensation of freshness that cuts through heavier accords. In laundry and home care formulations, Verdone performs exceptionally where heat and steam are present. Its unique ability to sublime when heated makes it invaluable in detergents and functional products - the material literally lifts into the air during hot water use, carrying your entire composition with it. Use Verdone to anchor aromatic fougères, add structure to citrus-heavy blends, or introduce sophisticated powdery transitions in masculine fragrances. It pairs brilliantly with aldehydes to amplify sparkle, with vetiver to emphasise woody-earthy facets, or with ionones to strengthen powdery heart notes.

missing.title: Vernaldehyde
missing.description: Vernaldehyde is a fresh, green aldehyde with a bright outdoor-air character. Underneath the aldehydic top sits a cool, dewy green freshness and a light waxy-citrus edge. The overall effect is airy and clean, closer to spring air than to the fatty aldehydes of the C-10 to C-12 range. Use it in muguet, lilac and freesia for a sense of open-air freshness. In citrus colognes it reinforces the top and keeps bergamot from collapsing. It also pairs well with cedar, vetiver and Iso E Super, adding a cool lift to woody bases. Overdose it in a chypre to update the aldehydic top, where the green reads cleaner and more modern than classic C-10 or C-11. A trace lightens a heavy amber without weakening its warmth. It also refreshes a muguet base that has lost its lift.

missing.title: Vertenex
missing.description: We stock Firmenich's Lorysia® — the finest quality of Vertenex, having the highest amount of the preferred cis isomer. Comparisons of Lorysia® against generic and even other big name produced versions of Vertenex illustrate how truly marvellous this Firmenich product is. While Vertenex (PTBCHA or p-tert-butyl cyclohexyl acetate) is a lovely volumising wood material, Lorysia builds on that with its soft fruitiness and almost edible quality. Arctander speaks thus: “Widely used in perfumery along with the Ionone, Cedarwood products, floral and non-floral perfume chemicals, a very versatile perfume material for soap and other low-cost fragrances, where volume is required. Generally as a blender / modifier in countless types of fragrances, from Pine to Rose, from woody to floral, it is one of the most successful perfume chemicals of the last few decades.” A far more radiant material than regular Vertenex, we recommend this as a wonderful alternative or blender to the now more common Iso E Super . See our demonstration formula below for Dior Dior to see how Edmond Roudnitska used Lorysia® to great effect in what he considered to be his greatest fragrance.

missing.title: Vertoliff
missing.description: Vertoliff (closely related to Triplal) smells tart, green, and aldehydic with a citrus-herbal brightness and a distinctive bark-like quality underneath. There is nothing subtle about the opening — it announces itself immediately. On dilution the tartness settles and a more rounded herbal character emerges. The strength is high, so work from a dilution. What makes vertoliff particularly useful is its breadth — it sits comfortably in citrus, herbal, floral, and green accords, lending crisp freshness to top notes without overwhelming the composition. That versatility across fragrance families is its chief virtue. Bergamot, galbanum, and clary sage complement its green-citrus character well. A trace in floral compositions contributes a green transparency that can lighten heavier hearts. In fresh masculine accords the citrus-herbal bite makes an immediate impression. Vertoliff appears in Chanel Bel Respiro (0.19%), Davidoff Cool Water (0.15%), Dior Rouge Trafalgar (0.09%), and Hermes Un Jardin sur le Nil (0.07%).

missing.title: Vertosine
tags: locale:heat needed for pure. Diluted is still thick.
missing.description: Broom, orange blossom, and leafy green — all at once. The green aldehydic character hits immediately, sharp and bright, but a warm floral quality saves it from harshness. You catch a gentle anthranilate-like warmth reminiscent of night-blooming flowers. The effect is intensely natural for a synthetic material. This Schiff base (Triplal and Methyl Anthranilate) excels at bridging green and floral notes in ways that simpler materials cannot. It naturalises mimosa and honeysuckle accords, giving them a green botanical depth that reads as freshly cut stems rather than perfumery abstraction. In gardenia compositions, it supplies the green-leafy top that expensive naturals provide at a fraction of the cost. Vertosine gives green top notes a depth and complexity they rarely have on their own. Use it to enrich galbanum and violet leaf accords. It also lifts citrus-peel notes — try it alongside bergamot and petitgrain where its floral warmth softens sharp hesperidic openings into something rounder and more complex.

missing.title: Very Violet™
missing.description: Very Violet™ can be used in combination with other colours in the Perfumer's Palette™ range or alone to reduce yellow tones caused by the use of naturals, or to add a purple touch. The Fraterworks® Perfumer's Palette™ is a range of dyes that can be used alone or in combination with each other to add vibrance and colour to your perfumes or cosmetic products. Our proprietary blend of FD&C and D&C colours are sold in liquid form. Perfumer's Palette colours contain distilled water which is perfectly safe for alcoholic perfumes in the quantities needed for colouration. Typical use is from 0.01–0.5% of finished product. At these low levels, staining of clothing or skin is minimal to none but you should always test your finished product against white cloth or paper.

missing.title: Vetikolacetat®
missing.description: There is no denying it: this smells like cannabis… and vetiver and rhubarb. Vetikolacetat (also called veticol or vetikol acetate) is a truly interesting material. In small amounts it adds a wonderful vetiver note in the complete absence of any natural vetiver, but it is also a magnificent nuancer and booster for the essential oil. We use it in our best selling Vetiver fragrance, Serge Lutens uses 0.4% as the sole vetiver note in his Ambre Sultan (1993) for ladies and gentleman, and 0.25% is found in the plush Amouage masculine Interlude Black Iris where it modifies 2% natural vetiver. It's relatively long lasting, novel and versatile, being able to be coaxed in a myriad directions depending on the skill of the perfumer; in one direction it is the memory of a hazy drug fuelled party, in another it is a dank barnyard beneath a lowering sky, and in yet another it is a fresh rhubarb note adding interest to a delicious gourmand; add Veratraldehyde and lactones for a custard note (with a trace of Sulfurol and Butyric Acid for enhanced egginess).

missing.title: Vetikone®
missing.description: Vetikone is vetiver made fresh and radiant. It keeps the cool, rooty, green-woody heart of the natural, but lifts it with a bright squeeze of grapefruit and a sweet gardenia floralcy. The effect is clean and tea-like, brighter and less earthy-heavy than raw vetiver. Use it to build modern vetiver accords or to pull vetiver up into the top of a fragrance, where it adds air and light. It brightens woody and chypre bases, freshens masculine colognes, and gives fern and floral structures a green, rooty spine. As with most vetiver synthetics, it pairs very well with grapefruit notes .

missing.title: Vetimoss
missing.description: Vetimoss is a fascinating long-lasting material with weedy, leathery, mossy and almost salty nuances. It is usually used in fairly small amounts (less than 2%) to add green herbaceous notes to a fragrance and can be a very interesting alternative to the usual Isobutyl Quinoline for a more refined leather note. Vetimoss blends well with Suralette™ Extra , Artemal ™, Fixomusk ™, 2-Isobutyl Quinoline , Fauxmoss ®, Corps Racine , the Cis-3 Hexenol family, Cedarome , Sophira and Saxon Moss . In terms of naturals, Vetimoss blends with Birch Tar , Castoreum , Vetiver ( Bourbon and Haiti), Vetiveryl Acetate and Vetiverol , as well as all the patchoulis and Oakmoss ( Green and Decolourised ).

missing.title: Vetiver Acetate 53281
missing.description: Vetiver Acetate is one of the most popular zizanoides products which is frequently blended with fine vetiver oil for a softening effect or used on its own as a fresh, long lasting and modern vetiver note. There are two types of the acetate: Vetiver Acetate and Vetiveryl Acetate. The first (this product) is produced from Vetiverol (a mix of vetiver alcohols) which is extracted from the Vetiver roots prior to the acetylation process. The second, Vetiveryl acetate is produced by direct acetylation of the whole Vetiver essential oil and contains more accessory alcohols so it has a slightly higher IFRA limit and a more complex drydown. It is also slightly lower in price. Our vetiver acetate from MANE (reference 53281) is more sheer and diffusive than most and is the star of Frater Perfumes' best selling Vetiver fragrance and Molecule 03 by Escentric Molecules. When other Vetiver Acetates fade away, this astonishingly good version keeps going and going. It has a presence and a royal quality that absolutely justifies its higher price point. This Vetiver Acetate has a woody character with spicy and citrus nuances. This makes for a more interesting inclusion in fragrances and far more lively blends with aroma chemicals like Iso E Super , Lorysia and Vertofix Coeur. This is the closest you can get to the famed Acetivenol of times gone by. NOTE: under IFRA 52 (in draft), vetiveryl acetate and vetiver acetate must be fortified with 1% Tocopherol. Our vetiver acetate is not (yet) so you should do this yourself when planning for IFRA 52 compliance. Blend it with Guerlain's favourite Vetiver Bourbon oil and the esteemed natural Vetiverol ex Vetiver Haiti as used in No 5 by Ernest Beaux for Chanel. Or blend it in a one to one ratio with Mysore sandalwood oil like Bois Des Îles (14% of each in the original formula).

missing.title: Vetiver Oil, Fractionated
missing.description: This molecular distilled speciality product of Floral Concept is outstanding. It is a 100% pure and natural vetiveryl acetate alternative. Vetiveryl Acetate is never a natural product even when it starts from pure vetiver oil, whereas this speciality uses a fractionation technique to get to a similar odour profile without the use of synthetic additives. This is not just a product for natural perfumery, this is a product for all perfumers with a passion for fine fragrance. It is a product we love so much that we use it ourselves extensively and know no equal. It is, perhaps, the nicest Vetiver oil you will ever smell. Floral Concept continues to prove itself a leader in the industry when it comes to total refinement and elegance. Blends of this MD Vetiver oil with Floral Concept's Patchouli Heart are out of this world. The source of this material is Haiti and owing to difficult circumstances in that nation global stock is low. We will always endeavour to keep this (and all) products in stock but we recommend buying more than you think you need until the situation in the area is resolved.

missing.title: Vetiverol ex Vetiver Haiti
missing.description: Vetiverol is the molecular distilled heart of vetiver oil and the raw material precursor for acetylated vetiver ( vetiver acetate ). Vetiverol is sweeter and softer than the acetate and, better still, it's completely unrestricted in use. Despite its name it is not a singular vetiver alcohol but rather the name given to the mix of naturally occurring alcohols inside vetiver oil. Our vetiverol is extracted from the most beautiful vetiver oil and is the same type as that used by Ernest Beaux in No 5 for Chanel and Jean Paul Guerlain in Guerlain's Vetiver (demo formula below). This is a perfect material for adding vetiver goodness without dominating a fragrance. It makes a wonderfully rich alternative to the various wood chemicals so overused in today's perfumes. Note: the price of vetiverol has increased significantly due to the tumultuous events in Haiti.

missing.title: Vetiveryl Acetate 20326
missing.description: Vetiveryl Acetate (and related Vetiver Acetate ) is one of the most popular zizanoides products which is frequently blended with fine vetiver oils for a softening effect or used on its own as a fresh, long lasting and clean vetiver note. There are two types of the acetate: Vetiver Acetate and Vetiveryl Acetate. The first is produced from Vetiverol (a mix of vetiver alcohols) which is extracted from the Vetiver roots prior to the acetylation process. The second, Vetiveryl acetate (this product) is produced by direct acetylation of the whole Vetiver essential oil and contains accessory molecules so it has a slightly less restrictive IFRA limit and a more complex and slightly more metallic dry down. It is also lower in price. While Vetiver Acetate (acetylated Vetiverol) is more popular due to being cleaner in the dry down, this wonderful Vetiveryl Acetate 20326 should not be overlooked. It blends particularly well with Orris materials and can be used anywhere Vetiver Acetate is used. We also stock Vetiver Acetate from V Mane Fils. Used in: Chanel No 19, Poison, Ma Griffe and Dior Homme. NOTE: under IFRA 52 (in draft), vetiveryl acetate and vetiver acetate must be fortified with 1% Tocopherol. Our vetiver acetate is not (yet) so you should do this yourself when planning for IFRA 52 compliance.

missing.title: Violettyne MIP
missing.description: Sharp violet leaf cuts through with real presence the moment Violettyne MIP hits a blend. A fruity-tropical undercurrent and galbanum-like depth give the note dimension beyond simple greenness. Distinctive cucumber and bell pepper facets set it apart from every other violet-leaf material. This Firmenich material offers what MOC and MHC cannot — a green-violet note with genuine stability across formulations. Twenty-four hours on blotter gives you green-violet persistence that those older materials rarely match. Use in florals, chypres, and fresh green accords where you need lasting impact. Blend with ionones for a complete violet accord, or combine with hexenyl acetate and galbanum for lush green-floral depth. The cucumber-pepper facet adds unexpected dimension to aquatic and aromatic compositions. Start at traces and work upward — the strength here is considerable. Note: MIP is simply the shortened form of IPM in French.

missing.title: Violiff
missing.description: Violiff opens with striking violet leaf intensity—green, fresh, and immediately commanding. The fruity banana facet adds unexpected sweetness, while tagette-marigold brightness contributes an almost medicinal edge that keeps the material interesting. The overall effect is heady and aromatic, bridging green and floral territories with remarkable confidence. This IFF material spent years as a captive molecule before its release to the wider market. The cyclooctenyl structure provides the violet leaf character, while the carbonate group adds stability and diffusion. Despite its 12-hour substantivity on blotter, the immense strength and projection mean Violiff punches far above its volatility—a little travels a very long way. The material works as both top note sparkle and heart note support. Work with Violiff at up to 2% of your concentrate, but approach with caution—the intensity demands serious dilution before evaluation. Use at 10% or less to appreciate its nuances without overwhelming your nose. It blends beautifully with woody-floral materials, galbanum products like Dynascone , and metallic-pineapple notes. The banana facet makes it valuable in fruity-floral compositions where green freshness needs tropical warmth. Note: may form acidic compounds under heat, so store cool.

missing.title: Woodol®
missing.description: Woodol® is a multifaceted heart note that delivers a warm, rich foundation to fragrance compositions. Its complex profile blends dry woody notes with sweet amber facets and a distinct patchouli-like earthiness. This material is particularly suited to functional perfumery due to its exceptional stability in alkaline products, h owever, it still has great potential in fine fragrances; it is just waiting for the right perfumer to exploit it. Incorporate Woodol® in formulations to impart a substantive woody-amber base with unique patchouli nuances. It pairs well with other woody, amber, and earthy notes, enhancing depth and longevity. Exercise caution with dosing, as its character can become dominant. Woodol® has synergies with Patchouli, Cedarwood (and related materials), and Ambroxan.

missing.title: Yellow Dawn™
missing.description: The Fraterworks® Perfumer's Palette™ is a range of dyes that can be used alone or in combination with each other to add vibrance and colour to your perfumes or cosmetic products. Our proprietary blend of FD&C and D&C colours are sold in liquid form. Perfumer's Palette colours contain distilled water which is perfectly safe for alcoholic perfumes in the quantities needed for colouration. Typical use is from 0.01–0.5% of finished product.
